en: The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Scroll One. Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty. Chapter One: The Introduction. Chapter One: The Introduction. Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling at the city of Vaiśālī, in the grove of Āmrapālī, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. All were arhats, free from outflows, free from afflictions, having accomplished what was to be done, laid down their burden, attained their own goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and whose minds were liberated through perfect wisdom. Among them were the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Aśvajit, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bāṣpa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahamaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Kapphiṇa, the Venerable Subhūti, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Rāhula, and others such as these. Furthermore, there were many thousands of bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, all of whom had already attained the stage of non-retrogression, possessed the power of the ten directions, and were skilled in the profound Dharma of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. They were: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ratnamati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, and others such as these. At that time, the World-Honored One was seated upon a lion throne, surrounded by this great assembly. He was preaching the Dharma for the sake of the fourfold assembly, causing them to hear, receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice it according to the teaching. He expounded extensively on the meaning of the Great Nirvāṇa, the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha, the meaning of the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure, and the meaning of the unconditioned. Having finished preaching this sutra, he entered into the samādhi called "The Lion’s Play. As soon as he had entered this samādhi, his body and mind became tranquil and motionless. His physical form appeared like a mountain of gold, emitting a great light that illuminated the entire world-system. From every pore of his body there issued forth hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light, each ray of light manifesting hundreds of thousands of millions of lotuses. Upon each lotus sat a transformed Buddha, preaching the Dharma for sentient beings. This light shone throughout the ten directions, reaching as far as the Avīci Hell and the Heaven of the Summit of Existence, illuminating all the worlds within the great trichiliocosm. Wherever the light reached, all sentient beings who encountered it were freed from suffering and attained peace and joy. Those who had not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment did so; those who had already generated the aspiration increased their resolve; and those who had already set their resolve increased their practice. All the evil paths were closed, and the gates to the heavenly realms were opened. The sun and moon shone with greater brilliance, and the five planets moved in harmony. The great ocean surged with waves, and the earth shook in six ways. The various heavens rained down celestial flowers, and divine music played spontaneously. Thus, the supernatural manifestations were vast and boundless. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robes to bare his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, why has the Tathāgata manifested such a great supernatural display? I pray that the World-Honored One will explain its cause and condition for the sake of the fourfold assembly. The Buddha told Ānanda: “Excellent, excellent! You have asked well. Listen attentively and reflect deeply; I shall now explain it for you. Ānanda replied: “Yes, World-Honored One, I am eager to listen. The Buddha said: “Ānanda, the Tathāgata has now entered the samādhi of ‘The Lion’s Play. Because he wishes to preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, he first manifests this great supernatural power. Why? Because this sutra is the most supreme among all the teachings of the Buddhas of the three times. It is the ultimate, the final, and the unsurpassed. It is the great white ox-king that can pull the heavy cart of the Dharma, and it is the great physician king who can cure all the diseases of sentient beings.

It is the great bridge that allows all sentient beings to cross over the river of birth and death. It is the great ship that carries all sentient beings across the sea of suffering. It is the great sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance. It is the great moon that cools the heat of the afflictions. It is the great wind that scatters the clouds of doubt. It is the great fire that burns away the fuel of karma. It is the great rain that moistens the seeds of the roots of goodness. It is the great mountain that cannot be shaken by the winds of Mara. It is the great jewel that fulfills all the desires of sentient beings. Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata now wishes to preach this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, and for this reason he has manifested this great supernatural power. The Buddha then spoke a verse: “The Tathāgata’s body is like a mountain of gold, Emitting a great light that illuminates the world. From every pore issue forth rays of light, Each ray manifesting lotuses of various colors. Upon each lotus sits a transformed Buddha, Preaching the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings. This light shines throughout the ten directions, Reaching as far as the Avīci Hell and the Peak of Existence. Wherever the light reaches, all are benefited: Evil paths are closed, and the heavens are opened. The sun and moon shine with greater brilliance, The five planets move in harmony. The great ocean surges with waves, And the earth shakes in six ways. Heavenly flowers rain down from above, And divine music plays spontaneously. Such are the vast and boundless manifestations, All for the sake of preaching this supreme sutra. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard the Buddha speak this verse, was filled with joy and said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, I pray that the Tathāgata will arise from this samādhi and preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for the sake of the fourfold assembly. The Buddha told Ānanda: “Wait a moment. The Tathāgata will now emerge from this samādhi and preach the Dharma for you. Then the Buddha emerged from the samādhi of “The Lion’s Play” and addressed the bhikṣus: “Bhikṣus, you should know that the Tathāgata has now attained the Great Parinirvāṇa. Why? Because the Tathāgata’s lifespan is immeasurable, and he has long since transcended birth and death. However, in order to teach and transform sentient beings, he manifests birth and death. Just as a skilled illusionist can manifest various forms, yet those forms have no reality, so too the Tathāgata manifests birth and death to teach and transform sentient beings, yet his true nature is eternally quiescent and beyond birth or death. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should not think that the Tathāgata truly enters parinirvāṇa. Why? Because the Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, the eternal, the blissful, the self, and the pure. He is the great physician king who cures the diseases of all sentient beings. He is the great bridge that allows all to cross over the river of birth and death. He is the great ship that carries all across the sea of suffering. He is the great sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance. He is the great moon that cools the heat of the afflictions. He is the great wind that scatters the clouds of doubt. He is the great fire that burns away the fuel of karma. He is the great rain that moistens the seeds of the roots of goodness. He is the great mountain that cannot be shaken by
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kauśāmbī, by the side of the River Hiraṇyavatī, amidst the twin śāla trees of the Sthiravana grove, surrounded before and behind by eight hundred billion bhikṣus.

On the fifteenth day of the second month, as he approached his parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings were individually filled with joy; they considered themselves pure and free from doubt or weariness. Suddenly, they realized:

"Today the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—out of compassion for the world, a protector of the world, and a refuge for the world—regards all sentient beings equally as if looking upon an only son. This tranquil and serene Great Muni is about to enter extinction. All you who have doubts or difficulties should come now to ask questions; let this be your final inquiry."
Having awakened to this, each harbored grief and sorrow.

At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various rays of light from his face—blue, yellow, red, white, crystal, and crimson—brilliant and extraordinary, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm and all Buddha-lands throughout the ten directions. Among the sentient beings of the six realms who were touched by these lights, their karmic defilements and afflictions were entirely extinguished. They all wept with such profound lamentation that their tears fell like rain, saying to one another:

"How strange! O virtuous ones, the world is now empty! How strange! O virtuous ones, the merit of sentient beings is exhausted! How strange! O virtuous ones, the dharma of suffering increases; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa!"

"How swift is the world becoming empty! How swift is the extinction of the eye of the world! We should go together at once to visit the Buddha to pay homage and make offerings, and entreat the World-Honored One not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to remain for a kalpa or even longer than a kalpa. If the Buddha enters nirvāṇa, who will be our kind and compassionate guide?"
"Who will act as our savior from these various calamities?
Therefore, O virtuous ones, whatever you do not understand, you should go to the Tathāgata to consult him and resolve your doubts.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways. Then, eight hundred billion bhikṣus—all of whom were arhats with minds attained to mastery, who had accomplished what was to be done and were free from all afflictions; who had subdued their faculties like great dragons, achieved the wisdom of emptiness, and realized their own benefit; whose retinues were like a grove of sandalwood trees, and who were fully endowed with merit—were the true sons of the Buddha.
Their names were:
the Venerable Kātyāyana, the Venerable Bakkula, the Venerable Upānanda, and others. These bhikṣus, at dawn, used willow twigs to rinse their mouths and purify themselves.

At that time, a wondrous light came to illuminate their bodies, just as when the sun first rises it shines upon green tree leaves so that their red veins all become visible; these bhikṣus were likewise thus. With blood flowing from all the pores of their limbs and joints like falling rain, they suffered great pain in their hearts. Yet, out of compassion for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings, desiring to bring forth the skillful and secret teachings of the Mahāyāna, and for the sake of the conditions for conversion, they quickly finished washing and rinsing themselves and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and stood to one side, respectfully inquiring after his well-being.

Furthermore, there were twenty-five billion bhikṣuṇīs, all of whom were arhats with minds attained to mastery; they had accomplished what was to be done, were free from all afflictions, and had subdued their faculties like great dragons; they had perfected the wisdom of emptiness and realized their own benefit.
Their names were as follows:

The bhikṣuṇī Koṭīviṃśati, the bhikṣuṇī Subhadra, the bhikṣuṇī Upānanda, the bhikṣuṇī Sāgaraprajñā, and others were like the rising sun illuminating green leaves so that their red veins all become visible; these bhikṣuṇīs were likewise. Blood flowed from all the pores of their bodies and limbs like falling rain, and they suffered great pain in their hearts. Out of compassion for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings, desiring to bring forth the secret teachings of the Mahāyāna expedient means, and for the sake of the causes and conditions of conversion, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and stood to one side, respectfully inquiring after his well-being.

Furthermore, there were bhikṣuṇīs who were all bodhisattvas, heroes among men, who had attained the practice of the ten stages (daśabhūmi). For the sake of teaching and transforming others, they manifested in female bodies; they roamed through the four immeasurables and were able to manifest various transformations as Buddhas.
Furthermore, there were Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River— heroes among men who had fully perfected all merits—
who, through bodies of skillful means, deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna; they were correctly oriented toward the Mahāyāna,
hungry for the Mahāyāna, greedily seeking the Mahāyāna, thirsting with longing for the Mahāyāna, and were well able to accord with all worlds.
To deliver those not yet delivered and to liberate those not yet liberated; for incalculable eons, one cultivates pure precepts to deliver and liberate sentient beings;
for incalculable eons, one cultivates pure precepts to comfort sentient beings;
for incalculable eons, one cultivates pure precepts to cause the Three Jewels to flourish; for incalculable eons, one cultivates pure precepts to turn the wheel of the True Dharma.
Cakra, throughout incalculable eons he cultivated pure precepts to achieve great adornment;
throughout incalculable eons he cultivated the firm ground of pure preceptual conduct.
Having thus accomplished such immeasurable merits, he regards all sentient beings equally, as if looking upon an only son.
Their names were:

Bodhisattva Sāgaramati, Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, and others. Just as when the sun first rises, its light illuminates green tree leaves so that their red veins all become visible, so it was with these bodhisattvas. With blood flowing from every pore of their bodies like falling rain, they experienced great anguish in their hearts; yet, out of compassion for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings, desiring to bring forth the esoteric teachings of the Mahāyāna expedient means, and for the sake of the conditions of conversion, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, and stood to one side, respectfully inquiring after his well-being.
Furthermore, there were laymen (*upāsaka*) observing the five precepts, as numerous as the sands of two Ganges Rivers, who deeply delighted in all methods of counteractive treatment (*pratipakṣa*):
suffering and pleasure, permanence and impermanence, self and non-self, emptiness and non-emptiness, dependence and non-dependence, sentient beings and non-sentient beings,
constancy and non-constancy, auspiciousness and inauspiciousness, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and *nirvāṇa* and non-*nirvāṇa*.
Deeply delighting in such methods of counteraction, desiring to hear the wondrous meaning and proclaim the Great Dharma,
they have purified their Brahma-conduct throughout countless eons without any lapse; desiring to practice the Mahāyāna and explain it extensively for others,
they cultivate pure precepts and desire to study the steadfast Mahāyāna, desiring to study how to accord with the world, and desiring to study...
To deliver the world; to study the flourishing of the Triple Gem; to study the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
to study the great adornment—thus endowed with immeasurable merit, they regard all sentient beings equally, as if looking upon an only child.
Their names were: the upāsaka King of Stainless Radiance, the upāsaka Good Virtue, and others such as these— upāsakas numbering as many as two Ganges-sands—
who, at the time of dawn, for the sake of making offerings to the Tathāgata, each [person] individually...
They fashioned five thousand bed-canopies of *candana* sandalwood, bed-canopies of aloeswood (*agaru*),
bed-canopies of various jewels, bed-canopies of celestial incense, and bed-canopies of saffron flowers;
all these bed-canopies were perfumed with ox-head *candana* incense and adorned with various wonderful and marvelous seven treasures, decorated with golden cords and nets to cover them.
Above, there were blue with blue light, yellow with yellow light, red with red light, white with white light,
crimson with crimson light, crystal-colored with crystal light, and the color of wish-fulfilling gems with the light of wish-fulfilling gems;
adorned with such various colors, this most excellent and rare canopy surrounded [the space].
All were covered above with nets of the seven precious gems, with various jeweled banners suspended around their four sides;
they were anointed with all kinds of blended incense, and tassels woven from gold thread hung down.
Within those jeweled canopies, various colors were adorned as described above, and cushions woven from the seven precious gems served as the bedding.
Soft, fragrant incense was spread within them. Each bed and canopy was mounted upon a precious chariot, these chariots being exquisitely adorned with the seven treasures.

Both before and behind each were precious banners, streamers, and canopies; every banner and canopy was further embellished with nets of the seven treasures—blue, yellow, red, and white—and decorated with the four kinds of flowers: the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*. These too were ornamented as before with the seven treasures. Various miscellaneous jewels were knotted together to form flower garlands, and fine white cotton cloths depicted images of the Tathāgata’s past lives (*jātaka*). These portrayed the Bodhisattva from his first resolution for enlightenment until his attainment of Buddhahood, recording in full detail all the various forms of suffering he endured during his successive incarnations.

On both sides of the path, a multitude of musicians performed various musical arts; all their instruments were made of the seven treasures, and their harmonious and elegant sounds all issued forth the tones of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. They all cried out, "How strange! The world is empty! Their lamentations and weeping shook heaven and earth. For the sake of making offerings, each person brought famous flowers and fine powdered incense, and prepared various foods of supreme flavor. Using mountain stream water and fragrant wood for fuel, they ensured the food was soft, savory, and complete in fragrance and taste.

Furthermore, he swept and sprinkled the interior and exterior of the Sāla Grove and spread sand made of the seven precious gems; precious robes scented with incense were laid over it. Around the perimeter, thirty-two rows of lion thrones were arranged, all adorned with the seven precious gems, their carvings and engravings shimmering in five colors. Various exquisite blended incenses were used to perfume the thrones, and cushions of the seven precious gems were spread upon them.
Having completed all these tasks, he formed this thought:

"Whatever all sentient beings may require or desire, I shall give it all to them—clothing, food and drink, wealth, treasures, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children; even my head, eyes, marrow, brain, blood, flesh, and limbs. Whether they be poor or wealthy, noble or lowly, I shall satisfy each according to their needs, with the sole exception of unwholesome gifts such as carnal desire, poisons, and things that cause harm to living beings."
These upāsakas, having resolved their minds upon awakening as bodhisattvas, thought to themselves:
"We shall offer these beds, canopies, precious chariots, and various articles of provision to the Buddha and the Saṅgha; this shall be our final great offering."
Each of them thought to themselves:
"After the Buddha and the great assembly have accepted my offerings, today the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Having formed this thought, their minds were overwhelmed with grief, like the rising sun shining upon green leaves so that the red veins all become visible.
The upāsakas were likewise; blood flowed from every pore of their bodies like falling rain, and they wept with hearts and bodies in agonizing pain.

Furthermore, beside the Śiṃśapā Grove, they erected a great canopy adorned with the seven treasures, lofty, vast, and magnificent, reaching up to the void of space. Within this canopy, they established a pavilion made of the seven treasures. Having completed the preparation of the offerings, they went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and filled the void with offerings of banners and parasols. They burned incense and scattered flowers like clouds and rain; all were moved by such sorrowful longing that it shook heaven and earth.
Beating their breasts and wailing, tears fell like rain as they said to one another: "How strange! O virtuous ones, the world is becoming empty! How swift is the extinction of the Eye of the World!"
They prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground and addressed the Buddha with one voice:

“We pray that the Buddha and the Saṃgha will take pity on us and accept our invitation together with the great assembly. Having accepted our invitation, may you enter parinirvāṇa, so that we may provide food for the Buddha and the great assembly and obtain the merit of the final offering.”
The World-Honored One, knowing the time was not yet right, remained silent and did not accept; thus, even after three such requests, the Buddha remained silent.

At that time, all the upāsakas lost hope and were filled with grief, sorrow, and distress, just like a compassionate father who has an only son that suddenly falls ill and dies, and returns from the funeral procession in grief, sorrow, and distress. The upāsakas’ grief, sorrow, and distress were exactly like this; they paid their respects, rose, and stood to one side.
Furthermore, there were three times as many *upāsikās* as the sands of the Ganges, all fully endowed with the merit of observing the five precepts.
They manifested in female forms to transform and deliver sentient beings, rebuking their own bodies as being like four venomous snakes.
They saw that eighty thousand families of worms infested and devoured their bodies; this body was foul and impure, deluded by lust, and was like a corpse.
First is that which is pleasant: this body is impure, with its nine orifices constantly leaking; it is a false city formed by the mutual dependence of flesh, blood, sinews, and bones;
the hands, feet, and limbs serve as its defensive walls; the nails, teeth, ears, and eyes serve as its watchtowers and openings;
the illusory and deceptive mental phenomena serve as its inner chambers and screens; and negligence, restlessness, and pride serve as its upper stories.
Contemplating this, one sees that within this city dwells the king of malicious and predatory intent; he greedily pursues profit and wanders restlessly through the six sense-objects.
Such a city of thieves is abandoned by all Buddhas and cherished only by fools;
it is inhabited by the rākṣasas of greed, hatred, and delusion, like a thicket of eranda trees that offers nothing lovely, resembling a mass of foam or a plantain tree.
It possesses no solidity; it is like a flash of lightning, a mirage, or the echo of a shout; like the moon reflected in water, a magical illusion, or the waves of the ocean;
like a swift current or a blade of grass set upright that does not remain for even a moment;
and like a cemetery thicket filled with filth, where foxes, wolves, vultures, eagles, crows, ravens, hungry dogs, and various evil insects vie to dwell within. Like...
How could this defiled body possibly be endured?

Even if one were to take a single hair-tip to drop from the waters of the great ocean, its number could still be known; yet this body, a tree of poison, possesses four hundred and four diseases and immeasurable, incalculable impurities. As the World-Honored One has taught through parable: even if all the grasses and trees under heaven were cut into counting-slips, and the earth, stones, and soil were ground into fine dust, their number might still be known.
This body is impure and filled with immeasurable, manifold evils, exceeding even this number; it is violent and harmful, destroying all wholesome dharmas.

These upāsikās are able to cast aside such a body as if discarding spittle; they practice the way of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, deeply delighting in the Mahāyāna and constantly preaching it for others.
Their names were:

the female lay disciple Jīvāśrī, the female lay disciple Śrīmālā, the female lay disciple Viśākhā, and others. At dawn, when the radiance had shone forth, they immediately perceived this auspicious omen; they each quickly prepared various offerings, twice as magnificent as before, and came to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves with their heads to the ground, and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The World-Honored One did not accept [the invitation]. He remained to one side, sorrowful, distressed, and afflicted by grief.

Furthermore, there were Licchavi youths as numerous as the sands of four Ganges Rivers—both those residing within the city of Vaiśālī and those who had come from outside—as well as kings, ministers, and officials from the bordering kingdoms of Jambudvīpa. All were delighted by the True Dharma and purely cultivated their conduct in the precepts; they were perfected in manifold virtues, having subdued various heterodox teachers and those who disrupt the Dharma. They were universally able to bestow the gift of the Dharma of fearlessness and expounded for the multitude the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma. They were all capable of practicing the wondrous nectar-like Dharma taught by all Buddhas, crushing and subduing the demonic hordes and the heterodox arguments of external paths. Maintaining the disciplinary conduct themselves, they enabled the monks who uphold the precepts to gain strength and dwell in peace. Maintaining the disciplinary conduct themselves, they delighted in hearing the Mahāyāna and extensively expounded it for others. Universally compassionate and sympathetic toward all sentient beings, their virtues were exactly as described above.
Their names were:

the Licchavi youth Vimalanetra-kośa, the Licchavi youth Nityaprahlāda-vimala, and the Licchavi youth Gaṅgā-nirmala-vimala. These various Licchavis each prepared eighty-four billion sandalwood couches and canopies, aloe-wood couches and canopies, saffron-wood couches and canopies, cypress-wood couches and canopies, and *turuṣka* incense-wood couches and canopies; each also prepared eighty-four billion items carved and engraved with patterns, adorned with the seven treasures and radiant with five-colored light, decorated as previously described. Each also prepared eighty-four thousand precious horses, eighty-four thousand great elephant kings, and eighty-four thousand chariots drawn by four horses, all bound and decorated with divine pearls and luminous gems, majestic and exquisite, moving like the swift wind.

Furthermore, eighty-four thousand divine moon-jewels were prepared, which shine constantly day and night; along with banners, canopies, streamers, flowers, and great precious curtains and hangings, as well as white cotton cloths and images, all arranged in succession as previously described.

The precious flower-canopy was one yojana in width; its painted and finely layered images were thirty-two yojanas in size; the curtains rose to a height of one hundred yojanas each; the banners were each one thousand yojanas long; they were adorned and embellished with the seven treasures as described before;
and the fragrance of the food perfumed an area of one yojana.

Having prepared seats and bedding in the Drḍhavana forest and provided all necessary requisites, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and requested the Buddha to accept his invitation; having completed his head-to-foot salutation, he stood to one side.

Furthermore, within Jambudvīpa, there were great householders as numerous as the sands of five Ganges Rivers, who deeply delighted in the True Dharma, purely cultivated their conduct of precepts, and had perfected all virtues; they subdued various heterodox teachers and those who disrupt the Dharma, and deeply delighted in the Mahāyāna.

Their names were King Candraprabha, the Elder Campakamukha, the Elder Dharmottara, and others such as these—five *gaṅgā*-sands of sons and daughters of elders. At the time of dawn, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they prepared a multitude of offerings even more magnificent than before. They came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves to request his presence, and having bowed their heads at his feet, stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were the King of Vaiśālī and his inner and outer retinues, as well as the lords of the various cities, towns, villages, and wilderness regions throughout Jambudvīpa—excluding King Ajātaśatru, these included King Candravimalagarbha, King Sūryavimala, and others numbering six *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* [sands], each leading a retinue of one hundred and eighty billion followers. All were valiant and strong like dragon-elephants, moving with the speed of a swift wind; they deeply delighted in the True Dharma and purely cultivated their conduct of precepts. Having accomplished all virtues, they subdued those of heterodox views and those who disturbed the Dharma. The offerings they prepared were twice as magnificent as those before. They came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and requested the Buddha’s presence; bowing their heads to his feet, they stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were the various great and small kings who ruled over Jambudvīpa, along with their queens and court ladies, numbering as many as seven Ganges-sands. With the exception of King Ajātaśatru, all these queens and court ladies were weary of their female forms; they practiced the path of emptiness, took deep delight in the Mahāyāna, and extensively expounded for others the merits they had cultivated, all as previously described.

Among the upāsikās were those named Lady Wondrous of the Three Realms, Lady Recollecting Virtue, and others. The offerings they prepared were twice as magnificent as before; at dawn, they came to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves, and requested the Buddha to teach. They bowed their heads to his feet and stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were celestial hosts as numerous as the sands of eight Ganges Rivers, including the Son of Heaven Samantaprabha and others, all of whom delighted in the Mahāyāna and extensively expounded it for others.

They practiced pure precepts and thirsted for the Mahāyāna; for those among the various classes of sentient beings who delighted in the Mahāyāna, they quelled their thirst through the Mahāyāna Dharma, practicing pure precepts with a longing for the Great Vehicle.
Mounting the vehicle, they are firm in the Great Vehicle and awakened to the Great Vehicle; they harbor no envy or pride regarding the Dharma of the Great Vehicle;
they subdue various heterodox teachers and those who disrupt the Dharma; they protect and uphold the True Dharma and practice pure precepts;
they accord with the world, delivering those not yet delivered and liberating those not yet liberated; they desire to turn the Wheel of Dharma and desire to cause the Three [Jewels] to flourish.
He ensured that the flow of precious offerings remained uninterrupted and desired to establish a Great Adornment;
thus, he was fully endowed with immeasurable merits such as these, treating all sentient beings with equal compassion as if they were his only child.
At dawn, when the light had shone forth, these devas perceived this auspicious sign and all thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."
They approached the place where the Buddha was and, seeing the various articles of offering, said to one another:

"Behold, you all, these human offerings; their adornment is so extraordinary that they are no different from those of the heavens. This is the final offering made to the Tathāgata—a grand final gift of various foods for the Buddha and the Saṅgha—yet now the World-Honored One accepts none of it at all."

"O virtuous ones, today we too shall, for the sake of the Buddha, the Saṃgha, and their retinues, perform our final offering and fulfill the perfection of giving. May the Tathāgata, the Saṃgha, and their retinues compassionately accept our final offering, as they are about to enter Parinirvāṇa. A Buddha appearing in the world is difficult to encounter; a final offering such as this is even more exceedingly rare."
"How strange! O Benevolent One, the world is empty; how swiftly the Eye of the World has perished!
All these hosts of devas thought to themselves:
"We, too, shall make offerings to the Tathāgata."

He immediately prepared offerings twice as magnificent as those of the human realm—beds, curtains, carriages, banners, streamers, flower canopies, images, and hangings—all adorned and embellished with celestial incense, celestial silks, and celestial jewels.
Having prepared the offerings, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, and stood to one side after paying their respects.
Furthermore, there were dragon kings as numerous as the sands of nine Ganges Rivers who came from the four directions;
their names were:

The Nāga King Vasuki, the Nāga Kings Nanda and Upananda, and others—endowed with manifold virtues and moved by compassion for the world—having illuminated the world with their radiance at the break of dawn, each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."

They prepared various offerings twice as magnificent as those of humans and devas, and coming to where the Buddha was, they prostrated themselves to request his presence; having circumambulated him hundreds of thousands of times, they stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were ghost kings and spirits numbering as many as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, including Vaiśravaṇa and all other ghost kings; their offerings were exactly like those of the former, and they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves to request his presence, and after circumambulating him hundreds of thousands of times, stood to one side.
Furthermore, there were twenty Ganges-sands of Kinnara kings, such as the Kinnara King Dragon-Enemy (Nāga-vairin) and others;
thirty Ganges-sands of Gandharva kings, such as the Gandharva King Narada and others;
and forty Ganges-sands of Kinnara kings, such as the Kinnara King Swift-Sight (Kṣipradarśin) and others.
Fifty Ganges-sands of mahoraga kings, such as the mahoraga king Mahādarśana;
sixty Ganges-sands of asura kings, such as the asura king Ākāśagocara;
and seventy Ganges-sands of dānava kings, such as the dānava king Dharmodgata-vimala-jaya.
Eighty *gaṅgā*-sands of rākṣasa kings, such as the rākṣasa king Vipulabhaya;
ninety *gaṅgā*-sands of forest-lord kings, such as the forest-lord king Gandharati;
and one thousand *gaṅgā*-sands of mantra-holding kings, such as the mantra-holding king Mahāmāyāvin.
One hundred million *gaṅgā*-sands of gods of the desire and form realms, such as the various Sudarśanas;
one hundred billion *gaṅgā*-sands of celestial maidens, such as the various Rambhās;
and one trillion *gaṅgā*-sands of kings, such as King Bhūtānanda and King Śakrāditya-Bhūtānanda.
There were hundreds of thousands of billions of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sons of gods, including the Four Great Kings;
hundreds of thousands of billions of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* wind-king spirits;
and one hundred million *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* cloud-and-rain-of-music king spirits.
The kings of all worlds, the Cloud-Rain Sovereigns,
having been awakened at dawn by the radiance of these kings, perceived this auspicious omen and each thought to themselves:
"The Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa."

A multitude of rain-like offerings, surpassing those of humans and devas, arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling; they prostrated themselves, requested the Buddha [to remain], and after circumambulating him hundreds of thousands of times, stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were twenty Ganges-sands of fragrant elephant kings, such as the golden-colored, deep-blue-eyed Elephant King; these elephant kings, according to their respective powers, had gathered various fragrant medicinal herbs from the Snowy Mountains, as well as famous flowers—blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), night-blooming water lilies (*kumuda*), and white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*)—each as large as a chariot wheel, along with all manner of flowers produced by mountains, rivers, waters, and lands, using them to adorn couches, canopies, and ritual implements.
With cries of lamentation that shook heaven and earth, they exclaimed: "How swift is the world becoming empty! How swift is the extinction of the eye of the world!"
They approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
Furthermore, there were three *gaṅgā*-sands of lion kings, such as the Great Roaring Lion King;

all of them universally bestowed fearlessness upon sentient beings. Also present were the various bird kings, such as the *kāraṇḍava* bird and the *kalaviṅka* bird king, whose offerings were all exactly like those of the elephant kings.
Furthermore, there were kings of oxen and sheep who went to the Forest of Solidity and produced fine fragrant milk, causing the milk in all the pits and ponds to overflow.

There were also kings of bees who filled their hives with fragrant honey. Such beings as these, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges River, all went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand *gaṅgā*-sands of five-attainment (*pañcābhijñā*) ṛṣis, together with all the various ṛṣis of the four continents, such as the ṛṣi Kṣāntivādin; they manifested various supernatural powers, and the offerings they presented were all twice as magnificent as those before. They came to where the Buddha was, spread their hair upon the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.

At that time, the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs from the sixteen great nations—all except for the two assemblies of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa and the Venerable Ānanda—gathered in full, filling an entire yojana, all exactly as before.
At dawn, the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and after circumambulating him a hundred thousand times, stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were ten thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of minor mountain spirit kings, great mountain spirit kings, various ghost spirit kings from the intervals between worlds, and the Sumeru mountain spirit king; those who consume the leaves, flowers, fruits, and various kinds of living beings of the trees—all possessed supernatural powers and emitted great radiance as they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and stood to one side.

Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of *Ganges*-sands of deities of the eight great rivers, the great oceans, and the great earth, as well as sons of gods and kings, both great and small, all possessed of supernatural powers. They emitted a great radiance that eclipsed the sun and moon. From the Forest of Solidity (*Sālaguhāvana*), they brought forth water of ambrosia (*amṛta*) that filled the river Hiraṇyavatī, making its flow gentle, clear, and transparent. Everywhere they constructed stairways of the seven treasures, so that the assembly of the gathering might drink of it without weariness.

At that time, facing north from the birthplace of the Malla warriors, there was a naturally formed multi-storied lecture hall of the True Dharma, adorned with carvings and embellished with the seven treasures, radiating light of five colors. Clear springs, bathing pools, flower gardens, and fruit orchards were likewise spontaneously manifested; they were as delightful as the Nandana Grove of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. All the devas, humans, and asuras beheld the signs of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, and all were moved by grief, filled with sorrow, and sighed deeply.
Furthermore, one hundred million asaṃkhyeya devaputras of the Four Great Kings all came to the assembly and said to one another:

"All of you observe these devas, asuras, and humans who, for the sake of making their final offering to the Tathāgata, have prepared these various excellent, wondrous, and extraordinary offerings of food and drink; once the Buddha and the great assembly have accepted those gifts, he shall enter parinirvāṇa. We, too, shall prepare a multitude of offerings that shall surpass theirs twofold."

They all brought celestial flowers, celestial incense, and celestial food—mandārava flowers, mahā-mandārava flowers, karkarava flowers, mahā-karkarava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahā-mañjūṣaka flowers, saṃtāna flowers, and mahā-saṃtāna flowers—as well as various other celestial flowers and celestial incenses to form their offerings. They approached the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and requested the Buddha to sit, remaining to one side.

The offerings made by Śakra Devānām Indra together with an incalculable multitude of the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens, and even those made by the King of the Sixth Heaven together with his retinue, were each many times more excellent than the preceding ones.

Excluding those in the four formless realms and the gods of the non-percipient heaven within the realm of form, all other devas likewise prepared offering articles that were twice as magnificent as before.

At that time, Brahmā, the Lord of the Sahā World, together with his immeasurable retinue of Brahmā-sons, each emitted bodily radiance that pervaded the four continents, such that the various lights from the bodies of humans and devas in the desire realm were all eclipsed and did not appear. They rained down celestial robes and famous celestial flowers, and prepared celestial food; furthermore, individual celestial banners, celestial pennants, and celestial canopies extended from the Forest of Solidity up to the Brahma Heaven.
Having prepared the various requisites, he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself, and stood to one side, requesting the Buddha [to accept his offerings].

Furthermore, the Asura King Vemacitra, together with immeasurable retinues of asuras, emitted bodily radiance that pervaded the four continents; the bodily radiance of Śakra Devānām Indra and the various Brahma Kings was all eclipsed and no longer appeared. He also prepared meals and various offering articles, such that the precious parasols completely covered the small chiliocosm.
Having prepared the various offerings, he approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated himself, and requested that the Buddha remain to one side.

At that time, the celestial Māra Pāpīyān, together with an immeasurable host of celestial Māra maidens, used his supernatural powers to open wide all the gates of the hells. He provided for and relieved all the sentient beings in those hells according to their respective wishes and desires, and further addressed the hell-beings, saying: "You all!..."

You should bring to mind the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and offer your final sympathetic joy; this is the merit of practice that you are capable of accomplishing through your own power, which shall cause you to long obtain peace and happiness, and forever attain liberation from the agonizing torments of hell.

Through the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata, Māra Pāpīyān’s mind was turned toward submissiveness; together with his retinue, he arrayed himself in full battle regalia—swords, blades, bows, arrows, golden mallets, battle-axes, nooses, long hooks, and all manner of martial implements. For the denizens of hell who have long been shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, who are far removed from the True Dharma and undergo various agonies, and for whose city gates the fierce fires were blazing, he raised great clouds and torrential rain that caused those fires to be completely extinguished.

At that time, the sentient beings in the hells were freed from suffering and attained peace. Having been freed from suffering and attained peace, each of the māras, together with their retinues, prepared various offerings twice as magnificent as before and came to where the Buddha was.

They prostrated themselves and entreated the Buddha, saying: "We only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our offerings. Once you have accepted our offerings, for any son or daughter of good family who invokes the name of the Mahāyāna—whether they be genuine or spurious—we shall all provide them with protection against fear."

And he spoke this mantra: “Ṭa ṭa ṭāṭala | Ṭa ṭa rūlu-re | Mahā-rūlu-re | Ara | Mara | Tara | Svāhā. This mantra can cause those with distracted minds to attain profound and wondrous concentration; this mantra can cause those who are terrified to be free from all fear; this mantra can cause those who act as Dharma-preachers to possess uninterrupted eloquence; and this mantra is able to subdue all non-Buddhists. Those who protect the True Dharma will be protected by this mantra as if they were wearing a divine sword. The words of this mantra-lore I have spoken are true and real. If there are those who can uphold this mantra, whether they encounter fierce and harmful beasts, water, fire, or other calamities in the wilderness, if they either uphold or recite it, all such hardships will be entirely eliminated, just as a tortoise withdraws its six limbs.

Today we have all become entirely free from the deceptions and crookedness of Māra; we only pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately accept our offerings, and that you will likewise grant your seal of approval upon the divine mantras we have spoken.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Māra, saying:
"I do not accept your offering of food; however, for the sake of bringing peace and security to all sentient beings, I shall now accept your gift of the Dharma, which is this divine spell."
Thus he requested three times, yet the World-Honored One remained silent three times and did not accept.
Then Māra Pāpīyas and the celestial maidens of Māra prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.

Furthermore, the Great Lord Śiva, together with immeasurable sons of heaven of great power, emitted a great radiance that illuminated the entire trichiliocosm. The bodily radiances of all the gods, from Brahmā and Śakra down to the hosts of asuras, were completely eclipsed and did not appear. He prepared various offerings twice as magnificent as before; the light of his flower-canopy illuminated the trichiliocosm, such that the hundreds of millions of suns and moons appeared like masses of ink, their radiance no longer visible.

Chapter Two: The Bodhisattva Mahākāya The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Two: The Bodhisattva Mahākāya To the east, beyond this world, past as many Buddha-fields as there are atoms in the lands of countless *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands, there is a world named Manojñābhiruta. There, the Buddha is named Ākāśasama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently dwells in the world teaching the Dharma. He addressed his foremost śrāvaka and bodhisattva, named Mahākāya, saying: "Good son!
In the western direction there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is about to enter parinirvāṇa.

I take this fragrant rice from my bowl, sufficient to fill the entire land, its fragrance pervading the trichiliocosm, and manifest my own mind before that great assembly; once that Tathāgata has accepted my food, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he presented various jeweled couches, canopies, and ritual implements to that Tathāgata, saying, "You and I shall together request a resolution for our doubts.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāya prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and with palms joined, received his instructions; then, accompanied by countless asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he set out toward this Sahā world.

At that time, the earth of the trichiliocosm shook violently. The great assembly gathered there—the Śakras, Brahmās, the Four Heavenly Kings, Māras, Asuras, and the gods of great power—saw this earthquake and their body hairs stood on end; each perceived that the radiance of their own bodies had vanished, appearing entirely like lumps of ink.
At that time, the entire great assembly rose up in alarm.
The youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, Māras, and the various celestial kings, saying:
"Do not be afraid, do not be afraid!"

To the east, beyond lands as numerous as the atoms within the dust motes of countless *asaṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands of Buddha-fields, there is a world named *Manojña-svara*. There dwells a Buddha named *Gaganasama-tathāgata*, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who addressed his foremost śrāvaka and bodhisattvas:

"Go to the Sahā world; there is a Buddha named Śākyamuni-tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is about to enter parinirvāṇa. Offer food to that Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and you yourselves shall together request the resolution of your doubts."

Immediately, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahākāya prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and with palms joined, received his instruction. Together with countless asaṃkhyeya bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he came to this Sahā world; by emitting light from his body, he caused all your own lights to be completely eclipsed and made invisible.
Those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, equal to space, have dispatched these bodhisattvas to make offerings to the World-Honored One; you all should rejoice with a single mind.
Then Śakra, the King of Devas, Brahmā, and the great assembly again exclaimed:
"How extraordinary! The world is empty; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa. How swift is the extinction of the Eye of the World!"
They all raised their voices in mournful wailing and weeping.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahākāya, together with immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, each emitting great radiance from every part of their bodies, came from the Buddha-land of Manojñābhigarjitasvara to this Sahā world.

From every pore of the Great Body Bodhisattva’s body, light radiated forth, transforming into immeasurable varieties of lotus flowers. Upon each flower were seven hundred and eighty million cities, lofty, vast, and magnificently adorned. Each city had seven tiers of walls; each wall was made of the seven treasures, with Jambūnada gold forming the battlements. Above these battlements, jeweled trees were planted in rows, from which grew various precious lotus fruits. Golden cords stretched continuously between the trees, and outside the trees, nets of the seven treasures were layered over them. When a gentle breeze blew, they produced the five musical notes; their sound was harmonious and elegant, like celestial music, while the people lived in peace, security, joy, and sovereignty.

Outside that city, there are ponds made of the seven precious substances encircling it on all sides, filled to the brim with water possessing the eight virtues; the water flows gently and purely, being neither cold nor hot. Within them grow four kinds of lotuses made of the seven precious substances, as large as chariot wheels, radiant with the five colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—and therein they sport upon boats made of the seven precious substances.

Furthermore, within that city there are also bathing pools. Four kinds of lotuses, as large as chariot wheels and adorned with five colors, grow therein. The four sides of these pools are made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; each side reflects the others through the brilliance of these respective jewels. The bottom is of rose-colored gems strewn with golden sand. Each bathing pool has eighteen flights of stairs made of yellow gold, decorated and embellished with various miscellaneous jewels. Along the sides of the paths, *jambu-river* gold *bālakṣa* trees are planted in rows. Heavenly *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as large as chariot wheels, cover the surface of the pools everywhere, while flocks of birds of diverse species sport amidst them.

Above those bathing pools were various kinds of celestial fragrant flower trees; when the winds blew from the four directions, they scattered [the flowers] everywhere over the pools, making the water fragrant and pure like celestial sandalwood.

Within and without that city there were eighty-four thousand great kings; each king had immeasurable consorts and court ladies who delighted themselves with the five desires. The dwellings of the people were each four *yojanas* in size, and their sevenfold walls were all made of the seven precious gems. Each also possessed gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools; they dwelt and roamed at will in the pleasures of the five desires without being subject to any ruler. The ground was soft and supple, strewn with flowers of five colors and perfumed with celestial incense.

Furthermore, in that place, even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist; it is purely and solely the Mahāyāna. Upon each flower there is a great king seated upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet, while canopies of various precious jewels cover him from above, as he transforms and delivers sentient beings through the Mahāyāna Dharma.
All those sentient beings were upon the flowers, listening to and receiving the Mahāyāna, copying, upholding, reciting, and contemplating it, and practicing according to its teachings.
The Bodhisattva Mahākāya’s light from his pores, his supernormal powers, and his transformations—these were likewise so for all the other bodhisattvas.

At that time, the sentient beings had no desire for pleasure; they were filled only with sorrow, distress, and lamentation as they traveled gradually along the road toward the great city of Kauśāmbī, saying to one another:

"Behold this extraordinary offering made by the devas and humans! The Bodhisattvas who have come have also prepared sacrificial requisites; the various flavors of the food are so fresh, pure, fragrant, and delicious that there is nothing to compare them to."

The Bodhisattva Mahākāya, together with his retinue, produced precious lotus flowers from the pores of their bodies. They presented the food they had brought as an offering to the Buddha and the Sangha; the fragrance of that food pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, and all sentient beings who smelled it were completely freed from every affliction. The precious canopies of lotuses, banners, pennants, and flowered parasols—indeed, all the offerings—were beyond compare. Departing from their own land for this realm, they traveled through the void like soaring towers, such that there was not a single sentient being among them who did not behold them.

The Bodhisattva Mahākāya and his retinue prepared various offerings that surpassed those of the devas; indeed, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s radiance, the light of Brahmā, Śakra, and all other devas was eclipsed and did not appear.

From every pore of the bodies of those bodhisattvas, lotus flowers rained down; the fragrance of these flowers pervaded the entire trichiliocosm, and all who smelled it were cleansed of their karmic defilements and inspired the resolve for enlightenment.

The Bodhisattva Mahākāya possessed a body of immeasurable size that filled all of space; except for the Tathāgata himself, no one else was able to fathom it. He prostrated, presented food and various offerings, and stood to one side.

The bodhisattvas who have come from the worlds of the southern direction emit precious lotus flowers from the pores of their bodies; like those in Jambudvīpa, these arise from upon lotus flowers to form cities of the seven treasures that are twice as magnificent as those in the eastern direction.

The lotus flowers from the pores of the bodhisattvas who have come from the worlds of the western quarter are as large as the four continents; their cities and various implements are twice as magnificent as those previously described.

The lotus flowers from the pores of the bodhisattvas who have come from the worlds of the northern quarter are as large as a small thousand-world system; their city walls and bathing pools are likewise twice as magnificent as those previously described.

Even the countless asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas who had come from the worlds of the ten directions were all like the Great Body Bodhisattva, their bodies filling the void; the lotuses in their pores were as vast as the trichiliocosm, raining down various flowers and manifold offerings. Their own bodies and radiance eclipsed those of the entire assembly, and they prostrated themselves, presented their offerings, and stood to one side.

At that time, the side of the Drḍhavana Forest became a ground of great auspiciousness. Thirty-two rows of seats were arranged all around; although the space was narrow, the bodies of the bodhisattvas were immeasurably large. Devas and humans from all quarters gathered like clouds, yet there was no crowding. Some seats occupied the space of a needle-point, some the space of a hair-tip, some the space of a fine bristle, and some the space of a minute mote. Each, according to the size of their body, found a place to stand securely without distress. Even the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as motes of dust, shook in six ways, and through supernatural transformations, rare signs appeared. Each, according to their capacity, made offerings as before.

At that time, throughout Jambudvīpa—with the sole exception of the retinue of the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the retinue of the Venerable Ānanda, and the retinue of King Ajātaśatru—all other sentient beings came to the assembly.

At that time, venomous snakes, poisonous stingers, and all other species of malevolent insects, as well as demons, spirits, rākṣasas, and those who employ various spells and sorcery, will all give rise to a heart of compassion and refrain from harming one another, regarding each other as if they were their only child—except for those belonging to the class of icchantikas.

At that time, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the ground of this trichiliocosm became entirely soft and supple, free of mounds, ravines, sand, gravel, thorns, or poisonous weeds; it was adorned with various jewels like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The assembly of devas, humans, and asuras present there all beheld worlds as numerous as the dust motes of the ten directions, seeing everything contained within them clearly before their eyes, as if observing reflections in a mirror.

At that time, the Tathāgata emitted various kinds of extraordinary and magnificent light from his face; the bodily radiance of all those gathered in the assembly was completely eclipsed and no longer appeared. All sentient beings prostrated themselves and entreated him, whereupon the light, having performed its purpose, returned through his mouth.
At that time, the devas, humans, asuras, and others were struck with great terror, their hair standing on end. They said to one another:

"The Tathāgata’s radiance has shone throughout the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions; having completed what was to be done, it now returns into his mouth with no further purpose remaining. This must surely be the sign of his final nirvāṇa."

He does not accept any offerings presented by devas and humans; how strange this is! The sprouts of the four virtues have been abandoned all at once; the sun of noble wisdom shall henceforth perish forever, and the precious ship of compassion has sunk right here.
Alas! How painful! The hopes of sentient beings are utterly severed.
Wailing and weeping with blood and tears falling like rain—just as a great cloud pours rain everywhere over the world—so too did the entire great assembly weep and shed tears at that time.

Chapter Three: The Elder Cunda, from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*. At that time, in the assembly, there was an elder from the city of Kauśāmbī named Cunda, who was accompanied by five hundred sons of elders. With dignified and composed deportment, he observed that the entire assembly had gathered; he adjusted his robes, prostrated before the Buddha, and was filled with sorrow and grief. He appeared like the rising sun shining upon green tree leaves, causing their red veins to become clearly visible;

the elder was just like this, with blood flowing from his entire body and tears falling like rain. Having circumambulated the Buddha a hundred thousand times, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha:

“I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly, will compassionately accept our final offering, so that I and all sentient beings may together attain liberation. It is like a poor farmer in the middle of spring who plows his fields and sows his seeds, looking up in hope for the rain from heaven; even so am I now, whose body, speech, and mind are afflicted by the many defilements of afflictions, having only just begun to cultivate the thought of weary detachment.”

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will bestow the rain of Dharma upon the great assembly; may you compassionately accept my invitation, so that this parched field may receive the moisture of your grace.
At that time, the World-Honored One, possessing all-encompassing wisdom and knowing all times, addressed Cunda, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with the great assembly, shall accept your invitation for our final offering.”

At that time, the devas, humans, and asuras, hearing that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha had accepted the final offering of the elder Cunda, felt joy within their hearts; with one voice and in unison, they marveled at this unprecedented event, exclaiming:
"Excellent!"
Excellent,
Elder Cunda! Your virtues and aspirations are fully realized.
"How extraordinary, Cunda!

You have now attained a rare benefit difficult to find among those born in the human realm. Like the udumbara flower, which is seldom seen in the world, it is difficult for a Buddha to appear in this world; difficult to gain faith, and difficult likewise to hear the Dharma. Yet, to offer the final供养 (pūjā) to a Buddha on the verge of parinirvāṇa is even more difficult than those."
Furthermore, Cunda!
It is like the fifteenth night of the spring month, when the moon is pure, full, and free from all clouds; there are no sentient beings who do not gaze up at it, and you are just like that.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, together with the great assembly, accepts from you this final perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Excellent, Cunda!
For this reason, it is said that you are like the full moon, whom all sentient beings gaze upon without exception.
How marvelous, Cunda!
You are a true son of the Buddha; though born into the human realm, you are now regarded by all as the God among Gods. Therefore, we shall bow our heads in prostration to you.
They all raised their voices together and praised him, saying:
"Though born among the human realm, You are fully endowed with celestial marks.
We and the entire assembly Now prostrate ourselves and entreat you:"
If you would now compassionately grant your consent, I shall proclaim my humble aspiration.
If you wish to deliver sentient beings, you should quickly offer this exhortation:
Today, O God among Gods, Tamer of Men;
With the perfect, responsive eye of supernormal power, Possessing the marks of immeasurable merit,
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he requests that you Relinquish the means of entering nirvana;
O God among Gods, remain in this world And extensively proclaim the Dharma of ambrosia.
“After the long-lasting suffering of birth and death, from this one attains peace and security.

At that time, the elder Cunda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, just like a person who has suddenly lost their parents and is overcome by grief, only to find them restored to life at the very moment they are being escorted to the grave; beholding them, his sorrow turns to joy and his feelings of reverence redouble.
The elder Cunda and his entire retinue were likewise filled with such joy and exultation; prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they joined their palms and spoke in verse:
"How joyous! I have now attained great benefit; The wondrous fruits among humanity have all been obtained.
How joyous! I have now attained great benefit; The gates to the hells and evil realms are forever closed."
How joyful! I have now attained great benefit; having been born into this world, I have encountered the unsurpassed fruit.
It is like seeking wondrous jewels from within the sand, only to suddenly encounter a diamond with great delight.
How joyful that I have now attained a noble liberation from the delusions of the animal realm wherever I may be!
How joyful that I have now attained this great benefit: the firm and steadfast faith of the udumbara flower!
How joyous that I have now successfully escaped the suffering of hunger and thirst born of the stinginess and greed of hungry ghosts;
how joyous that I have now attained great benefit, having reached the further shore through the perfection of giving, which is so difficult to obtain.
From now on, the various evil realms shall be closed forever; The Asura King has attained ultimate liberation.
How joyful that I have now gained this great benefit! A Tathāgata appearing in the world is most difficult to encounter;
To meet the Udumbara flower now is like A mustard seed being cast onto the point of a needle.
How joyful it is that I have now attained a noble liberation; the Four Great Kings abandoned their notions of permanence.
How joyful it is that I have now attained great benefit; the great treasure of the Dharma King is now fully seen.
Even regarding the ten realms of birth among the desire heavens, I have clearly and distinctly understood them, remaining free from attachment.
How joyful am I now that I have attained this great benefit; the Hero of the World is difficult to encounter, yet today I behold him.
Just as a mustard seed might be cast upon the point of a needle, it is even more difficult than that to meet a Buddha.
Even the twenty-five sources of the three realms, when compared to the point of a needle, are likewise so.
How joyful! I have now attained great benefit; meeting the Tathāgata, my vows are fulfilled.
All manner of evils are crushed and destroyed—the thieves of immeasurable ignorance and darkness.
How joyful! Now I have attained great benefit, Born to encounter the Venerable One, the Stainless Lotus.
How joyful! Now I have forever escaped, The surging waves of the ocean of birth and death.
How joyful it is to be born in this world and encounter a Tathāgata, like a blind turtle in the ocean meeting a floating log!
How joyful that I have now forever escaped the delusions of the blind turtle in the great ocean of birth and death!
How joyful! I have now attained a great benefit, Unprecedented in the world and without peer;
Though gods and men entreated me with grief, I accepted none; This most difficult-to-request treasure, I have now obtained.
How joyful! Now I have attained great benefit, honored by devas, humans, and asuras; how joyful!
Now I have attained the fruit of the present life, for the Great Sage has accepted my final invitation;
how joyful! Now I have attained great benefit, having exhorted him together with all the devas and humans.
Having set aside those exquisite and sublime foods of devas and humans, he compassionately accepted my coarse and rough offering;
how wonderful that I have now attained such great benefit, whereas the offerings presented by devas and humans failed to fulfill his wish.
I offered food as coarse and bitter as the eranda tree, yet the Tathāgata, out of great compassion and pity, accepted it;
the devas, humans, and asuras, filled with grief and weeping, prostrated themselves and entreated him.
The Tathāgata, with great compassion and universal kindness, regards all sentient beings as his only child;
even if he does not accept this offering of food from the multitude, we pray that he will have pity on devas and humans and not enter parinirvāṇa.

Those gods and humans have no other pursuit; they pray only that the Tathāgata may dwell forever in the world, like Mount Sumeru standing in the great ocean, firmly established upon the vajra-circle, secure and unmoving.
The mountains and waters reflect his majestic and beautiful form; thus the Tathāgata dwells within this great assembly.
The Dharma King’s radiant majesty shines upon the fourfold congregation, just as when the sun emerges from thick clouds to dispel the darkness of the world.
Now all these devas and humans are likewise; for a long time they have been shrouded in the darkness of sorrow, grief, and delusion.
We only pray that the Tathāgata will dwell long in the world, so that the sunlight of his noble wisdom may utterly extinguish it.
May the World-Honored One of Great Wisdom dwell long in the world; may the Great Hero dwell long in the world.
May our minds be freed from sorrow and fear, remaining as stable and unmoving as Mount Sumeru.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying: "It is so, Cunda!
A Buddha’s appearance in the world is extremely difficult to encounter, just as a single grain of diamond among the sands of the ocean."

A human body is difficult to obtain, and even more so than that is the complete possession of faith; it is like a blind turtle encountering the hole of a floating log. To encounter a Tathāgata at the very moment he is about to enter parinirvāṇa and to perform the final offering of *dānapāramitā* is even more difficult than that, occurring only once in a great while, like the appearance of the udumbara flower.
"You, Cunda, should not give rise to sorrow or distress;
rather, you should feel great joy.
Why is this? You should form this thought:"
"Today the Tathāgata, together with the great assembly, accepts my final and greatest offering of alms; for this merit and benefit, you should rejoice.

Cunda, you should not now request that the Tathāgata remain long in this world; you should observe that all things in the world are impermanent, and the nature of all conditioned phenomena is likewise so.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for Cunda:
"Even if one were to remain in the world for a long time, In the end, one must inevitably perish;
Though one may be born in the heavens of long life, One's lifespan will likewise surely come to an end."
All things accomplished must come to ruin; that which exists is entirely subject to extinction.
The vigorous are destroyed by old age; the strong are beset by illness.
All human life ends in death; how can impermanence ever endure?
There is no form and no physical strength, nor is there any life-span.
Wives and children, as well as elephants and horses, and even wealth—all are likewise so.
All the various kinsmen of the world and one's retinue must all be parted from.
The great terrors of the three realms, even the sufferings of the evil destinies—all these shall return to extinction;
how could one not find weariness and dread in them?
There are the characteristics of birth and old age, which are what we call the laws of shame and modesty.
Though constantly subjected to injury and deception, one still claims it endures forever.
Yet the sublime Dharma of purity and coolness is far removed from all terror;
it also brings liberation from the great calamities of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The defilements of a distracted and deluded mind—these are all said to have been transcended;
it is the immeasurable, the remainderless, the wondrously supreme nirvāṇa.
Its meaning is truly impermanent, nor is it a dharma protected by the aggregates.
Yet this mass of suffering is hollow and not solid;
it is incapable and cannot be endured, nor can it be maintained forever.
These beings are like silkworms, weaving a web with which they entangle themselves.
Within the cycle of the three realms, there is not a single place of delight;
there is only the suffering of birth and old age, and the great affliction of sickness and death.
Those who understand the truth can see that the span of life flows away day and night.
Subject to decay and deception, terrifying and without even a moment’s joy;
filled with disease, grief, sorrow, and affliction, it is overflowing with all that is unwholesome.
The wheel of the fire of desire blazes fiercely, and a multitude of hardships converge upon it in competition.
The wise do not dwell forever in this great suffering;
they clearly understand the afflictions of the five desires as being devoid of merit or benefit.
Free from desire and without greed, they perceive reality with lucid clarity.
This is the contemplation of liberation, which abandons all that is born;
it censures harmful fetters and enmity, ultimately casting off all states of existence.
From this, one swiftly transcends all conditioned phenomena, just as a blazing fire is extinguished when the fuel is exhausted.
Exquisite form is serene and ever-abiding in peace, Unwasted or eroded by aging and decay.
Immeasurable sickness and suffering do not oppress him; His lifespan endures long, without end or limit.
The boundless ocean of suffering has been entirely crossed; He does not shift with the passage of seasons or kalpas.
How joyful is the Tathāgata, who has transcended the three realms;
no longer deluded by the cycle of birth and death, do not regard me as having entered final nirvāṇa, for I remain like Mount Sumeru standing firm within the great ocean.
Cunda, I shall now enter parinirvāṇa; the equal and true Dharma shall abide forever in peace and joy.
When those of clear wisdom hear this meaning, they will understand it with perfect clarity and feel no grief or sorrow.
Do not attempt to measure the Buddha with a fragile body subject to birth and death, nor with shallow wisdom;
my body dwells in true tranquility, and only the World-Honored One can fully comprehend it.
At that time, Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“World-Honored One!
We common and inferior beings have come to know that the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa* is inconceivable. World-Honored One!

We now become no different from those great beings—the assembly of bodhisattvas and the arhats—just like Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and the arhats. Within this assembly, if one first receives the precepts, at the moment of receiving them, they are said to be included within the ranks of the Saṃgha.”
I, who am now but an ordinary and inferior being, am likewise thus; having received the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, I have been permitted to join the ranks of such great and worthy ones.
Truly so, World-Honored One!
I pray that the Tathāgata will remain long in the world, and do not enter parinirvāṇa like a scorched and ruined seed.
Mañjuśrī said to Cunda, "Do not make such a vow. Why is this? Because..."

One should contemplate in this way: the nature of conditioned phenomena is inherently thus. One who contemplates in this manner is fully endowed with the wisdom of emptiness; those who seek the True Dharma should awaken to it in this way.
Cunda replied, “Mañjuśrī!
The Tathāgata is the Honored One among men and the God among gods; he is named the Worthy of Offerings (Arhat). How could he be a conditioned practice?”

If a practitioner were subject to the dharma of arising and ceasing—like a bubble on water that quickly forms and quickly vanishes, or like a chariot wheel in its constant coming and going—and if the Tathāgata were likewise subject to such conditioned phenomena, he would ultimately never transcend the realms of humans and devas; he would not be the God among Gods, nor the Worthy One (Arhat).
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

Have you not heard that there are gods of long life, yet the Tathāgata has not even reached a hundred years? How can the Dharma of birth and death be called 'the God among Gods' (Devātideva) and named 'Worthy of Offerings' (Arhat) in comparison to humans and devas?"

Mañjuśrī! It is like a person who serves as a village headman; according to his merits, he gradually advances to a high position, becoming honored by the multitude and possessing mastery over wealth and power. Yet, once his merit is exhausted, he returns to being a poor and lowly person, no longer accounted among the ranks of men.

If the Tathāgata were likewise subject to such conditioned processes, he would be just the same: he would not be the supreme among humans, nor the god among gods, nor an Arhat worthy of offerings, but would instead become inferior.
Why is this? Because it is a phenomenon that arises and ceases. Therefore, Mañjuśrī!
"Do not hold such a view that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is a conditioned phenomenon.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, do you speak thus because you know it to be so?"
Is this spoken out of ignorance?
How can you, through such false conceptualization, claim that the Tathāgata is subject to the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*)?
If the Tathāgata were subject to the conditioned factors, he would not be called the Dharma King who possesses mastery over the triple world.

Why is this so? It is like a king who is courageous and possesses great strength, such that one man can match a thousand; because he is able to subdue a thousand strongmen, people of the time call him the "King of a Thousand Strongmen.

In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise subdues the Māra of Afflictions, the Māra of the Aggregates, the Māra of Death, and the Māra of the Lord of Heaven (Māra-pāpīyas). Having thus subdued the pride of all these Māra-warriors, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained the status of the Sovereign Dharma King of the Three Realms. If the Tathāgata were subject to the law of death, he would not possess the true merit of the King of a Thousand Strongmen.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī! Do not give rise to conceptualizations of calculation regarding the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

For example, suppose there is a wealthy elder who has only one son. An astrologer examines the boy and finds signs of a short lifespan. Upon hearing this, the parents' hearts are filled with great sorrow and distress, thinking: "We are of poor fortune; our household is not auspicious. Having fathered a short-lived son, we shall no longer hold him in high regard."
Why is this? Among gods, humans, and brahmins, those who possess short lifespans are not themselves respected or honored by their peers because of that very shortness of life.
