In this way, Mañjuśrī!

If the Tathāgata were to have a lifespan equal to that of worldly people, he would not be loved and respected by his parents, just as worldly people are not; likewise, if the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha were subject to the cycle of conditioned existence, he too would not be loved and respected by humans, devas, and asuras, because he would be seen to undergo transformation.

Why is this? Because, while sharing in the decline and failure of all dharmas regarding knowledge and vision, one nonetheless preaches the teaching of liberation for sentient beings—how can such a principle be called "right awakening"?
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, do not give rise to conceptualizations of enumeration regarding the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī:

It was like a poor woman who had no home and was further afflicted by illness; wandering about to beg for alms, she stayed in another's guesthouse and gave birth to a son there. When the owner of the guesthouse drove her out, she carried her child along the road toward a prosperous and happy land. On the way, she grew exhausted and was bitten all over her body by mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects. Upon reaching the Ganges River, she carried her child across it; as the current flowed with great force, she did not let go of her child, and consequently they both drowned and died.
By virtue of this merit of saving his child with a compassionate heart, when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Pure and Wondrous Heaven. Why is this?
It is because he protected his child without regard for his own life.

Mañjuśrī! A bodhisattva who wishes to protect the True Dharma in this way does not engage in the contemplation of the Tathāgata as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). One should know that anyone who engages in such contemplation is blind and lacks the eye of wisdom. Regarding the World-Honored One, one should correctly contemplate him as inconceivable; one should know that the Tathāgata is not a conditioned phenomenon, for he manifests through emanations to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings. Just as that poor woman, by protecting her son and not begrudging her own life, was reborn in the Pure and Sublime Heaven, so too is it with the bodhisattva who protects the Dharma.

Being able to know that the Tathāgata is not a conditioned phenomenon, but a permanently abiding dharma and an eternally dwelling dharma, such a protector of the Dharma attains the fruit of the present life and swiftly achieves liberation.
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī! It is like a man traveling far who stays as a guest in another's house;

exhausted, he falls asleep when a great fire suddenly breaks out and consumes the dwelling. Startled awake, he sees the fire pressing against his body and seeks to escape the calamity. His clothes are completely burned away, and he feels ashamed of his nakedness; yet, failing to leave the burning house, he eventually perishes in the flames."

By virtue of the merit of shame and modesty (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*), when his body perishes at the end of life, he becomes the king of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven eighty thousand times; furthermore, he becomes the Brahmā king one hundred thousand times; and when reborn among humans, he always becomes a wheel-turning sage-king (*cakravartin*). He does not fall into the evil destinies but dwells forever in peace and happiness—such is the result of shame and modesty.

Mañjuśrī! You should know that the Tathāgata acts through skillful means; one should die with shame and remorse like that man, rather than, like the non-Buddhists, indulge in and practice false views. One must not, for the sake of a precept-observing bhikṣu, falsely speak by conceiving of the unconditioned Tathāgata as being conditioned.
If one conceives of the Tathāgata as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), you should know that such a person shall have the Avīci Hell as their constant dwelling.

Therefore, do not reckon the Tathāgata as conditioned. One who can conceive of the Tathāgata as unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) will thereby cross the great ocean of wisdom and will not be deluded by corpses. This is the accomplishment of the profound perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); by means of this fruit of wisdom, one swiftly attains the Tathāgata’s complete marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*).
At that time, Mañjuśrī said to Cunda:
"Excellent, son of good family!
You should know this: the Tathāgata abides eternally in the unconditioned, a dharma that is not subject to change.
You, son of good family!

Possessing such wisdom, you are likewise able to conceal the conditioned through skillful means and manifest it as the Buddha does. Before long, you shall attain the path of Buddhahood; such supreme, wondrous, and extraordinary merits can only be praised and described by the World-Honored Buddha.
Furthermore, Cunda!
Timely giving and the gift of Dharma surpass all other forms of giving. As for timely giving:

if a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā—whether traveling from afar or on the road—one provides what is needed according to their capacity and with promptness, this is the seed of the *dānapāramitā* that gives rise to great fruit and retribution.
Cunda! Now, according to your capacity, you should offer the final alms to the Buddha and the Sangha; you should know that this is the time, for the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One is imminent.
Cunda replied: "Mañjuśrī!
Why trouble yourself to urge me to offer this defiled food?"
"Would the Tathāgata truly wait for this food?

For six years beneath the Bodhi tree, the Tathāgata performed difficult and painful ascetic practices, sustaining himself on only a daily meal of hemp seeds and rice; how much more so now—could he not endure it for a mere moment?"
"Do you think that the Tathāgata eats this food?
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a body sustained by impure food.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mañjuśrī:
"What Cunda has spoken is a true teaching.
He then addressed Cunda again:
"You have attained great wisdom and clearly understand the Mahāyāna."
Mañjuśrī said to Cunda:
"You have now become worthy of the Tathāgata and are held in the Buddha's thoughts.
Cunda replied:
"How could the Tathāgata harbor partial thoughts?
He regards all sentient beings with equal mindfulness.
Do not speak such inverted views; both the one who minds and the object of mindfulness are non-existent—this is how you should practice."

As for this affectionate mindfulness, it is like a dairy cow that, though hungry and thirsty and wandering in search of water and grass, will suddenly think of her calf and quickly return home regardless of whether she has had enough;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have no such suffering-filled thoughts. They regard all sentient beings as their only child; this mindful wisdom is the realm of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
Just as elephant-drawn, horse-drawn, and precious chariot carts differ in their speed, so too these ninefold vehicles of ours are unable to inquire equally about the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!

It is like the king of golden-winged birds (garuḍa) soaring through the void; as it passes over the great ocean, its reflection appears in the water with a body vast and long, such that no aquatic creature can measure the size of its form—just as an infant suffering from illness cannot endure a potent medicine.
Mañjuśrī said: “It is as Cunda has stated;
however, it is for the sake of the bodhisattvas that I have established this discourse regarding profound merit.”

At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted rays of various colors from his face. When the youth Mañjuśrī saw this light, he knew that the time for the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa had arrived. He then addressed the elder Cunda, saying:
“You have made an offering as the very last one to the Tathāgata as he approaches parinirvāṇa; the time has now come, and you should provide it with all haste.”

Cunda! You should know that the Tathāgata does not emit this radiance for no reason; there is a specific purpose for it. You must act with haste, you must act with haste, lest you let the opportunity pass like a flower already plucked.
The elder Cunda remained silent.
The Buddha said to Cunda:
"The Tathāgata will enter parinirvāṇa shortly; this is precisely the time for you to make offerings to the Saṃgha."
Thus he spoke a second and a third time.
Cunda, filled with grief and distress, raised his voice and lamented:
"How strange! The world is now empty; the Tathāgata has passed away forever. Alas! My wailing brings forth tears."
He further entreated him, saying, "I pray that you will compassionately remain for a long time.
The World-Honored One replied, "Cunda!"

Do not weep and disturb your own mind; you should practice correct contemplation by cultivating the perception of a mirage, and realize that things are as unsubstantial as a plantain tree, a dream, an illusion, a flash of lightning, or a clay vessel. You should know that all conditioned phenomena are a dwelling place of calamities and afflictions.
Cunda addressed the Buddha: “Tathāgata!
If you do not take pity on us by remaining in the world, the world will become empty; how could we help but weep?”
The Buddha said, “Cunda!
It is out of compassion for you and all sentient beings that I enter parinirvāṇa. Such is the nature of all Buddhas’ dharmas; the nature of conditioned phenomena is likewise so.”

Regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), you should reflect upon the verses on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self that I have previously taught; and the verses I spoke on this body as a source of affliction, and the verses on its arising and ceasing like a bubble upon the water. Do not merely grieve and lament according to the way of ordinary people.
Cunda addressed the Buddha:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I truly know that the Tathāgata’s entry into parinirvāṇa is a skillful means; nevertheless, I am so overcome with grief and distress that I cannot sustain myself.”
The Buddha said to Cunda:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!

You should know that the Tathāgata’s expedient nirvāṇa is like this: you should understand that the Buddha’s sūtras are like traversing a great ocean—whether longevity or non-longevity, the arising of dharmas or the cessation of dharmas, illusory dharmas or expedient dharmas, time or non-time, nature or non-nature—all such things should be fully understood."

Cunda! If you wish to swiftly cross the ocean of the three realms of existence, you should quickly prepare offerings. The various articles of worship brought by devas, humans, and asuras shall now serve as your final offering, enabling all sentient beings to obtain from me the bliss of immovability. You and others have encountered this excellent field of merit; the *dānapāramitā* you have established toward the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, shall—without hindrance—also spontaneously become your own field of merit as a Tathāgata.

At that time, the elder Cunda, desiring to deliver all sentient beings, bowed his head and wept with tears falling like rain; just as when the sun rises and shines upon green tree leaves, their red veins all become visible, so it was with the elder Cunda, whose blood and tears flowed together as he addressed the Buddha:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
We shall now follow your instructions.

However, the profound meaning of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is beyond the capacity of measurement for us ordinary and limited beings; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, but belongs solely to the realm of the wisdom of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

At that time, Cunda, together with his retinue, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and circumambulated him to the right. Having offered incense and scattered flowers as an offering to the World-Honored One, and having also made offerings to Mañjuśrī, he returned to his home because he had prepared the meal.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume One;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Two.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Lamentation.
At that time, the entire earth shook in six ways; the villages, cities, mountains, and seas, even extending to the ten directions, all trembled greatly.

At that time, all sentient beings were filled with great terror; devas, humans, and asuras raised their voices in mournful lamentation. Having prostrated themselves at his feet and completed their offerings, they all simultaneously spoke in verse:
"Homage to the Hero among Men! Have pity on us, now left orphaned and exposed.
We cast ourselves beneath your venerable feet, Gazing up with devotion at your wondrous merits."
Listen as I speak of birth and death, And their manifold, immeasurable sufferings;
Upon hearing this, all gods and humans Will surely give rise to weary detachment.
It is like an orphaned child, Afflicted by illness within his own body.
Though he encountered a skilled physician for treatment, his illness remained undiminished.
Yet the physician suddenly abandoned him midway and departed for another land;
we and all others are likewise in such wretched suffering.
Having just begun to receive the treatment of skillful means for the various heterodox afflictions and views,
the World-Honored One, the Great King of Physicians, will suddenly abandon me and depart.
I am like a destitute and sick child who, having lost his physician, has no one to rely upon.
Alas! This world, from this day forth, shall be forever desolate.
It is like a kingdom in chaos that has further lost its wise and enlightened ruler;
how lamentable it is for all devas and humans, who shall now be beset by the calamities of rākṣasas.
Just as in an age of famine when grain is scarce, The people suffer the pain of hunger;
Alas for all devas and humans, Forever losing the taste of the nectar of immortality!
It is like a great fire breaking out, Where living beings are all burned to death.
Alas, all you gods and humans! The evil realms burn forevermore.
Alas, all you gods and humans! You undergo great suffering through the long night;
you revolve in the stream of birth and death like an elephant mired in deep mud.
Alas! Today these gods and humans, with blood flowing from their bodies, are filled with sorrow and grief; their longing and devotion are such as this.
Even though the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa, his deeds and practices remain difficult to fathom.
The sun and moon are hidden by heavy clouds, and the light of wisdom perishes from this point on.
Alas for the multitudes of devas and humans, dwelling in the darkness of the long night!
Therefore, they harbor sorrow and suffering that cannot be described by any worldly thing.
Beholding the body as having nothing to delight in, one wishes to cast it away like spittle;
not desiring to remain forever in the world, one hears the sound of the Buddha’s nirvāṇa.
We pray only that the Honored One of Great Wisdom will remain in the world to preach the nectar of the Dharma.
"When the clouds disperse, the sunlight appears, and all deep darkness is utterly extinguished;
so too the sun-like light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom forever dispels the obstacles of birth and death.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"O bhikṣus! Do not grieve, lament, or weep like ordinary worldlings and devas; you should instead apply yourselves with diligent effort to uphold the true Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, maintaining it with focused mindfulness and steadfast practice."

At that time, when the devas, humans, asuras, and others had heard the Buddha preach the Dharma to the bhikṣus, their hopes and requests were severed and they endured the pain of their grief and longing. It was like a filial son and a compassionate mother who have recently lost [a loved one]; having escorted them to the grave for the final farewell, they suppress their sorrow and distress with great effort.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"You all should open your minds; such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma.
Each of you return to your seats and listen attentively to what I shall say."
Gather your mind and do not be negligent; maintain the pure precepts;
settle all distracted thoughts, and skillfully protect your own mind.
"Furthermore, O bhikṣus!

If there are any doubts, you should all ask them now—whether regarding emptiness or non-emptiness, permanence or impermanence, refuge or non-refuge, dependence or non-dependence, eternity or non-eternity, sentient beings or non-sentient beings, reality or unreality, truth or untruth, nirvāṇa or non-nirvāṇa, the secret or the non-secret, the duality of dharmas or their non-duality. Whatever doubts you have among these various kinds of dharmas, you should all ask them now; I shall explain them for you accordingly, and I shall open for you the gate of the Deathless before leading you to parinirvāṇa. Therefore, each of you should now ask according to what is currently in your minds.
Why is this? The appearance of a Buddha is difficult to encounter;

a human body is difficult to obtain; and to attain faith is likewise difficult. To be free from the eight states of no-leisure and to be fully endowed with the precepts is even more difficult—just like seeking golden grains amidst the sands of the Ganges, or like the udumbara flower.
Furthermore, bhikṣus!

The hundred grains, medicinal herbs, trees, and all manner of precious treasures all emerge from the earth, and all sentient beings rely upon them for their growth and development. In this same way, the Tathāgata gives birth to the various sublime and wondrous nectar-like dharmas, and sentient beings thereby nourish and develop their *dharmakāya*. Therefore, bhikṣus, you should ask whatever doubts you have; the Tathāgata will fully explain the definitive meaning for you before entering *nirvāṇa*, so as to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the Tathāgata was definitively entering nirvāṇa, their hearts were filled with grief and terror, and the hair on their bodies stood on end. It was as if the rising sun shone upon green leaves, causing their red veins to become fully visible; likewise, their entire bodies and all their limbs were covered in a mingling of blood and tears. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent!
“World-Honored One!

It is well that you have preached the teaching of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. Just as among all the tracks of living beings, the track of the elephant is supreme, so too, World-Honored One, the perception of impermanence is the foremost among all perceptions. By diligently practicing it, one can become detached from all craving for the realm of desire, craving for form, and craving for existence; ignorance and arrogance will thereby be extinguished forever.”
Furthermore, World-Honored One!

It is like a farmer who, during the autumn months when the grass and grain have not yet ripened, deeply plows his field; thus, when he plants the five grains in spring, weeds and impurities do not arise. In the same way, when a practitioner deeply contemplates the perception of impermanence and practices it with diligent effort, they are able to leave behind all craving for the realm of desire (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*), craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*), and craving for existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*); ignorance and arrogance will never arise again.
Just as a farmer considers autumn plowing to be the most important task, so too, within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, the perception of impermanence is foremost.

Furthermore, it is like a sovereign who, knowing his life is about to end, grants a general amnesty to all prisoners and those in confinement throughout the realm, ensuring they all receive liberation before he passes away.

Today the World-Honored One is likewise; as he approaches his final passing, he preaches the Dharma of ambrosia to benefit and bring profit to sentient beings, so that they may all be liberated from the prison of craving before he enters *nirvāṇa*.
Just as a person possessed by an evil spirit attains liberation upon encountering a master of incantations,

so too do sentient beings possessed by the rākṣasa of craving and attachment fortunately receive the Great Incantation of the Tathāgata’s Noble Wisdom, thereby escaping all the malevolent rākṣasas of affectionate love.
Just as a person suffering from malaria is completely freed from their painful affliction upon meeting a skilled physician and medicine,
so too have we— possessing immeasurable physical ailments, wrong views, and afflictions— been granted healing through the Dharma-medicine of the World-Honored One.

Just as a person intoxicated by wine fails to distinguish between kin and stranger, noble and base, elder and younger, yet upon later regaining sobriety feels shame and remorse, deeply reproaching himself;
so it is with us: within the boundless cycle of birth and death, we were drunk on sensual desires and deluded by false views, until now we have finally attained awakening.
"Just as the reed and the eranda tree have no core of solidity, so too is this body; the self, the person, and the life-span are likewise devoid of any firmness.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you cultivate the perception of non-self in this manner?"
The bhikṣus replied:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
We constantly cultivate the perception of non-self, and others likewise cultivate the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.”
“World-Honored One!
Just as people say that the sun, moon, stars, mountains, and earth revolve, yet this is not actually revolving;

it is only because sentient beings are deluded that they call it revolving—so too, when people speak of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, one should know that these sentient beings are likewise deluded by worldly conventions. What we cultivate is the cultivation of equality.”
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Regarding the analogy you have spoken, you still do not understand the flavor or the meaning explained within this parable; I shall explain it further for you."

It is like when people say that the sun, moon, mountains, or earth are moving; this is not actually movement, but rather a visual illusion they perceive as movement. In the same way, sentient beings, out of ignorance and perversion, conceive of a self, permanence, pleasure, and purity. However, for those Buddhas, "self" refers to the meaning of the *dharmakāya*, "permanence" refers to the meaning of the *dharmakāya*, "pleasure" refers to the meaning of *nirvāṇa*, and "purity" refers to the meaning of all phenomena as mere designations.
"O bhikṣus, do not harbor deluded thoughts by saying, 'I have cultivated the perceptions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity regarding all phenomena.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“We also practice three kinds of cultivation for purification.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“These three kinds of cultivation within my Dharma also lack true meaning. Because the nature of intermittent painful cultivation fluctuates between rising and falling, there arise the inversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure, the inversion of perceiving pleasure as suffering, the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the inversion of perceiving the permanent as impermanent, the inversion of perceiving what is not-self as self, the inversion of perceiving the self as not-self, the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure, and the inversion of perceiving the pure as impure. Those who possess such four inverted perceptions do not recognize equality; the cultivation they practice is not right cultivation.”

To cultivate what is suffering as not suffering, to cultivate the impermanent as permanent, to cultivate what is non-self as self, and to cultivate the impure as pure—these four modes of cultivation pertain to the worldly notions of pleasure, permanence, self, and purity. Beyond the worldly, there are likewise four kinds of pleasure, permanence, self, and purity;
you should know that the "name and flavor" are worldly dharmas, while the "meaning" is the supramundane dharma.
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How should we practice, as the World-Honored One has taught, regarding the three perceptions and the vision that overcomes the four perversions?”

We only pray that the Tathāgata will remain in the world for one kalpa, or even longer than a kalpa; as the World-Honored One has instructed us, we shall practice accordingly. If the Tathāgata does not remain in the world, how could we long share the same dwelling with poisonous snakes while remaining forever separated from the Tathāgata?
"Who shall remain in the world to uphold the True Dharma?
We should follow the Tathāgata into Nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak such words; do not speak such words.

Monks, you should know that the Tathāgata has entrusted the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa. Mahākāśyapa shall serve as a place of refuge for you all, and he shall universally protect and deliver all sentient beings no differently than the Buddha."
"Monks, you should know!
Just as when a great king governs various kingdoms, if he wishes to travel to another land, he must first appoint a chief minister to oversee state affairs as if the king were still present;
I am likewise doing so, for I shall soon establish Mahākāśyapa here in this world."

"However, O bhikṣus, that which you have previously practiced—the notions of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—is not true practice. It is like a group of merchants in the spring month who, during a festive gathering, were playing by the water's edge when one among them lost a lapis lazuli gem, which fell to the bottom of the deep water. At that time, each of the merchants entered the water to search for the treasure; some found tiles, stones, or sunken wood and, thinking these were the treasure, joyfully brought them out, only to realize they were not the real thing.

That lapis lazuli gem remained as before in the water, its radiant color penetrating and illuminating more brightly than the sun and moon. When the people saw the light, they knew it was a famous treasure and marveled at its rarity, each desiring to obtain it. Then, there was one man of skillful wisdom and expedient means who succeeded in obtaining the true treasure."
"Thus it is, bhikṣu!

Regarding all that is suffering, empty, impermanent, and impure, you conceive the notion of exhaustion and claim, 'I am practicing,' just like that person who holds what is not a jewel in his hand and deceives himself."
"You, bhikṣus!
Do not like that man who merely deceives himself; you should instead be like the merchant who possesses wisdom.
Bhikṣus!"
You should know that there is a self, permanence, pleasure, and purity; all that you have cultivated and grasped is inverted, like those who fail to recognize a lapis lazuli jewel.
"O bhikṣus, cultivate the dharma of true reality as if you had obtained a precious jewel; regarding unreal dharmas, cultivate the perception of impermanence.
The bhikṣus said:
"As the World-Honored One has taught:"
"All dharmas are entirely without self; one should practice in this way.
When one practices in this way, the notion of a self is extinguished; once the notion of a self has been extinguished, one proceeds directly toward Nirvāṇa."
"What is the meaning of this?
We only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will explain it further.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent, monks!”
If you wish to eliminate the delusion of self, you should ask in this manner.

For example, suppose there is a king who is dull-witted and of little wisdom, and there is a physician who is likewise not discerning; this physician deceives the world while receiving the king’s stipend. He knows only the medicinal use of milk, yet lacks skill in its application, and he constantly treats patients with it. Furthermore, the people do not know what is appropriate for diseases of wind, phlegm, or spittle, yet the dull-witted king considers him a supreme physician.
At that time, there was a skilled physician who was proficient in the eight branches of medical science;
coming from a distant land, he said to the former physician, "You shall be my teacher and I shall be your disciple; I must study under you."
The former physician said: "Excellent!
I shall teach you the method for the medicine of immortality; you must study diligently for forty-eight years so that you may fully master this unsurpassed medical art."
He then took the latter physician in and out of the royal palace, and the dull-witted king also grew fond of him.
That latter physician then addressed the king, saying:
"Great King!..."
"One should study all arts and crafts.

The king was greatly delighted and accepted the instruction; as his wisdom gradually increased, he realized that the former physician was ignorant and deceitful, so he drove him out of the country and showed even greater respect to the latter physician.
Later, when that physician knew the time had arrived, he again addressed the king, saying:
"I wish to make a request; please grant it according to my wishes.
The king replied:
"Yes," the physician said,
"Great King!"
"The former physician’s milk medicine is poisonous, harmful, and dangerous; it must no longer be administered, and this practice should be abandoned.
The king then followed these instructions and issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom: "Henceforth, anyone who administers milk medicine shall be severely punished."
At that time, the latter physician used five kinds of medicines—the five flavors of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent—to treat all ailments.
Then, when the king fell ill and invited a physician to treat him, the physician examined the king’s condition and saw that milk medicine should be applied; he then addressed the king, saying:
"Only milk medicine can ensure that you do not die."
The king said to the physician,
"Are you now mad?
Previously you said this was poison and told me to expel it, yet now you say that I should take the medicine of milk."
The physician replied later, "No,
Great King!"

These words have a specific meaning. For example, suppose there is a mark on a wooden plank gnawed by insects that resembles the name of a king; one unskilled in writing might take it for a genuine character, whereas one skilled in writing would know it is not real.

It is the same with the former physician: although he prepared a medicinal decoction of milk, he did not know how to distinguish the appropriate timing. One should know that a milk medicine can either kill a person or not kill them. When a cow is raised for its milk in a wilderness free of poisonous plants, where she drinks from selected waters, is not subjected to whips or sticks, and moves in and out at the proper times—if, when her milk is drawn, no froth or bubbles arise, one should know that this milk cures all diseases and serves as the medicine of immortality.
The king said,
"Very well," and immediately took the milk medicine.
At that time, the people of the kingdom, hearing that the king had taken the milk, were all struck with terror and came before the king, saying:
"Is this master perhaps a ghost?
Previously he spoke of killing people, and now he has caused Your Majesty to take back the medicinal milk."

At that time, the king extensively explained to the people the benefits and risks regarding the consumption of milk. The king and the people increased their reverence and made offerings to the latter physician, adopting his methods and constantly taking the medicinal milk.
“Bhikṣus, you should know!

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—the Great King of Physicians—has appeared in the world for the purpose of destroying the heterodox and false medical arts of others. Having gradually become familiar with the King of Beings and having understood his inclinations, he taught him to abandon the heterodox and false attachments, saying to him:
‘There is no self, no sentient being, no life-span; these are like letters carved by insects. It is because the various followers of other paths cling to a self that they speak of “no-self.”’”

"All sentient beings, receiving the words of the Tathāgata, teach one another in succession, all proclaiming non-self. This is because the Tathāgata, knowing the proper time and employing skillful means to deliver sentient beings, declares that the nature of all phenomena is non-self; it is not like the 'self' as conceived by worldly people, and thus he says that the nature of all phenomena is non-self."

At that time, he further spoke of the "self," just as that skilled physician who understands the methods of medicinal milk explained it: "One should know that this 'self' is real; the self is eternal, not subject to change or decay. The self is virtue; the self is sovereign. Just as the physician skilled in medicinal milk, so too does the Tathāgata preach the true Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; all members of the fourfold assembly should train themselves accordingly.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you have any doubts regarding the various laws and teachings, you should ask the Tathāgata.
The bhikṣus said:
“Yes, World-Honored One!
We have already cultivated that which is supreme among all cultivations, and we understand and know that the characteristics of the body are entirely empty and quiescent.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Do not speak as you have, following the words of the All-Knowing One, saying: 'I cultivate all bodily marks as being entirely empty and quiescent.
Furthermore, he addressed the bhikṣus:
'If you still have doubts regarding the Dharma and Vinaya, you should ask further.'"
The bhikṣus said:
“World-Honored One!
The meaning of equality of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is not within our sphere; how could we dare to ask again?”

The teachings spoken by all Buddhas are inconceivable, and the practices performed by all Buddhas are inconceivable; therefore, we and this entire assembly are all unable to pose further questions to the Tathāgata.
“World-Honored One!

It is as if there were a person one hundred and twenty years old, afflicted by a chronic illness and lying prostrate upon a bed. A certain man, lacking wisdom yet possessing immeasurable wealth, comes to his side, takes the sick man’s hand upon the bed, and says to him:
‘Good son!...’”
"You should take possession of my precious storehouse; I wish to travel elsewhere to another country for ten or twenty years. When I return later, it shall all be restored to me."

At that time, the patient had neither children nor kinsmen; as his illness grew increasingly severe, he passed away, and the wealth he had entrusted was entirely lost. Later, when the owner of the wealth returned wishing to seek it back, he did not know where it was.
Thus the World-Honored One has spoken to us, saying: "If there is anything you doubt regarding the various laws and teachings, you should now all ask about it.
Yet, if we were to allow the śrāvakas to question the Tathāgata, we fear that this True Dharma would not endure for long;
furthermore, we do not know what should be asked so as to enable all sentient beings to receive its blessings.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
We are currently unable to endure further questioning.
It is as if there were a man whom a physiognomist predicted would live for one hundred and twenty years, possess a complete circle of kinsmen, and enjoy immeasurable wealth.
Furthermore, suppose another person comes and says to that man:
"I have wealth and treasures which I now entrust to you; you should manage them for me to generate profit and interest, and after ten or twenty years, return them all to me."
"At that time, the man would take those goods and generate profit from them; when the owner later came to reclaim them, he would return them all.
In the same way, World-Honored One, it is impossible for the Venerable Ānanda and the other śrāvakas to preserve the Dharma-treasury taught by the Tathāgata so that it might endure forever."
Why is this? Because it concerns the Śrāvaka vehicle.

Only the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, such as Kāśyapa and others, should be permitted to inquire and receive [this teaching]; they are capable of upholding the Tathāgata’s treasury of Dharma for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, so that all sentient beings shall receive its blessings.
"Therefore, World-Honored One!
You should cause the Bodhisattvas to resolve their doubts for the sake of sentient beings; this is not something that we, who are of ordinary caliber, are capable of undertaking.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Excellent! Excellent! You, bhikṣus!"
Having attained the untainted dharmas and become an Arhat, you are thus able to make this true statement and deeply understand my intention.

There are two causes and conditions by which a Bodhisattva should uphold the True Dharma, enabling the treasury of the Mahāyāna teachings to endure for a long time and allowing all sentient beings to receive its blessings.
Chapter 5: On Longevity. From the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Five: On Longevity. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the entire great assembly:
"O sons and daughters of good family!
"Regarding any doubts you may have concerning these three dharmas and the various teachings of the Vinaya, you should now all ask about them.
This was said three times.

At that time, among those in the assembly was a Bodhisattva from the village of Nāla, of the Kāśyapa clan and of Brahmin descent. Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes and bared his right shoulder, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him a hundred thousand times, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and having finished making offerings of celestial incense and flowers, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a question; I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will explain it for me.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kāśyapa, saying:
“The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, grants you leave to ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

All that I have asked is due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata and also because of the roots of goodness of all sentient beings. Today, the Tathāgata has as his retinue the four great assemblies of noble ones, the various great lions, the various Vajra-holders, and the great ocean of wondrous wisdom; the Bodhisattvas in this assembly have all fully accomplished immeasurable merit. With such a multitude as his retinue, if we ordinary and inferior beings wished to ask questions, we would be unable to do so without being sustained by the Tathāgata’s spiritual power. Therefore, that I now venture to ask these questions should be known to be entirely through the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he asked in verse:
"By what cause does one obtain long life And a vajra-like indestructible body?
How should one uphold the profound meaning Of this sūtra?"
When Bodhisattvas transform sentient beings, how many kinds of Dharma do they preach?
What kind of person is capable of this, and is called a true refuge?
Though not an Arhat, their measure is equal to that of an Arhat.
The Tathāgata, the Conqueror of Māra, has taught: how can one discern them?
How does one know the meaning of the Four Noble Truths and the nature of the four perversions—suffering, emptiness, and non-self?
How does one perceive the Bodhisattva, whose nature is as difficult for a Tathāgata to see?
How does one attain full perfection and thoroughly understand the meaning of the "half-syllables"?
How does one skillfully manifest transformations, like a wild goose, a crane, or a śarīka bird?
How does one attain wisdom, like the sun, moon, and the kings of the constellations?
How does one become a bodhisattva? We pray that you will compassionately and definitively explain these various Dharma-gates and their immeasurable, most profound meanings.
"What we ought to know, we have therefore been able to ask;
how could we dare to question the Tathāgata regarding the realm of all Buddhas?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Excellent! Excellent,
son of good family!”
Only by gradually ascending to the Tathāgata’s knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) can one inquire into the meaning of this profound sūtra.

In every direction, there are *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; from the very beginning, they have sat beneath the Bodhi tree in their respective worlds and attained perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) in immeasurable numbers. Originally, while they were bodhisattvas, they attained the path to awakening through a gradual process of realization, all because they inquired into the Tathāgata’s profound treasury of Dharma.
"You all are likewise today; you are able to question me regarding the realm of the knowledge of all modes, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

I am not capable of questioning the Blessed One regarding the realm of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Just as a mosquito cannot fly across the great ocean of space nor drink up its waters entirely, so too am I; I am unable to fathom the profound wisdom of the Blessed One, which is like the great ocean of space, and thereby attain fearlessness.
World-Honored One!

It is just as when a great king possesses a bright pearl within his topknot; its guardian increases his protection of it as if guarding his own crown. I am likewise now asking the Tathāgata about the profound and true Dharma, so that the Tathāgata may explain it extensively and resolve my web of doubts.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Good son! I shall now speak of the karma of long life. When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice this karma, it becomes the cause for Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi). You all should listen attentively and reflect well upon it; hear the root of that practice and explain it extensively for others, so that through this cause they may give rise to Equal Enlightenment."
"Good son!
I too, by practicing those deeds and extensively explaining them to others, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
It is like a great king whose son has committed a crime and is imprisoned; for the sake of his son, he grants a general amnesty to all prisoners to rescue him."

In this way, the Bodhisattva cultivates the karma of long life, regarding all sentient beings as his only child. Toward all sentient beings, he maintains great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity. Upholding the pure precepts, he does not harm sentient beings; he establishes all sentient beings upon the tracks of the five precepts and the ten wholesome karmas. According to their capacities, he rescues those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. To sever the karmic conditions for all evil destinies, he liberates those not yet liberated and delivers those not yet delivered. With firm resolve and mindfulness, he accomplishes the wisdom of skillful means. Through these karmic practices, he attains the fruit of reliance and the fruit of retribution: infinite longevity, the attainment of great and wondrous wisdom, fearlessness, and sovereign mastery. In this manner, the Bodhisattva is forever free from the law of death.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards all sentient beings as if they were his only son.
What is the meaning of this?”
If one says that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regard all sentient beings as their only son, such a thing is impossible.

Why is this? Within the Buddha-dharma, there may be those who violate the precepts, commit the five heinous crimes, or slander the true Dharma; should one cultivate the perception of them as an only son toward all such sentient beings?
The World-Honored One said:
"It is so, Kāśyapa!
I regard all sentient beings as I do Rāhula."
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:

"If that were the case, how was it that once, on the fifteenth day of the month during a great *poṣadha* assembly when the community of monks was pure, there was one who had not yet received full ordination who stealthily entered to listen to the Vinaya? At that time, the Vajrapāṇi, perceiving the Buddha’s divine intent, took up his vajra-pestle and crushed him into dust."
"How is it that you regard all beings equally as your own children?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Do not speak such words. That youth was merely a transformation; he was created to clarify that those who commit offenses against the True Dharma must be expelled, so as to solemnize the future and cause those who harbor thieving intentions, as well as the Icchantikas whose evil minds lie latent, to be restrained."
Just as a king’s ministers seize those who have committed offenses and punish them according to their crimes, so too does the Buddha:
he uses reason to penalize those who destroy the Dharma, causing those who have committed evil to see for themselves the retribution for their sins.

The Tathāgata constantly comforts sentient beings with the radiance of his own body, so that they are neither terrified nor harmed; yet even if there are sentient beings who die without receiving this radiance, the Tathāgata does not abandon his great compassion toward them.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
If you are able to skillfully understand the subtle and secret meaning of the Tathāgata, I shall now speak further.
For example, Kāśyapa!

In another place, there were certain bhikṣus who maintained pure precepts, whose moral conduct was uniform, and whose deportment was complete; however, the Tathāgata in that region had already entered parinirvāṇa, and the community of bhikṣus lacked anyone to sustain them. Because that assembly of monks was without a Great Teacher, those who lacked the Path troubled the bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a king who cherished the Buddha-dharma; he either executed those evil persons or banished them from the country. Because he established the True Dharma by expelling those evildoers, he obtained immeasurable merit.
Why is this? Because their grave transgressions are punished so that the Great Dharma may be established.

Furthermore, just as one must swiftly cut down various poisonous trees in a household, so too within this Dharma, those who violate the precepts and disrupt the teaching—like harmful masters or slaves—must all be expelled. Know that if they are not expelled, such persons remain far from my Dharma; if they are expelled, they are my true disciples.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"For this reason, it is not the case that all sentient beings are equal as one's only son; the statement that one regards them with equanimity whether they are smeared with sandalwood paste or cut with a blade is contradictory."
"If it is said that the Tathāgata disciplines those who destroy the Dharma, how can such a principle exist?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose there were a king’s minister, a householder, or a lay devotee who had a son who was handsome, intelligent, and wise, peerless in the world and beloved by all. His father took the son to a teacher's gate to study various arts and crafts, and addressed the teacher, saying:"

"Although this son of mine was born with merit and physical excellence, he has not yet learned any arts or skills. I must have him taught so that he may surely achieve success; if he does not follow the proper method, I shall diligently apply the cane. Even if three of my four sons were to die from the cane while studying under you, there remains one son who must still be strictly disciplined. I would have no regrets as long as he is made to achieve success."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"What do you think?
If parents or a teacher should instruct their child with such severity that it even leads to the loss of life, would the parents or the teacher incur the offense of killing?"
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“No, World-Honored One.”

"Because he loves his son and desires him to achieve success, although he inflicts the punishment of the rod, he has no intent of hatred or harm; his merit is immeasurable, and there is no sin of killing.
Thus it is, good son!"

The Tathāgata is likewise: toward those who destroy the Dharma or violate the precepts, he regards them as his own children with compassionate pity and instructs them, desiring to bring them to fulfillment despite their destruction of the Dharma and violation of the precepts; it is therefore no fault for him to discipline them strictly.

Therefore, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas regard all sentient beings as their only child, cultivating such a mind of impartial samādhi and harboring no malice, this constitutes the karma for a Bodhisattva’s longevity and mastery over wisdom.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one regards all sentient beings as being like an only son, will a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who practices this perception attain long life?"
The Buddha said, “It is so.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will not speak of this matter, for it is like the dual speech of a child at play.
World-Honored One!

It is as if a child at play, in the midst of a great assembly, were to praise and speak of various offerings made to his parents, yet upon returning home, he would instead act with rebellion and lack of filial piety, distressing his two parents and failing to repay their kindness and nourishment."

The World-Honored One is likewise in this regard: you have stated that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards all sentient beings with the thought of them being as one's only son; by virtue of this merit, they attain long life, sovereign wisdom, and abide eternally in deathlessness. Yet now, the World-Honored One possesses a lifespan like that of ordinary humans. Could it be that throughout incalculable kalpas, the World-Honored One has constantly harbored thoughts of swords and blades toward all sentient beings?
How strange it is, World-Honored One!
To undergo such a fruit of harming sentient beings as a short lifespan, equal to the hundred-year life span of worldly people—this is not even the case for a bodhisattva, let alone for a Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"Do not utter such coarse words before the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
O son of good family!"

One should know that the Tathāgata’s longevity is immeasurable; one should know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma; one should know that the Tathāgata is not a subject to transformation; one should know that the Tathāgata is not a subject to extinction.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How can it be known that the Tathāgata is long-lived?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Just as the eight great rivers of Jambudvīpa and all its springs and streams flow entirely into the ocean without ever reaching exhaustion, one should know that the great ocean is the vessel for these springs and streams."

The Tathāgata is likewise; the lifespans of all devas and worldlings all return to the great ocean of the Tathāgata’s lifespan. For this reason, one should know that the lifespan of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!
Just as space is eternally abiding and unchanging, so too is the Tathāgata eternally abiding.

Just as the medicinal drug of clarified butter (sarpis) is cool and refreshing and can eliminate feverish afflictions, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, constantly employs the cool and refreshing medicinal dharma of clarified butter to extensively remove all sufferings and calamities for sentient beings; therefore, the Tathāgata eternally abides in coolness, free from all suffering and affliction.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If the Tathāgata’s lifespan were indeed immeasurable and long, and if you wish to bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, then today the World-Honored One should remain in the world for one kalpa or even more than one kalpa, raining down the cool water of the Dharma universally upon all beings.”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and remain in the world.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Do not conceive the thought that the Tathāgata has reached extinction. If even bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and followers of other paths who possess five virtues can remain for a kalpa or more than a kalpa, walking upon the void and sitting or lying down with ease, emitting fire from their left side and water from their right side, producing smoke from their bodies, making their own bodies infinitely large or entering the most minute spaces—possessing these five virtues, they attain such sovereign spiritual powers. How much more so for the Tathāgata, who has accomplished all immeasurable merits; could it be that his power is unable to remain in the world for a kalpa or more than a kalpa?”

Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding; he is neither a subject to change nor a subject to extinction. You should know that this body is not a body sustained by impure food; it is a manifested body within this world, like a poisonous medicinal tree, which I shall now relinquish.

"Therefore, Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternally abiding; it is neither a subject to transformation nor a subject to extinction. I have extensively taught this for the sake of others.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the difference between the mundane and the supramundane?
The Buddha says that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, yet worldly people also say they are eternally abiding.”

I, of the Kāśyapa clan, declare that our former teacher Brahmā possesses an eternal spirit that wanders to and fro; if the Tathāgata were likewise eternally abiding, there would be no perceived distinction between worldly dharmas and supramundane dharmas.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose, for example, there is an elder who has a milch cow which he entrusts to a cowherd to raise and feed. He places it in a vast wilderness where there is no poisonous grass, not tethering it in the same stall with the herd of cattle; he protects and nourishes it, desiring to obtain fine ghee to provide for his kinsmen."
Before long, that man passed away, and the cowherd died shortly thereafter. At that time, a wild man wandering through the marshland found this milch cow;

he milked her to provide for his own livelihood. Desiring to make curds and butter, he did not know the proper method: he used a worn-out vessel and the temperature was unsuitable. Consequently, he failed to produce either curds or butter, and instead ruined the quality of the milk. The spoiled milk became thick and turbid, and he mistook it for curds and butter; perceiving it as such, he took it and ate it.

The ignorance of sentient beings is likewise so. The pure moisture of the True Dharma and its profound, vast, and wondrous meaning have now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa—just as when the master of the oxen has died. Those sentient beings dwelling in the wilderness of saṃsāra are like those wild folk who, using worldly wisdom, form perverted conceptions regarding the pure moisture of the Buddha’s True Dharma and its discipline, saying: "There exist sentient beings, a self, a person, and a life-span; this is liberation; this is eternal birth."

These sentient beings are shrouded by false delusions; they do not recognize liberation, nor do they recognize the eternal abiding. They cultivate various heterodox views and fail to attain the essential way out. They remain far removed from the true reality, the moral discipline, and the sphere of practice. Not knowing that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma, they are like ignorant country folk who, failing to obtain cow’s milk with its five seasonal flavors, claim to be eating ghee while actually obtaining not even a single flavor among those five.

They merely cling to worldly notions of Brahmā and creation, asserting that this is eternal, that this is the self, and that this is liberation. Because they seek Brahmā, they practice a limited form of pure conduct—abstaining from sexual misconduct and dutifully supporting their parents—and thus they occasionally gain birth in heaven with natural, blissful food, much like those country folk consuming spoiled milk.
"Good son!

Worldly pure conduct consists of making offerings to one's parents without knowing the Three Refuges; you should know that the fruit of this is not eternal. Although by making offerings to one's parents and refraining from sexual misconduct and so forth, one may attain something like the transformations of a Buddha, these are merely impermanent, husks of worldly dharmas. Only the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and never extinguished."
Therefore, son of good family,
you should employ skillful means to abandon all doubt and diligently contemplate that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma.
Furthermore, son of good family:
At that time, a rustic man was tending those milk cows when it happened that a Wheel-Turning Sage King appeared in the world.

According to the law of a Wheel-Turning King, he ought to possess milk cows; by the power of the King’s virtue, the rustic man was made to abandon the cows and go on his way, and the cows went spontaneously to the presence of the Wheel-Turning Sage King’s minister in charge of the treasury.

The Minister of the Treasure-Treasury knew that this milch cow would surely yield milk of five-seasonal essence; he was certain it was the response to the merit of a holy king. It is likewise when the Buddha, the Dharma King, appears in the world:

just as that milch cow’s ordinary worldly sounds are transformed into the voice of the Tathāgata’s eternal Dharma, so too do the vulgar and the common folk, having been subdued and dispersed, abandon the cow. Once the sound of the milch cow of the eternal Dharma has departed from them, it proceeds before the precious minister who is the disciple of the Tathāgata. By the power of the merit of sentient beings, the milch cow of the eternal Dharma yields milk of constant fragrance.

Therefore, good son, you should know that the eternal nature of the Tathāgata is not subject to change; it is something that worldly fools cannot comprehend, and it is only through the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding voice that they can come to understand it.
Those people of the world should think thus:
"The Dharma-sound of permanence is indeed the Tathāgata’s Dharma-sound of permanence.
From this sound, one should know that the Tathāgata is incalculable and immeasurable."
"In this way, good sons and good daughters!

If you uphold these two characters, 'Tathāgata' and 'Eternally Abiding,' and practice them throughout kalpas, such sentient beings will before long attain the path of Equal and Right Enlightenment, no different from me."
"You, son of good family!
Be careful not to be negligent; constantly cultivate these two characters and uphold them with firm resolve.
Today the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa; this is the fixed law of all Buddhas."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘Dharma’?”
"What is the meaning of 'Dharma'?
I wish to hear what the nature of the definitive Dharma is.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do you now wish to hear about the nature of phenomena (dharmatā)?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha,
"I pray that you will explain it extensively."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is the relinquishing of the body.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"The Discourse on Increasing Doubt Regarding the Sacrifice of the Body.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not hold such a view as to say that the Tathāgata sacrifices his body and then receives another body."
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha,
“I did not ask about receiving a body.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not speak thus, that all phenomena are annihilated.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, consider the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception; how do those sentient beings dwell there, being devoid of the form-aggregate?"
What is death?
What is manifestation?
How do those mental conceptions revolve?
This is the realm of the Buddha; you should inquire about it, and you should also ask me how I receive another body.
If someone were to ask you:
"How do those non-percipient beings experience pleasure while abiding in their physical forms and perceptions?"
"How shall one answer this?
It is simply not within the sphere of experience of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas; it is solely the sphere of activity of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, son of good family!"
The body of the Tathāgata is even more difficult to comprehend than that; it is not within the reach of the spheres of any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or bodhisattvas.
Where does the Tathāgata abide?
How is it manifested?
The inconceivable body of the Tathāgata’s skillful means is not within your realm,
O son of good family!
Regarding me, you should simply hold this thought:

"The Tathāgata is eternally abiding; so too are the Dharma and the Saṃgha. These three things are not impermanent dharmas; they are eternally abiding, unchanging, cool, real, and free from all afflictions and sufferings.
If it were otherwise, those sons and daughters of good family would not fully accomplish the pure Three Refuges."
"One should cultivate the inconceivable, eternally abiding Dharma in this manner. Good son!
For example, where there is this tree, there must be this shadow; if that tree does not exist, then that shadow will also not exist. It is impossible to see the shadow while not seeing the tree."
Thus, since there is a Tathāgata, he must necessarily act as a great tree for all, providing shelter and protection for sentient beings and serving as their refuge;
if the Tathāgata were impermanent, he could not be called an Arhat worthy of offerings, nor would he be the supreme refuge for devas and humans.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One, how is it that the shadows of trees appear in the darkness of night?
The Buddha said:
“There is a shadow. Since the tree exists, how could there be no shadow?
It is simply that it cannot be seen by the physical eye.”
Therefore, you should know that because the Tathāgata exists, he is eternally abiding; he is neither a phenomenon subject to transformation nor a phenomenon subject to extinction.

Just as the shadow of a tree cannot be seen by the physical eye in the midst of darkness, so too, although the Buddha remains eternally abiding and unchanging after his parinirvāṇa, he is likewise not seen by the physical eye.
Yet those deluded thoughts conceive notions of impermanence regarding the Tathāgata.
Good sons, if you, your parents, and those whom you revere should conceive the notion of non-eternality toward the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, then all your three refuges will be impure.
"You should now exhort and instruct them by means of the three dharmas that abide eternally, so that they may attain the name of 'Bodhisattva's Three Refuges' regarding these three dharmas.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

From this day forward, I shall cause my parents, and even those up to the seventh generation of my lineage, to be awakened to the eternal abiding of the Three Jewels—the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—and cause them all to uphold the Dharma of eternal abiding.
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!

These three dharmas are eternally abiding; I shall receive and study them, and extensively expound them for others. If they do not accept this truly wondrous teaching, one should know that such people are deluded regarding impermanence; nevertheless, I shall expound it for them three times every day, causing them to draw near."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!

One should protect and uphold the True Dharma in this manner, and also constantly cultivate the compassionate mind of non-harming. Through the fruit of that non-harming, one shall attain the Bodhisattva’s infinite longevity and mastery over wisdom."
Chapter Six: The Diamond Body. From the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Six: The Diamond Body. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son!

The body of the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding body, the indestructible body, and the adamantine body; it is not a body sustained by impure food. It is the Dharma-body; one should contemplate it in this way.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is not something that can be observed by an ordinary person such as I.”

Why is this? If the Tathāgata were to enter parinirvāṇa, he would be destroying this body—a body of dust, a body of filth, a body sustained by impure food. If the Tathāgata were never to enter nirvāṇa, one should accordingly cultivate the contemplation of equality.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Good son! Do not say that my body is the same as those of worldly people—perishable, fragile, and subject to the cycle of birth and death throughout the long nights of kalpas."
Regarding death: the body of the Tathāgata is an indestructible body; it is not the body of a worldly person, nor the body of a deva, nor a body sustained by impure food.
It is a body that is no-body; it neither arises nor perishes, it does not accumulate nor undergo transmigration, it is boundless and without end.
It is neither wisdom nor conditioned activity, for its intrinsic nature is fundamentally pure.
It is without anything existing and without anything received; it is without coming or going, neither abiding nor moving; it is without savoring and without contact;

it is without consciousness and without thought; it is without equal and without superior; it is not a destination, yet all destinations and the act of going are forever severed, yet it is not a state of annihilation;
it is neither a phenomenon nor a reality; it is neither perception nor ideation; it is neither created at the beginning nor completed at the end; it is without establishment.
It is not fullness; it is not a location, nor a dwelling; it is not cessation, nor quiescence. It is vast purity, free from all afflictions;
it is neither grasping nor defiled attachment, neither contention nor free from contention. Because it is eternally abiding yet non-abiding, it does not submit and does not die.
It is neither dharma nor non-dharma; it is neither a field nor a non-field, and it is inexhaustible.
Neither a bhikṣu nor a non-bhikṣu; free from names, free from praise, free from verbal expression, free from cultivation, and free from thought or aspiration;
neither in union nor in separation; neither measurable nor immeasurable;
neither arrived nor not arrived; neither penetrating nor obstructed; neither possessing marks nor separated from marks—yet adorned with every mark.
Austere, it is neither maintained nor existent, being apart from existence;
it can serve as a field of merit, yet is truly invisible and cannot be demonstrated. It is suchness and ultimate reality;
it delivers all sentient beings without anything delivered, liberates all sentient beings without anything liberated, and purifies all.
Sentient beings are not something to be purified; they cover all sentient beings yet there is nothing that covers them. They instruct sentient beings without duality;

they are equal to the unequaled, equal to the immeasurable, equal to space, equal to the non-localized, equal to the unarisen, equal to non-existence, equal to the peerless, and equal to the detached. They are quiescent, yet their activity is not annihilated.
Non-turning and ultimate, it encompasses all while severing the profound and subtle; it manifests the teaching of non-duality without abandoning its own nature.
It is neither formed nor extended nor short; it is not the aggregates, the elements, nor the sense bases;
it is not the characteristic of the conditioned, nor the state of the unconditioned, nor that which is nurtured. It is neither high nor low; it is not accumulation, nor is it non-accumulation.
Accumulated and stored, it is neither earth nor non-earth; thus, immeasurable and inconceivable merit constitutes the body of the Tathāgata.

There is no one who knows it, no one who sees it, no one who speaks of it, and no one who debates it. It is not comprised within the world; it is neither caused nor uncaused. All conceptualizations, grasping at signs, and even the term "nirvāṇa" cannot serve as its comparison. The perfection of such immeasurable merit is called the body of the Tathāgata.
Thus it is, Kāśyapa!
The physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are not known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; such is the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s body—it is the Dharma-body, not a body sustained by impure food.
How could there be illness, affliction, or decay, as if one were made of fragile pottery?
To those who are to be transformed, the Tathāgata manifests old age, sickness, and death; yet the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is adamantine and indestructible.

Kāśyapa! From this day forward, you should understand this: the body of the Tathāgata is not a body sustained by impure food. It is for the sake of people that I have extensively taught it to be born from sublime causes; it is the Dharma-body, the Vajra-body, and the Body of Purity. You should understand it thus as the eternally abiding Dharma.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Since the Tathāgata’s merits are thus fully perfected, how could there be illness or death?”

"From this day forward, I shall contemplate the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body as eternally abiding, not subject to change, supremely excellent, and tranquil; I shall explain this extensively for the sake of others.
So it is, World-Honored One!"
“The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible like a vajra, yet one does not yet know what its cause is.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“The merit of upholding the True Dharma is its cause.”
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha,
saying, “How does one protect the Dharma?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Those who protect the Dharma do not merely observe the five precepts nor practice the virtuous discipline;

rather, in this evil age, they do not spare their own bodies or lives, but take up sharp weapons to defend the Dharma teachers and those who uphold the precepts—this is what it means to protect the Dharma.”
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
“If a bhikṣu travels and stays together with those who carry weapons, would he not cease to be a bhikṣu?
The Buddha said:
"No," Kāśyapa Bodhisattva replied again to the Buddha,
"this is merely a shaven-headed layman."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Do not speak such words. Why is this? Because..."

If there is one who dwells alone in seclusion practicing the nine dhūta ascetic practices—begging for food, having few desires, remaining silent, meditating, contemplating the body, and walking in meditation—and who also explains to others the causes and effects of the practice of giving, morality, and virtuous deeds, yet cannot widely proclaim fearlessness nor subdue and transform deceitful and evil people, you should know that such a person cannot save themselves nor save others; they merely cultivate the holy life for their own private benefit.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu practices the dhūta austerities and attains fearlessness, he extensively proclaims the ninefold canon—sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, nidāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, and adbhutadharma—to transform sentient beings, thereby delivering himself and others. Moreover, for the sake of others, he explains the essential passages of the sūtras, stating that a certain sūtra declares one must not keep slaves, oxen, horses, livestock, or items contrary to the Dharma; if one were to keep such things, it would not be the way of a renunciant, and such a person would violate the regulations, lose their status as a practitioner, and be expelled.

When those who have violated the precepts hear such a teaching, their factions will become enraged and harm that Dharma master; yet even though he may come to his end, he will still be able to deliver himself and deliver them as well.
Therefore, Kāśyapa,
lay followers who are kings or ministers should protect and uphold the Dharma, and they should also subdue those householders who have shaved their heads.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa:

In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in the world named Nandivardhana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who appeared in the world and likewise resided constantly in this city of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, this world was vast, magnificent, and pure, like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; all its sentient beings were entirely at peace and free from thoughts of hunger or thirst, consisting solely of bodhisattvas.

That Buddha remained in the world for immeasurable billions of kalpas before entering parinirvāṇa; his bequeathed Dharma also remained in the world for immeasurable billions of kalpas, such that for another forty years the Buddha-dharma had not yet perished.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Buddhadatta who appeared in the world, surrounded before and behind by a great assembly of followers. Having attained fearlessness, he preached the Dharma, instructing the bhikṣus with the ninefold scriptures, saying:
"The sūtras state that one must not keep slaves, livestock, or any items that are contrary to the Dharma."
Those who had broken their precepts then gave rise to anger; forming a faction to assist one another, they sought to harm the Dharma Master.

At that time, there was a king named Bakaḍāta who, hearing that those evil men intended to harm the Dharma Master, took up sharp weapons for the sake of protecting the Dharma. He engaged them in a bitter struggle and utterly destroyed the evil men. The king’s body was covered in wounds as he approached the Dharma Master, who then expounded to the king the merits of protecting the Dharma. Having heard the Dharma, the king immediately passed away and was reborn in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha. Those among the king’s retinue who had likewise protected the Dharma passed away in succession and all attained rebirth in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha; those who had given rise to the mind of sympathetic joy all achieved Bodhi.
Buddhadeva soon passed away and was reborn in that land as the foremost disciple of Akṣobhya Buddha; King Bhagadatta became his second disciple.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Was that king at that time anyone else?
It was I myself."
The Dharma Master at that time was Kāśyapa Buddha.

Kāśyapa, you should know that the merit of upholding the True Dharma is immeasurable. Because I formerly protected the True Dharma without begrudging my own body or life, I have attained this indestructible diamond-like Dharma-body.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has taught, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is truly and eternally abiding, not subject to decay or destruction; I believe this with all my heart, as firmly as if it were engraved upon stone.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Therefore, son of good family!

Whether they be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās, you should diligently employ skillful means to protect and uphold the True Dharma, and you should also extensively explain the karmic rewards for protecting the Dharma."

Furthermore, Kāśyapa, a Dharma-preacher who maintains the pure precepts should always protect himself; he must not move about lightly without defensive equipment. If there are lay followers (*upāsaka*) who have not received full ordination but study the Mahāyāna and carry weapons for the sake of protecting the Dharma, he should rely upon such as these as his companions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have already stated that to be in the company of those who carry staves is contrary to the Vinaya.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"After my parinirvāṇa, in this turbid world, due to the high price of grain and the prevalence of pestilence, there will be many and countless instances of those who feign outward forms for the sake of profit and sustenance. At that time, there may be Dharma masters who uphold the precepts and the Vinaya and are fully endowed with dignified deportment, yet they will be driven away, harmed, or even killed by such people.

During such times, these precept-keeping Dharma masters shall travel through various cities, towns, dangerous places, and wildernesses; I permit them to take as companions kings, ministers, forest-dwellers, lay devotees, and even *caṇḍālas*, provided they have not received full ordination but are able to protect the Dharma."
Although those people do not receive the precepts, the merit and karmic fruit of their protection of the Dharma are immeasurable, surpassing even those who have received the precepts.

As for that Dharma Master, he upholds the practice of the precepts with pure deportment; he deeply delights in the Mahāyāna and expounds it extensively for others. He is able to offer fragrant oils, banners, flowers, and ritual implements, mutually presenting them to kings, ministers, and elders, yet without ever violating or losing the conduct of a śramaṇa; such a person is called a Dharma Master who maintains the precepts.
To uphold the true Dharma within oneself like a great ocean and to be complete in one’s dignified deportment is called upholding the precepts (*śīla*).

Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts yet takes no pleasure in happiness, finds no joy in reputation, and feels aversion toward gain and offerings; if one constantly preaches to others on having few desires and being content with little—yet in such cases, one’s own benefit diminishes and one’s followers are displeased, this is not called being a Dharma Master.
To give rise to thoughts of weariness and distaste toward one’s own disciples, and thus to ruin one’s own following, is also called destroying the Sangha.

“There are three kinds of Saṃgha: the Saṃgha that violates the precepts, the Saṃgha of the ignorant, and the pure Saṃgha. Among these three, one may destroy the Saṃgha that violates the precepts and the Saṃgha of the ignorant, but one cannot destroy the pure Saṃgha.”

Regarding "monks who violate the precepts": foolish ordinary persons who follow those who violate the precepts, who do not examine one another and yet join together for the sake of greed and corruption—these are called monks who violate the precepts;
even those who themselves are able to maintain the precepts are likewise reckoned among the number of those who violate the precepts.
Regarding such monks who engage in conduct that ought not to be practiced, if one can transform these practitioners of unrighteousness, they are called a Dharma Master.
