As for the ignorant monks—those who habitually practice non-action, possess dull faculties, and are foolish—even if they obtain offerings to provide for themselves and their retinues, each acts independently without living in harmony with others; even in the *pravāraṇā* and *poṣadha* ceremonies, they do not associate with those who have transgressed the precepts. If one can transform these ignorant and unrighteous ones, they are called a Dharma Master.

Regarding the Sangha of Dharma and Vinaya: such a community cannot be thwarted or destroyed by hundreds of thousands of Māras; since the nature of the Bodhisattva Sangha is eternally pure, these two kinds of Sangha are the Teacher.

A Vinaya master who upholds the precepts while having transgressed them is one who skillfully teaches others, knowing the proper time, and knowing what is grave and what is light; such a person does not sever that which is non-Vinaya, nor do they sever what is appropriate, acting in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
What is meant by "skillfully teaching with knowledge of the proper time"? Those to be taught may be either bodhisattvas or the ignorant and simple-minded.

If the teacher is a bodhisattva, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, they do not examine whether it is the right or wrong time, nor whether there is anything remaining or not; whether it is an allowance or a prohibition, they act according to what is appropriate. Whether staying or traveling freely among villages or cemeteries, because their heart is set on protecting the Dharma, they commit no transgression—except for the houses of actors, widows, prostitutes, and young maidens, which are places where those training in the Śrāvaka path should not go. Aside from these, a bodhisattva who protects the Dharma may come and go and circulate through all other places throughout the entire day without fault; this is called a Dharma Master who teaches with knowledge of the proper time.

To know what is grave means that if one sees the original circumstances for which the Tathāgata established the precepts, and yet violates them with a mind of negligence—even regarding the four pārājika offenses—one is no longer called a renunciant; this is called knowing what is grave.

To know what is light means: if one sees that for each specific causal origin (*nidāna*) of an offense, the transgression of a light precept is not regarded as grave by the mind, or if one reflects upon it oneself and realizes that, according to the Tathāgata’s rules, the matter of the offense is incomplete, this is called knowing what is light.

Regarding "not severing what remains in the Vinaya": if one possesses slaves or other impure things, these remain within the Vinaya and should not be severed; one should always refrain from disputing with those who have committed offenses. This is called "that which is not Vinaya and should not be severed."
Although it is not the Vinaya itself, when other sūtras speak in a manner identical to the Vinaya, these too are called "Vinaya" and should not be rejected.

Those who merely follow the literal words are said to "guard the text" without understanding a single character; whereas those who can understand them will attain fearlessness within the sūtras spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods. Such followers of the Buddha’s teaching—profound, vast, and immeasurable—who are able to uphold it, shall attain the inconceivable state of a Tathāgata, the Dharma King.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is inconceivable; the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and not subject to change. I shall uphold this and expound it extensively for others.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
Kāśyapa!

Those who uphold the indestructible Vajra Dharma-body and wish to train in the equal contemplation of the Tathāgata’s body should cultivate the contemplation of the indestructible Vajra Dharma. When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice in this way, they will attain the equal contemplation of the unsurpassed Dharma-body.
Chapter Seven: On Upholding and Retaining the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* "Furthermore, son of good family!

I shall now explain the merit of upholding this profound sūtra. Any sentient beings who hear this sūtra will, in birth after birth, never fall into the four realms of misery; wherever they are born, they will always remain in the presence of the Buddhas."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This sūtra is named 'Mahāparinirvāṇa.

Its beginning is excellent, its middle is excellent, and its end is excellent; it is excellent in meaning and excellent in phrasing, pure, unified, and complete. I shall now speak this diamond-treasury."
"Good son!

Just as the waters of the eight great rivers of Jambudvīpa all flow into the great ocean and are inexhaustible, so too is the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. It extinguishes afflictions, subdues the multitudes of Māras, turns one's back on birth and death, and abandons the transformation body; therefore it is called Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas share this wondrous Dharma, which is without end or limit."

Furthermore, just as in medical science one who possesses subtle and secret techniques is called a great physician, for all prescriptions and medicines are contained therein; so too is the subtle and secret Dharma-treasury taught by the Tathāgata, for all nine divisions of the scriptures are contained within it. Therefore, it is named "Mahāparinirvāṇa."
For example, during the summer months, when one has plowed the fields and sown the seeds, there is constant expectation; yet once the fruit is harvested, all such expectations come to rest.

In the same way, the practitioner constantly maintains expectation while cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) through all the sutras; having studied this sutra, they will swiftly achieve liberation and transcend the existence of the three realms.
Furthermore, good son!

It is like a person with a grave illness who first takes *sarpis* (clarified butter) and then takes medicines of eight kinds of sweet flavors; these medicines are most excellent. In the same way, when sentient beings have the disease of confusion regarding the Buddha’s esoteric teachings, they are gradually taught and transformed by means of the Mahāyāna sūtras, and only thereafter is the eight-flavored medicinal dharma of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* expounded for them.

These eight flavors are: the dharma of permanence, the dharma of quiescence, non-aging, non-death, coolness, emptiness-and-penetration, immovability, and bliss. These eight flavors are called the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
If there are bodhisattvas who abide in this Great Parinirvāṇa, they are constantly able to manifest parinirvāṇa in every place; for this reason, it is called "Great Parinirvāṇa."

If a son of good family wishes to enter parinirvāṇa through the Great Parinirvāṇa, he should train himself in this way: that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, and the Dharma and Saṃgha are likewise so.
If there are good men or good women who practice this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they should study the Tathāgata as eternally abiding.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One!

The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; the wondrous Dharma he expounds is inconceivable; the merit of the Saṃgha is inconceivable; and this sutra is inconceivable. From this day forward, for all those sentient beings whose minds are stubborn and rigid, I shall extinguish for them the ignorance and remaining darkness of birth and death throughout the long night.”
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Two.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Three.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Four Dharmas.
The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa: “Good son!
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes four dharmas, he is able to preach the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra for others.
What are these four?
He is able to be self-restrained and upright; he is able to correct others; he is able to answer according to questions; and he is skillful in understanding causes and conditions.
These are the four dharmas.

As for those who are self-restrained and upright, upon hearing the Buddha’s urgent teaching, they are able to follow it with such revulsion and dread that their body hairs stand on end. As the Buddha has said: "It would be better to embrace a blazing dry tree until one's entire body is scorched and rotten than, while the Tathāgata’s subtle and secret teachings have not yet been realized by one's mind, to hear the doctrine of permanence and immediately give rise to slander, claiming it is the teaching of Māra, worldly discourse, or mere song and praise; whereas one regards as true those who preach impermanence."

One would rather lick a withered tree ablaze with one's tongue than speak of the Tathāgata as being truly impermanent. If one hears others say such things, one should immediately feel alarm and fear, giving rise to thoughts of compassion for the speaker; one should have deep faith that the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata exists eternally and cannot be destroyed by the laws of old age, sickness, or death. One should know that the World-Honored One is inconceivable, and his teaching is likewise so. As I have taught in the *Kūṭadanta Sūtra* and other scriptures, one should properly uphold them; this is what it means for a bodhisattva to be able to maintain self-restraint and correctness.

"One who can correctly guide others is like the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One: there was a woman nursing an infant who came to where the Buddha was; she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, having something on her mind, stood to one side reflecting."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their thoughts, immediately used his own son as an analogy to preach the Dharma, saying:

"Suppose there is a woman who skillfully nurtures her child; at first she places clarified butter on her fingernails for him to suck, and once it has been digested, she gradually increases the amount."
At that time, the woman’s mind was immediately opened and liberated; she then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Great Sage, you know my thoughts and have spoken these words. This morning, I gave much ghee to my child; will it not shorten his lifespan?”
The Buddha said, "No;
this child is already large enough to eat [the meat] without harm.
The woman, filled with joy, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How marvelous, World-Honored One!

You have well expounded the Dharma of conforming to what is digested and what is not digested. For those to be converted, you first speak of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity. If, when a sentient being’s faith is not yet firm, one were to preach the Dharma of eternal permanence to them, it would destroy their faculty of faith, and the constant [poison] would never be digested.”
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, virtuous woman!"

One should train in this way: the initial method for raising a child is to gradually provide food that is easy to digest and soft; once the child has grown up, one may give solid foods that can be digested without harm.

I am likewise: for the sake of my disciples, I first speak of the soft food of impurity, impermanence, suffering, and emptiness. Once their aspiration for the Way has increased and they are capable of receiving the Mahāyāna, I then speak to them of this Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa—the solid food possessing the six flavors of sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and bland. By means of the flavor of bitterness and sourness (impermanence), the flavor of saltiness (non-self), the flavor of suffering (suffering), the flavor of sweetness (joyful bliss), the flavor of blandness (the self), and the flavor of pungency (the Dharma of permanence), I take the fuel of afflictions to ignite the fire of illusory formations, thereby cooking the ambrosial food of the Great Parinirvāṇa Dharma.
Furthermore, good woman!

Suppose there is a sister who, having some business, leaves her home to travel to another village or does not return for a long time. You have two sons: one is purely virtuous and the other is wicked. As she is about to depart, she entrusts a hidden treasure of precious jewels to the virtuous son, without telling the wicked son.
The woman said to the Buddha,
“It is truly so,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked the woman,
"For what reason did the treasure storehouse not speak to its wicked son?
The woman replied to the Buddha:
"That wicked son acts contrary to what is righteous and indulges in heedless conduct, consuming without moderation; therefore, I do not speak to him.
That good son, however, is able to establish the household and bring glory to the clan; for this reason, I entrust it to him."
The Buddha said: "It is so.
My Dharma is likewise:

when I wish to enter the skillful means of parinirvāṇa, I shall entrust all the secret essentials of the Tathāgata’s treasure-store to my disciples, and not to those who have broken the precepts or hold false views."
"Do you now conceive of me as subject to extinction,
or do you conceive of me as eternal?
The woman replied to the Buddha:
"I conceive of the Tathāgata as being eternally abiding.
The Buddha said, "Sister!

As you have said, you should contemplate in this way and not conceive the notion of extinction. You should know that the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, a non-transformative dharma, and a non-perishing dharma. Any sentient beings who cultivate the perception of permanence toward the Tathāgata should know that in each of their successive households there will be a Buddha.
This is called being able to correctly guide others.
Regarding "being able to respond to questions accordingly," it is like someone coming to ask the Tathāgata:
"How may I attain the reputation for great generosity that spreads throughout the world, yet without giving away my wealth?"

The Buddha told the son of good family: "Only one who is pure and simple, who keeps no servants and practices the holy life (brahmacarya), yet delights in giving away slaves, servants, wives, and concubines; who has abandoned the taste of meat yet delights in giving meat; who avoids and does not drink alcohol yet delights in encouraging others to drink it; who always observes the practice of eating at the proper time yet gives food outside of that time; and who is free from perfumes, flowers, ornaments, and vessels, yet gives them all away with perfumes, flowers, and decorative implements—such a person, according to these various acts of giving, returns all merit to themselves as a great donor. If one acts in this way, they shall attain the reputation of a 'Great Donor' throughout the world, without ever having suffered the loss of even a single hair’s breadth of their own wealth."
"Thus, through such analogies, one is able to provide answers according to the questions.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"As the World-Honored One has said, if one who does not eat meat gives meat as a gift, the one who eats it incurs no great transgression; yet would this not increase the heterodox views of outsiders? Therefore, the rule of abstaining from eating meat should be established."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Good son! One who skillfully examines the Buddha’s intention and protects the Dharma should act as a Bodhisattva in this manner. Good son!"
From this day forward, I decree that my disciples shall not eat meat; even if they obtain leftover food, they should always regard it as the flesh of their own son.
How could my disciples ever permit themselves to eat meat?
"The Buddhas have taught that those who eat meat sever the seeds of great compassion.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, why did you permit the eating of the three kinds of pure meat?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"These three kinds of meat were spoken of as a gradual regulation according to circumstances.
Kāśyapa asked again:
“For what reason?
The Buddha said:
“There are nine kinds of acceptance and one should abstain from ten kinds of meat.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This, too, was established through gradual regulation; you should know that it manifests as the present prohibition against eating meat.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, World-Honored One, that you praise fish and meat as fine food?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“I do not say that fish and meat are fine food; I say that sugarcane, non-glutinous rice, rock honey, and various sweet fruits are fine food. Just as I praise various garments as ornaments, yet also praise the three kinds of dyed robes [of the ascetic], you should know that fish and meat are merely foods of filth and stench that accord with craving.”
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the World-Honored One has prohibited the eating of meat, then those five kinds of dairy products, sesame oil, silk, cotton, conch shells, and leather should also not be accepted."
The Buddha said:
"Do not harbor divergent thoughts, nor hold the views of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What should we do now?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Good son! From this day forward, I decree for my disciples that they shall not eat the three kinds of pure meat, nor shall they consume the nine kinds or the ten kinds of meat, nor even a single instance of meat from an animal that died naturally.”

Why is this so? Those who eat meat—whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down—are feared by all sentient beings upon seeing them. When they smell the odor of slaughter, it is like people smelling the scent of *hing-pu* (asafoetida) or garlic; if they enter a gathering, everyone feels loathing. It is the same for those who eat meat: all sentient beings, upon smelling the odor of slaughter, are terrified and fear death. Whether moving in water, on land, or through the air, living creatures all flee in haste upon seeing them. For this reason, a Bodhisattva never eats meat; though he may manifest eating it at times to transform sentient beings, in reality, he does not eat it.
Furthermore, good son!
Long after my parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who, though practicing the Way, will be conceited and say:
"I am a srotāpanna, a sakṛdāgāmin, an anāgāmin, or an arhat."

"In this degenerate age, there will be those who leave the home life out of exile, poverty, or hardship—monks with various false interpretations and mere names—who, for the sake of gain and offerings, show reverence to laypeople; their appearance is haggard like that of herdsmen, and though they wear the *kāṣāya*, they resemble hunters. Craving worldly profit like a cat stalking a mouse, emaciated by illness and afflicted with scabies and leprosy, their bodies are impure; yet they don the robes of the Muni and the noble sages. Their forms are like hungry ghosts, impoverished and shivering with cold; they are not true śramaṇas, yet they bear the likeness of śramaṇas."

In a future age when the True Dharma is in decline, within the sphere of the laws and precepts I have established, people will completely contravene the scriptures and orthodox treatises; each will compose their own sutras, treatises, and codes of discipline, claiming, "My code of discipline regarding the purity of eating meat was taught by the Buddha. They will compose verses and treatises that contradict one another, yet all will claim to be śramaṇas and disciples of Śākyamuni.
Furthermore, noble son!
I have taught that receiving gifts of grain and rice, as well as eating fish and meat, or preparing food with one's own hands, is not pure.
Likewise, engaging in the business of pressing oil, learning various crafts, or working as a carpenter or a leather-worker is not pure.
They travel back and forth to observe the movements of kings and the stars, compose medical prescriptions, study phonology and treatises on sound, and master worldly literary composition;
they keep slaves and accumulate wealth, such as gold, silver, coral, conch shells, jade, precious stones, and various gems;
they raise lions, tigers, leopards, bears, rats, cats, and wildcats; they store poisons and maintain incantations and sorcery, and engage in painting.
The teacher composes written documents; Māluṅkyaputra practices the way of sorcery, using song and dance for deception,
contending in physical strength, staining the teeth, perfuming and anointing the body, wearing flower garlands, and adorning the physical form,
as well as various other such unlawful appearances and unlawful implements and garments— I declare that these are not pure dharmas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If there are lands where meat-eating is prevalent, such that all alms-food is entirely mixed with meat, how should the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās maintain a pure livelihood therein?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa: “Good son!
If food is mixed with meat, one should place it in water so that the food and the meat are separated; only then may it be eaten, and this does not constitute a violation of the Vinaya.”
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If food and meat cannot be separated, what should be done in such a case?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

“Good son! If in a country where meat is constantly eaten, such that meat appears in all food, I permit that one should remove the meat and the broth, destroy its original flavor, and only then eat it. If fish, deer, or other meats are recognizable as such by their own nature, those who eat them incur an offense. Today I declare that for those with specific causes and conditions, I have prohibited the eating of meat; for those without such causes and conditions, through this teaching of the Mahāparinirvāṇa, I likewise prohibit that they should not eat meat.”
This is called being able to provide answers in accordance with questions.
Regarding "one who is skillfully proficient in causes and conditions": if a bhikṣu or upāsaka asks such a question as this:

"Why is it that when the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, first appeared in the world, he did not establish the precepts for his disciples one by one, nor did he explain these Dharma-gates one by one, nor did he fully expound the Prātimokṣa? What is the meaning of this?"
"What is the meaning of *vinaya*? "Good son,
listen as I analyze the meaning of *prātimokṣa*."
The Prātimokṣa consists of having few desires and being content, accomplishing dignified deportment, and not accepting or accumulating much while remaining free from all defiled attachments.

Regarding those who fall from all forms of pure livelihood: they fall into the four evil destinies and the hells to be burned and boiled; such persons, through their lack of deportment, fewness of desires, and failure to refrain from accepting and accumulating, fall from all forms of pure livelihood.
Regarding the term "non-falling": falling into the Avīci hell is what is called "falling.
*Poṣadha* (Uposatha) has two meanings: nourishing and increasing.
*Prātimokṣa* means being free from false teachings.
*Vinaya* refers to subtle instructions for the regulation of deportment; it also means not accepting unrighteous objects and not giving them to others—this is called *vinaya*.

Within it, there are those who commit the four grave offenses (*pārājika*); those who commit the thirteen remaining offenses (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*); those who commit the thirty offenses involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); those who commit the ninety-one offenses of falling (*pāyattika*); those who commit the four offenses requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*); those who commit the various rules of training (*śaikṣadharma*); those who commit the two indeterminate offenses (*aniyata*); and those who commit the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*). There are also those who slander the scriptural teachings and the group of *icchantikas*. For those with such transgressions who do not confess and repent before a wise person, but instead conceal them single-mindedly like a tortoise hiding its six limbs, the sins of violating the precepts increase day and night.
Why is it that the World-Honored One knows there is such an offense yet does not establish a precept, thereby causing those sentient beings to fall into the evil realms?

It is like a person leading a great multitude toward another land and showing them the essential path; if among them someone loses the correct way and proceeds along a wrong path, that wise person pursues and calls them back so they may regain the original, correct road.

The teaching of the Tathāgata is likewise: he first proclaims the direct path; if the bhikṣus subsequently commit many transgressions, he then explains the retribution for such offenses and establishes the precepts for them.

Thus, World-Honored One, you who show the path of the True Dharma and speak of the merits of the ten wholesome actions for the sake of sentient beings; you, the God among Gods, the King of the True Dharma, who universally pities all beings and speaks of the merits of the ten wholesome actions, viewing all beings equally as if they were your only child—if even a single being were in hell, you would remain in that hell for an eon or more than an eon in order to deliver that person and free them from hell. How could you allow a bhikṣu who has violated the precepts to fall long into the evil realms?
It is like a weaver who, after weaving a new garment, repairs it again once it has been torn.

It is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King who initially instructs the people through the ten virtuous actions; later, when the evil conduct of sentient beings increases, he again relies on the divine treasure of the sovereign golden wheel to establish laws and regulations to bring them under control.

The World-Honored One is likewise in this regard: at first, he had not yet established the Prātimokṣa precepts; later, as the offenses committed by the bhikṣus increased, he then took those causes and conditions of transgression as the basis for formulating the prohibitions. Those sentient beings who delight in practicing the Dharma, seeing those originating causes and conditions as testimony, find their faith increase, until they come to contemplate equally the profound and subtle meaning of the Four Noble Truths. Just as the golden wheel of a Cakravartin King possesses sovereign power, so too is the Wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas.

This is the teaching of the Dharma of immeasurable Buddhas; these Buddhas are inconceivable, the teachings they have proclaimed are inconceivable, those who hear this Dharma are inconceivable, and those who can believe in this sutra are also inconceivable—this is called skillfully understanding causes and conditions.

This is for a bodhisattva-mahāsattva to accomplish four dharmas, enabling them to preach the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* for others—preaching both present causes and conditions as well as the causes and conditions of the Great Parinirvāṇa. By means of this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they are well-versed in explaining causes and conditions.

"Regarding 'being self-restrained and upright': it means that having spoken with sincerity, one directs oneself exclusively toward this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*; you should know that this is called being able to be self-restrained and upright."

One who can correctly guide others knows the sincere inclinations of the minds of the bhikṣus and, for their sake, preaches this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, declaring that the Tathāgata exists eternally; you should know that such a person is one who can correctly guide others.

Regarding "answering in accordance with questions": as I have explained to you, Kāśyapa, the subtle and sharp wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, along with their various secret and essential expedient means and esoteric teachings, cannot be fathomed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; that which is called the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—you should know that this is termed "answering in accordance with questions."

According to what is appropriate for the thoughts and mental inclinations of those sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for them; it is not false. For example, it is like a person who gives many names to space—calling it "empty," "void," "non-existent," or "innumerable"—yet all such descriptions are not false. The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is also like this.
"The four kinds of teachings in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* all have their appropriate applications and are not false.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the Tathāgata were to exist eternally, it would contradict the sūtras spoken by the Buddha:"
"Just as when a glowing iron ball is cast into cold water,
its heat gradually dissipates until one knows not where it has gone."
"Through such liberations as these, they cross the abyss of birth and death;
secure, blissful, and forever unmoving, no one knows where they have gone.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“O son of good family!

Do not misinterpret these verses by conceiving the notion that the Tathāgata has entered eternal extinction. It is not as when an iron ball is thrown into water and its heat gradually subsides; the parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is not like that either.”
Just as when an iron ball is thrown into water, its heat is extinguished, so it is with the Tathāgata: his immeasurable afflictions and fetters are extinguished.

Just as when an iron ball is thrown into water, although the fire's power is extinguished, the nature of the iron remains, so too the blazing fires of the afflictions of the Tathāgata over immeasurable kalpas are all completely extinguished; yet the diamond-like nature of the Tathāgata remains eternally, being neither subject to change nor to destruction.

Those who, through such liberations, have crossed the abyss of birth and death—the river of birth, death, and afflictions spanning immeasurable kalpas—have already been delivered by the Tathāgata into nirvāṇa; their place of eternal cessation within the various realms of existence is unknowable.
Therefore it is said:
"Through such liberations as these, they cross the abyss of birth and death;
secure, blissful, and forever unmoving, no one knows where they have gone."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is this so, World-Honored One?

Just as when an iron ball is cast into water and its heat is extinguished, it can still be placed back into fire; [yet why is it that for others, once the roots of goodness are severed, they cannot be restored?]"

Although the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa is in truth eternally abiding, he intentionally enters into the boundless raging fires of birth and death for the sake of sentient beings, in order to sever all the afflictions and fetters of sentient beings.
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
May the Tathāgata definitively declare that he is eternally abiding.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"So it is, so it is. O son of good family!"

For example, when a Wheel-Turning Sage King enters his inner palace to enjoy himself with his ladies-in-waiting, he may for a moment go out to stroll through gardens and gaze upon bathing pools in joyous freedom; yet because he is not visible within the palace, one must not conclude that he has been lost forever.
It is the same with the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones: when they leave Jambudvīpa to manifest impermanence, it should likewise not be thought that they have been extinguished forever.

Just as that king abandoned his deep palace to sport in the gardens with ease and joy, so too does the Tathāgata abandon the deep palace of immeasurable afflictions to enter the garden of dhāraṇī and the lotus pond of the seven factors of enlightenment, where he dwells in joyful observation; riding upon the wisdom of skillful means, he manifests transformations with mastery, and the immeasurable fetters and ailments have long since been extinguished.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has said, throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, the Tathāgata has completely extinguished the afflictions of birth and death and has already crossed the ocean of the five desires.”
For what reason did the Tathāgata, while still a bodhisattva, dwell in the deep palace amidst court ladies for his own amusement and become the father of Rāhula?
Therefore, one should know that he did not exhaust all afflictions before crossing over the ocean of desires.
The Buddha told him:

"Good son, do not speak in this manner regarding the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. That which is called 'Great Parinirvāṇa' is so named because it is able to establish the Great Meaning."
Listen attentively now, and explain this extensively for others without giving rise to doubt or wonder.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells in this Great Parinirvāṇa, he is able to place Sumeru, the king of mountains, into a single grain of rice husk; yet those sentient beings who dwell upon Sumeru suffer no harm or disturbance, remaining unaware of who has come, gone, stayed, or rested there.

Other sentient beings who possess knowledge and vision recognize that this is a Bodhisattva dwelling in Great Parinirvāṇa who has placed Sumeru within the grain of rice husk and then restored it to its original state. Such is the realm of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in Great Parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa takes this great trichiliocosm and places its earth within a grain of millet husk; yet the sentient beings therein are not harmed or disturbed, and each is unaware of who has brought it there or who has placed it here.

As for other sentient beings who possess knowledge and vision, they know that this is a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa who has taken this great trichiliocosm and placed it within a grain of millet husk, and then restored it to its original state.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva dwelling in this Great Parinirvāṇa further takes the trichiliocosm and places it within a single pore of his own body, yet he causes no harm to those sentient beings therein. Each being is unaware of who brought them there or who has placed them here.

Among the other sentient beings, those with knowledge and vision recognize that this is a bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa who has taken this trichiliocosm and placed it within his own pore, and then restored it to its original state.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa, while remaining in this world, can lift all the buddha-lands of the ten directions and place them upon the point of a needle—just as one might hold a jujube leaf with the tip of a needle—and transport them to other buddha-lands in different directions, without causing any harm or distress to sentient beings; each being remains unaware of who brought them here or who placed them there.
As for those other sentient beings who possess knowledge and vision, they know that this is the work of the supernatural power of a bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa takes the lands of the ten directions and places them upon his right palm as if they were a potter’s wheel, casting them into other worlds as numerous as motes of dust. Yet he causes no harm or distress to any sentient beings; each remains unaware of who is bringing them or taking them away, or who is placing them here.
As for those other sentient beings who possess knowledge and vision, they recognize that this is the work performed by the supernatural power of a bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, son of good family!

A bodhisattva who dwells in the Great Parinirvāṇa takes a single atom from within the worlds of the ten directions; yet he harms no sentient beings, and each of them is unaware of who brought it there or who placed it here.
As for those other sentient beings who possess knowledge and vision, they know that this is the work performed by the power of the bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa.
In this way, son of good family!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells in this Great Parinirvāṇa possesses great supernormal powers and manifests various manifestations; therefore, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.

The deeds performed by a Bodhisattva dwelling in the Great Parinirvāṇa cannot be fathomed by any sentient being; how then can you now know that the Tathāgata associated with the five desires and became the father of Rāhula?
Furthermore, good son!

Abiding in this Great Parinirvāṇa, I am able to perform great deeds. Within this trichiliocosm of ten billion suns and moons and ten billion Jambudvīpas, I manifest various transformations as described in the Śūraṃgama Samādhi Sūtra. Within the Jambudvīpas of the trichiliocosm, I manifest parinirvāṇa through the Great Parinirvāṇa, yet there is no one who undergoes ultimate parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, within the five desires of Jambudvīpa, I manifested birth from a womb; my parents regarded me as their son, yet for countless kalpas past, my craving and desire have been forever extinguished. I possess no defiled body and no body that consumes impure food; my pure Dharma-body has severed all further rebirth. By means of skillful wisdom, I accord with the ways of the world and am born in Jambudvīpa to manifest as a youth.
Walking seven paces toward the north, I declared of myself: "Among devas, humans, and asuras, I am the Unsurpassed Honored One."
The parents, filled with joy, raised their voices and exclaimed:
"It is unprecedented in this world that our son, upon being born and falling to the ground, walked seven steps!

At that time, all sentient beings spoke of it as marvelous; yet I have never been a child, for throughout incalculable kalpas I have been free from infantile conduct. My pure Dharma-body does not grow from flesh, bone, or impure food; rather, the Dharma-body manifests as a child to accord with worldly ways, walking seven steps to the south to manifest as the unsurpassed field of merit for all.
Walking seven steps toward the west, he manifested the ultimate severance of birth, old age, sickness, and death, showing that he was the final limit for all sentient beings;
walking seven steps toward the east, he manifested himself as the guide for all sentient beings;

walking seven steps toward the four intermediate directions, he manifested the severance of the various wrong afflictions and demonic activities, the subduing of all the *Īśvara* devas, and his destined attainment of the path of the Worthy One, the Truly and Fully Enlightened One.
As for his treading through the air and walking seven steps toward the zenith, he manifests that, like empty space, he cannot be defiled by anything.

Furthermore, as for his walking seven steps toward the nadir, he manifests the extinguishing of the raging fires of all hells, raising great clouds of Dharma and pouring down great rains of Dharma to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings; raining down great bolts of Dharma, he shatters all evil precepts. He is born in Jambudvīpa manifesting the hair remaining upon his crown, desiring to let sentient beings know that this youth’s crown-hair was born simultaneously [with his body], such that no deva or worldly person could take up a blade and stand over his crown to shave it; having already been parted from crown-hair for countless kalpas, he now manifests possessing crown-hair.

In accordance with worldly custom, he entered the celestial shrines; there, the powerful devas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors bowed their heads, paid him homage, took refuge in him, and prostrated at his feet. For countless kalpas he has been the Honored One among gods and humans, yet he manifested entry into the celestial shrines to conform to the ways of the world.

In Jambudvīpa, he sometimes manifested having his ears pierced, though in reality no one dared to pierce his ears. His hair hung down, curling to the right like the mane of a lion; all the people saw the youth with his lion-like hair hanging down, yet for countless kalpas he had already abandoned wearing hair, manifesting the hanging, right-spiraling lion-manes only to conform to the ways of the world.

In Jambudvīpa, he manifested entering a schoolroom; within the three realms, there was none who could act as his teacher. Only I should serve as the teacher for devas and humans; therefore, I am called the One with All-Knowledge (*sarvajñā*). Having already studied writing throughout incalculable eons, I have attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

He manifests the study of scripts in accordance with worldly custom; he manifests riding elephants, horses, and precious chariots, and possessing various treasuries; though his body dwells within the deep palace and he amuses himself among the court ladies, he manages the affairs of state without any defilement or attachment, having long since abandoned them as if discarding spittle. He manifests the enjoyment of the five desires and the management of state affairs as a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over Jambudvīpa, yet he has already relinquished the royal throne for countless kalpas and is able to turn the unsurpassed Dharma-wheel of ambrosia;

thus, manifesting as a Wheel-Turning King, he accords with the ways of the world. Within Jambudvīpa, he manifests old age, sickness, and death, and abandons the various sensual pleasures of the inner palace to leave the home-life and study the Way, such that all people see the youth renouncing the world; for the sake of delivering sentient beings, he manifests leaving the home-life in accordance with the ways of the world.

I manifest as the four fruits of the śramaṇa—srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat—and practice the nine successive meditative attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) while cultivating the Four Noble Truths. Although all sentient beings see me thus, I have already swiftly attained unsurpassed arhatship; indeed, throughout incalculable kalpas, I have reached the ultimate state of an arhat, yet for the sake of delivering others, I manifest the initial attainment.

I go beneath the tree and manifest sitting upon a mat of grass to subdue the hosts of Māra and achieve the Unsurpassed Way; yet throughout incalculable kalpas, I have already subdued all the afflictions of the Māras and obtained the Dharma of Ambrosia (*amṛta*).

I manifest inhalation and exhalation, as well as the passing of stool and urine, though my pure Dharma-body is free from such ailments; I manifest these human activities in order to accord with the ways of the world.

He manifests the consumption of food and drink for the sake of sentient beings, yet in reality he has no perception of hunger or thirst; he manifests eating and drinking to accord with the world, while throughout incalculable eons he has constantly attained the profound *pāramitās*.

He does not manifest dwelling in houses according to the seasons, yet in reality he has no sleep, indigestion, yawning, stretching, or any physical pains; he manifests reliance on houses to accord with the world, though his true *dharmakāya* possesses none of these physical forms.
He manifests sitting, lying down, walking, looking ahead, glancing around, bending, stretching, bowing, and raising himself, yet in truth the *dharmakāya* has no such categories of form.

He manifests bathing, anointing his body with sesame oil, cleansing his teeth with *dantakāṣṭha*, and applying eye medicine; yet these are not required by the pure Dharma-body. His hands and feet are as soft as lotus petals, the fragrance of his breath is as pure as the *utpala* flower, and his eyes are as clear as the bright moon; he manifests these practices to accord with the ways of the world.
He manifests practicing few desires, begging for food, and wearing coarse rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), though he has already perfected all the ascetic practices of a *śramaṇa* over immeasurable eons.

He manifests dwelling among humans as the father of Rāhula, the son of King Śuddhodana and Queen Māyā; having accomplished his kinsmen and become weary of worldly pleasures, he leaves home to study the Way and dwells amidst the forest trees.

Manifesting the distinctions between superior and inferior desires and the gradations of pleasure, he abandoned his status as a prince and a member of the great Gautama clan to demonstrate the practice of renunciation for the sake of delivering sentient beings. It is not because the Tathāgata is defiled by and attached to the five desires that he became the father of Rāhula; rather, manifesting parents, he accords with worldly conventions.
While sentient beings regard him as a mere worldly man, in reality the Tathāgata is neither a deva nor a human.

Furthermore, within Jambudvīpa he manifests parinirvāṇa, yet he does not ultimately enter into nirvāṇa; sentient beings all say that the Tathāgata has been forever extinguished, but now the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is eternally abiding, being neither subject to transformation nor to decay—the constant law of all Buddhas is to manifest nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he may appear as a bhikṣu who has committed the four grave offenses (pārājika) so that all people see it, yet in reality he does not engage in such indolent conduct;

or he may manifest the conduct of an icchantika, or manifest the breaking of the Saṃgha, with all people seeing him commit an act of immediate retribution (ānantarya), yet in reality he lacks any intention to destroy the Saṃgha, nor is there any Saṃgha to be destroyed.
Within Jambudvīpa, he protects and upholds the True Dharma, and all sentient beings see him as a Great Being who guards the Dharma; this is the constant law of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
In Jambudvīpa, he manifests as a celestial Māra, seen by all sentient beings, yet in reality he does not perform the deeds of Māras;
in Jambudvīpa, he manifests in the form of a woman, and when sentient beings see him, they all exclaim in wonder:
"How marvelous! Today a woman has become a Buddha!"

In reality, the Tathāgata does not possess a female body; yet, in accordance with their desires and following various causes and conditions, he manifests the forms of men and women to conform to the world.

Within Jambudvīpa, he manifests birth among the four kinds of animal realms; all sentient beings claim these are truly animals, but in reality, he does not perform the deeds of those animals, manifesting entry into the animal realm only to conform to the world.

He enters among the Brahmā devas and manifests as a Brahmā to act as their teacher and leader; for those sentient beings who serve the Brahmā devas, he uses skillful means to lead them forward into the True Dharma so they do not practice those [worldly] karmas, manifesting the form of a Brahmā to conform to the world.

Manifesting entry into brothels to deliver those of lustful nature, they do not give rise to thoughts of desire; their minds are like lotuses, unsullied by dust or water, as they adorn their bodies and travel through the four crossroads to skillfully entice and transform sentient beings with defiled hearts.
Entering the quarters of courtesans, they manifest as women to transform others through the True Dharma; entering schools and lecture halls, they manifest as teachers to transform young children.
Or they enter wine gatherings and places of gambling and play; for the sake of teaching and transforming them, they do not participate in those activities.

He goes to the charnel grounds to deliver birds and beasts, yet does not grasp at the perception of seeing them; he enters among the elders and bestows upon them the True Dharma; he enters among the great ministers and instructs them in righteous governance; he enters among the princes and transforms them so they protect the Dharma; he enters among the kings and transforms them to rule the nation with the righteous Dharma of former kings.

He manifests the kalpa of pestilence and provides medicine for it, causing those who are ill to become weary of bodily suffering and guiding them with the True Dharma, while sentient beings believe this to be a true kalpa of pestilence.

He manifests the kalpa of famine when grain is precious, giving ambrosial food to hungry and destitute sentient beings and guiding them with the True Dharma, while sentient beings believe this to be a true kalpa of famine.

When manifesting the kalpa of weapons where sentient beings each harm one another, he transforms them to bring about harmony and guides them with the True Dharma; yet sentient beings believe this to be a true kalpa of weapons.

When manifesting as the conflagration at the end of a kalpa for those who cling to the notion of permanence, he demonstrates the mark of impermanence; yet sentient beings believe this to be a real conflagration at the end of a kalpa.

To all sentient beings, he speaks in their respective tongues, his voice being more subtle and excellent than that of each respective class; through these musical sounds, sentient beings thereby attain liberation.
They manifest as the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, each according to their respective natures, so that beings attached to them may thereby attain liberation;
they manifest as medicinal trees to heal and save sentient beings, so that they may thereby attain liberation;

they enter various heterodox paths and manifest leaving the household life, acting as teachers for those respective groups; though they have already been free from external paths for countless eons, they manifest leaving the household life to guide others with the True Dharma.

Manifesting as artisans, physicians, and masters of incantations and arts, he appears in various transformations among all sentient beings and non-Buddhists who harbor pride. He subdues their various heterodoxies, arrogance, and haughtiness by guiding them with the True Dharma; yet when sentient beings see him, they think he is merely a worldly man, for the Tathāgata eternally abides apart from worldly dharmas.

Even manifesting as lowly servants to deliver people according to their kind, there is no variety of diverse occupations in Jambudvīpa that he does not manifest; however, in reality, the Tathāgata does not engage in those same activities, but manifests such forms to accord with the world.

In the twenty-five locations, including Uttarakuru in the north, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Pūrvavideha in the east, as well as throughout the trichiliocosm, he manifests emanations in accordance with the world;
this is explained in detail in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*.
The Tathāgata has accomplished the wisdom of great skillful means; there is nothing he does that is not manifested through transformation. For this reason, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas abide in these merits, they are able to manifest various transformations according to the capacities of beings with sovereign ease and fearlessness. One should no longer doubt that Rāhula’s father is [an ordinary being]; one should know that the Tathāgata, throughout incalculable kalpas, has already transcended the great ocean of birth-and-death, craving, and desire. Therefore, the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, not a subject to change, nor a subject to extinction.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If the Tathāgata is a permanently abiding dharma, not a dharma subject to decay, and not a dharma subject to change, why does the Tathāgata praise nirvāṇa?"
"It is like a lamp that has gone out; no one can know where it has gone.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "I have presented this analogy, but I do not speak in such a manner."
"Good son!
It is like a vessel filled with ghee and oil used to light a lamp: when the ghee and oil are exhausted, it is called the extinction of the lamp, yet the vessel remains.
The Tathāgata is likewise: although the blazing fuel of the afflictions has been entirely extinguished, the lamp-vessel of the Tathāgata remains forever and is never extinguished."
If the ghee and the vessel were to perish together, then the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa would likewise perish together with them;
however, while the lamp is extinguished, the vessel remains. Therefore, the Tathāgata neither perishes nor is born, abiding in the bliss of parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, good son!
When I speak of the metaphor of the extinguished lamp, I refer to the Arhat, not to Nirvana.

An Arhat has attained the supreme fruit; the worldly defilements of food and craving have all been extinguished, having reached the ultimate cessation of the craving for food, just like the extinguishing of a lamp.
"The meaning of 'Anāgāmin' (Non-returner) is likewise so; therefore, I have taught this subtle and esoteric doctrine through skillful means, rather than teaching [the final] Nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the meaning of 'Anāgāmin'?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa,
"One who does not receive another body is named an Anāgāmin.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How is it, World-Honored One? Does the Tathāgata also possess secret teachings, like a magician?
The Buddha said: “No.”
The Dharma I teach is like the full moon in autumn, free from lust, anger, and delusion, without any obstructions or concealments;

it is also like a householder with billions in wealth who has an only son whom he holds dear. Taking the boy to a teacher’s gate to learn the "half-syllables," before long the father fears he will not achieve mastery quickly, so he brings him back himself and diligently teaches the half-syllables day and night.
"Good son, when a father teaches his son the study of the 'half-syllables,' can he possibly know all the treatises on grammar?
If he could indeed know all the treatises on grammar, why would the father teach him only the half-syllables?
Would he conceal anything from his beloved son and fail to teach him the treatises on grammar?"
Kāśyapa replied:
“No, World-Honored One.”

Because his son is young and ignorant and unable to understand the treatises, he does not teach him; this is not called "concealment. If one were to keep it secret out of stinginess, that would be called concealment; however, to encourage him with an open mind and teach him gradually according to his capacity is not called concealment.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"Good son!
As you have said, to harbor resentment, stinginess, and parsimony while keeping things secret is called 'concealment.

However, I regard all sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness and affection, regarding each as my only child. Because they are immature and not yet capable of receiving the profound Dharma, I do not preach it to them. Just as one teaches a child who is first learning the half-syllables, I likewise preach the ninefold canon, the ten powers of wisdom, the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths, the eightfold noble path, and the profound discourses; yet I do not at all preach the Vaipulya Mahāyāna to them."
Furthermore, good son!

It is like an elder who instructs his beloved son: first he teaches him the half-syllables; once the half-syllables are mastered, he then teaches him in succession the profound treatises to bring the son to full accomplishment.

I am also like this: I teach only the ninefold canon to my disciples; once I know they are capable of receiving it, I then explain the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras, teaching that the Tathāgata is eternally present and not subject to change, so as to cause the eye of wisdom of all sentient beings to open wide.
Furthermore, noble son!
It is like the summer season, when clouds arise with thunder and lightning, and a great rain must surely fall, so that the hundred grains, grasses, and trees all receive its moistening nourishment;

so too is it today for the Tathāgata, who raises the subtle and secret Dharma-cloud of Great Nirvāṇa and thunders the sound of the Great Dharma, so that he must surely rain down the nectar-like rain of the Dharma to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

“As the World-Honored One has said that there is nothing to store up and that one clearly understands the nature of morsel food—just as the tracks of a bird flying through the sky are difficult to find—what is the meaning of this?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Accumulation (caya) means the sense of gathering and piling up; receiving and taking up (upādāna) means the sense of increase; a treasury (kośa) means the sense of a storehouse. Because there is that which is received within a treasury, it is called 'accumulated in a treasury' (kośa-caya)."
There are two kinds of treasuries: the conditioned treasury and the unconditioned treasury.
The conditioned treasury refers to the śrāvakas; the unconditioned treasury refers to the Tathāgata.
There are two kinds of Saṃgha: the equal Saṃgha and the unequaled Saṃgha.
The equal Saṃgha refers to the Śrāvaka Saṃgha.
Since the Śrāvaka Saṃgha likewise has no hoarding or accumulation, why now do they accept and keep servants, money, treasures, and storehouses?
If one does not even store up things such as sesame oil and salt, how could the Tathāgata permit the keeping of servants and the like!
Those who speak thus, claiming that the Tathāgata permits it, shall fall into the Hell of the Severed Tongue in every successive life.

The Sangha of Śrāvakas and others who possess no hoarded stores are able to comprehend the nature of morsel food and harbor no thoughts of craving for its flavor; the footprints of such as these are difficult to find wherever they go, and they swiftly attain the path of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Because their footprints are difficult to find, they are called Tathāgatas.
If even the conditioned Saṃgha does not hoard or accumulate, how much less so the unconditioned Saṃgha?
The unconditioned Saṃgha refers to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; how could the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess anything hidden or secret?
If there is that which is hidden, it is a concealed accumulation.

That which is difficult to seek is called the immovable bliss of *nirvāṇa*. It is devoid of such things as empty space, the sun and moon, clouds and rain, earth, water, fire, and wind, as well as the various marks of birth, old age, sickness, death, and affliction; it is eternally abiding, unchanging, blissful, and immovable, and is therefore named *nirvāṇa*.
Because one attains this *nirvāṇa*, it is called the Tathāgata’s Great Parinirvāṇa.
That which is "great" is so because it accomplishes great matters;
what is called "great" is a designation for a large number—for instance, if there were a person whose lifespan were immeasurable, they would be called a "great man."

If a person can practice the Dharma, they are the greatest among men; if they further accomplish the eight thoughts of a great man, they are called a "great man. Therefore, "great" is a designation based on conditioned phenomena.

Nirvāṇa is so named because it is free from all wounds and sores. It is like a person whose body has been struck by a poisoned arrow and suffers great agony, who then encounters a skilled physician; the physician treats the wound, and the suffering is entirely removed. This good man, having become free from the wound, travels through various lands to universally treat the wounds and ailments of sentient beings.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this: for all sentient beings within Jambudvīpa who have suffered the poisonous pain of afflictions such as lust, anger, and ignorance throughout immeasurable kalpas, he preaches the ambrosial medicine of the Mahāyāna Dharma to treat their wounds and ailments. Once these sentient beings are freed from their wounds and ailments, he further manifests in other lands to treat the various diseases of all beings; therefore, it is called the Great Parinirvāṇa.
The meaning of reality and the meaning of skillful means are both termed Mahāparinirvāṇa.

Manifesting entry into the various realms of existence as well as entry into liberation, appearing everywhere in accordance with those to be transformed—this is the essential meaning; therefore, it is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, how is it that the Dharma of the skilled physician can cure all ailments and, once they have been healed, further manifest other methods to treat various diseases?"
The Buddha said:
"In this way, good son, one can heal all and cause them to be free from illness, with the sole exception of those with terminal illnesses that cannot be cured.
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise; with the sole exception of the icchantikas, they cure all other remaining ailments."
Kāśyapa asked again:
"What is the nature of liberation?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"As for that liberation, it consists of form and formlessness. Formlessness is the liberation of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; form is the liberation of the Tathāgata.
Although this liberation possesses form, it is not said to be form."
Why is this? Just as the formless states of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are neither form nor non-form, they are likewise not the existence of form.
Question:
“The realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is neither form nor formlessness, yet it is not non-form either; how does one abide therein?
What is its pleasure?
This matter should be explained.”
"This is the realm of the Buddha; it is not something known by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will again explain the meaning of the Tathāgata’s Great Parinirvāṇa liberation."

The Buddha told Kāśyapa: "As for that which is liberation, it is entirely free from all fetters and combinations. That which is free from combination is a 'birth' that is not born; just as a child is born because of parents and is therefore called 'born,' liberation is not like this. It is like *ghṛta-maṇḍa* (clarified butter), whose original nature is pure and which does not grow through the nourishment of parental desire. For the sake of delivering sentient beings, it manifests birth; therefore, liberation is a 'birth' that is not born."
Furthermore, that which is born is like planting grain to produce sprouts;
liberation is not like this. Therefore it is said: "Liberation is unborn," and that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.

Therefore, the arising of the Tathāgata’s non-arising is neither an agent nor an action. As for actual agents, they are like the construction of cities, walls, or towers by human hands; true liberation is not like this. Thus, liberation has no agent, and that which is liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is not a product of conditioned activity; this is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

That which is conditioned is like a potter who shapes clay to make vessels—there is both creation and destruction. However, true liberation is not like this: it is neither created nor destroyed. Therefore, liberation is without creation and without destruction, and that which is liberation is the Tathāgata.

One should know that the Tathāgata is neither born nor dies; therefore, the Tathāgata is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), and for this reason it is said that the Tathāgata enters the Great Nirvāṇa without the characteristics of aging or decay.
A withered form, an emaciated body, white hair, and fallen teeth—these are the marks of old age;

yet true liberation is not like this, for it is forever free from all aging, decay, and transformation, and is thus called liberation. That which is liberation is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata has no mark of senescence.
Therefore it is said that there is no illness; as for the names of illnesses, there are four hundred and four types of diseases, and other accidental ailments beyond counting.
To be free from all these afflictions is called liberation, and this liberation is none other than the Tathāgata.
The Dharma-body is pure and free from illness; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is without illness.
Because he is without illness, he is without death. Sentient beings die constantly because they lack liberation, and thus for them there is exhaustion and death.
Because he has forever transcended the name "death," he is called liberated; this liberation is precisely the Tathāgata.

The Tathāgata has accomplished such immeasurable, supreme, and wondrous merits; it is impossible that he should die. His Vajra-Dharmakāya is pure and indestructible; how could it possess the characteristics of impermanence or decay? Therefore, he does not die and is free from all defilements.
For example, it is like fine, white cotton cloth stained with ghee and oil;

true liberation is not like this. Rather, it is like a white lotus, pure and stainless; the liberation of the Tathāgata is likewise so, forever free from the defilements and impurities of craving and desire. Therefore, the Tathāgata is named "Stainless" (Vimala).
It is free from all limitations and obstructions;

that which is subject to the control of a master is called limitation and obstruction, but in reality, liberation is devoid of all limitations and obstructions. This liberation is itself the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is unimpeded and cool.

Regarding the "place of coolness," worldly temples are called "cool," but this is a false claim; only those who have attained liberation possess true coolness. Those who have attained liberation are the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is cool and tranquil.
That which is peaceful and secure is like a road free from bandits, which is called "peaceful and secure";

true liberation is not like this, for its nature is fearless, and thus it is called "peaceful and secure. This liberation is itself the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is peaceful and secure, fearless, and free from all terrors.
Those who possess fear are like kings who constantly dread their enemies; those in true liberation are forever free from such fear.

Just as a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) has no fears, so too is one in true liberation. This state of liberation is itself the Tathāgata; as the Dharma King, the Tathāgata turns the unsurpassed wheel and has no enemies. Therefore, the Tathāgata is fearless and without anxiety.
Those who possess anxiety and fear are like a king who has a traitor plotting rebellion; unable to subdue them, he constantly harbors anxiety and fear.

Those in true liberation have no such anxiety or fear; they are like a king who, having subdued his enemies, dwells in joy and happiness. This state of liberation is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is without anxiety and is free from all defilements.
That which is defiled is like a spring wind that raises up clouds of dust;

true liberation is free from all such dust and grime, just as the bright pearl in the topknot of a Wheel-Turning King is devoid of any stain or impurity. This liberation is itself the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is free from all defilements and free from all falsehoods.
That which is false and deceptive is likened to an unbaked earthen jar;

true liberation is not like this, for it is like a diamond, devoid of falsehood. This liberated one is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is free from all falsehood and is liberated from lack of mastery.
Lack of mastery is like a poor person who owes another wealth; held in check by the creditor, they lack freedom.
True liberation is not like this. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is sovereign, unimpeded, and free from all afflictions.

As for those afflicted by injuries, it is like a person who, by wading through heat in spring, drinking alcohol in summer, or wading through cold in winter, harms their own body and thus gives rise to afflictions;
one who has attained true liberation is not like this and is free from all such afflictions. This liberated one is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is free from all afflictions.

Free from all turbidity, just as space is free from all turbidity, so too is true liberation free from all turbidity. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is free from all turbidity and free from all entanglements.
Those who are entangled are friends and kinsmen;

those who have attained true liberation are free from such entanglements, like a wheel-turning monarch who is uniquely virtuous and without peer. This liberated one is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is uniquely virtuous and extraordinary.

Just as a lotus born from water is not extraordinary, whereas a lotus born from fire is indeed extraordinary and beloved by all, so too is the one who has attained true liberation beloved by all. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is rare and extraordinary.

There is no one capable of doing so; for example, just as an infant whose teeth have not yet emerged cannot cause them to grow, so it is with true liberation. It is impossible for one to attain it at an improper time, just as it is impossible for an icchantika—who is indolent, lazy, and lies like a corpse all day long—claiming he shall become a Buddha;

if he were to become a Buddha, such a thing would never occur. Even if lay followers who faithfully uphold the Dharma desire to seek liberation and cross to the other shore, this would still be impossible, let alone one who lies like a corpse.

Why is this so? Because its nature is not established by anything else; therefore, liberation is something that cannot be produced by another. That which is liberation is itself the Tathāgata; thus, the Tathāgata is something that cannot be produced by another.
The immeasurable and incalculable may, for example, still be measured like the great ocean;
but true liberation is both incalculable and immeasurable. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is immeasurable and most supreme.

That which is most supreme has nothing with which it can be compared; just as the great ocean has no equal, so too is liberation itself the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Tathāgata is most supreme, exalted, and manifest.
That which is most exalted is like space, beyond reproach; this liberation is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the sovereign king among all the holy ones.

For example, just as the lion is the king of all beasts, the one who has attained true liberation is the king of all dharmas. The light of liberation illuminates all phenomena; that which is liberated is the Tathāgata, who is supreme and unsurpassed.

Just as among all directions, Uttarakuru is considered supreme, so too is liberation the most supreme. That which is liberation is the Tathāgata; therefore, the Tathāgata is the highest and unsurpassed.

For example, just as among all directions, Uttarakuru is the most supreme, so too is liberation supreme; that which is liberation is the Tathāgata, and therefore the Tathāgata is the unsurpassed, eternal Dharma.

Just as death is the constant law for all devas and humans, the law of liberation is not like that; that which is liberated is the Tathāgata, and therefore the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and firm.
The plantain tree and foam have no solidity; true liberation is not like this. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
Free from all defilements and outflows—just as a dilapidated wall is a dwelling place for mosquitoes and gnats—liberation is not like this.
For example, on a painted wall, nothing can take up residence; likewise, liberation cannot be stained by any unwholesome dharmas. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
There is no limit [to it], unlike villages or lands which have limits;
those who have attained true liberation are not like this. For example, just as space is boundless and blissful, that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
Subtle and unmanifest, it is like the tracks of a bird flying through the sky that do not appear; liberation is likewise unmanifest, and that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.

It is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom; the kindness and virtue of parents who give birth and raise one are so profound that no one can measure them. True liberation is likewise so; that which is liberated is none other than the Tathāgata.

It is profoundly deep and difficult to perceive; just as all sentient beings each possess within their own bodies the nature of the Tathāgata, which is subtle, secret, and difficult to see, so too is true liberation subtle, secret, and difficult to see. That which is liberated is itself the Tathāgata.

There is no one who can see it, just as the mark on the crown of the head cannot be seen; liberation is likewise not something seen by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. That which is liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

There is no cave-dwelling; for that which is called a "cave-dwelling" is merely a name for a house or a place of residence. True liberation is not like this: it is like space, wherein the twenty-five abodes of birth and death can never be found. That which is liberation is the Tathāgata.

There is nothing that can be grasped; as for what is called "grasping," it is like a hand holding an *āmalaka* fruit. One who has attained true liberation is not like this; they are like the transformations produced by a magician, which cannot be grasped. That which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
It is free from all impurities; those impurities are like a garment made of multicolored leprosy-tainted cowhide.

True liberation is not like this; it is like fresh milk, uniform in color and flavor. The subtle and wondrous single characteristic of true liberation is likewise so: that which is liberation is itself the Tathāgata.
Its nature is pure; it is only when there is mud and turbid water that it is called impure.
One who has attained true liberation is not like this: just as rain falling from the sky is of a single, uniform purity, so too is the one who has attained liberation the Tathāgata.
Its nature is truly wondrous, like the full moon free from all clouds and obscurations; liberation is likewise stainless and truly wondrous, and that which is liberation is the Tathāgata.

It is truly wondrously tranquil; yet one who is like someone whose hair is on fire is not tranquil. Those who have attained liberation have forever extinguished the blazing calamities of afflictions; those who have attained liberation are the Tathāgata.
Its nature is equal; those that are not equal are like two madmen whose natures are unequal.
Those in true liberation are not like this; their nature is equal, just like that of a mother and her child. This liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

Its nature is quiescent; having attained the supreme state, it is free from any further seeking or conceptualization. It is like a hungry person who, upon obtaining fragrant and delicious food, feels fully satisfied and has no further desire for more. True liberation is also like this; that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
Its nature has already been severed; it is like a hook, bait, and line that have all been broken. True liberation is also like this, and he who is liberated is the Tathāgata.

To cross over to the other shore: for example, just as a river has both this shore and the other shore, immeasurable birth and death are called "this shore," and true liberation is called "the other shore"; that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
It is pure and deep-still; that which is deep and still is not like the various rivers, but is like the great ocean. Emancipation is also like this; that which is emancipated is the Tathāgata.
Its flavor is pure and exquisite; it is like the *jyotiṣmatī* seed, whose taste becomes increasingly bitter as it matures.
True liberation is not like this; that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
They are free from all negligence; for those who are negligent are addicted to the pleasures of the five desires.
Those with true liberation are not like this: their nature is pure and they are free from lust, anger, and delusion. Such liberation is itself the Tathāgata.

One subdues all craving; there are two kinds of craving: craving for sensory objects and craving for the Dharma. Craving for the Dharma consists of compassionately regarding sentient beings. One who has attained true liberation is free from craving for sensory objects and is detached from the notions of "self" and "mine. Such a liberated one is the Tathāgata.
When its nature is extinguished and all the fetters of the habitual tendencies of birth and death are completely extinguished, this is called liberation; that which is liberation is the Tathāgata.
He is a shelter for the world, providing cover and shade for all conditioned beings; he who has attained liberation is the Tathāgata.
He is a refuge for the world, like a king traveling through various kingdoms and towns;
true liberation is not like this—it is immovable bliss, which is called liberation, and he who has attained liberation is the Tathāgata.
That place is eternally peaceful, unlike the wilderness which is perilous, difficult, and terrifying;
those who have attained true liberation are not like this. They are like the lion king, who has no fear among the various beasts; such a liberated one is the Tathāgata.
Free from all oppression, he is like a person who, when pursued by a malevolent beast, has no protector to deliver him from his peril;
true liberation is not like this. Rather, it is like a mariner who obtains a sturdy ship and is able to cross the great ocean; such a liberated one is the Tathāgata.

Free from all dregs and impurities, it is like the process where curd is produced from milk, fresh butter from curd, clarified butter from fresh butter, and ghee from clarified butter; only ghee is by nature pure and free from all dregs and filth. Liberation is just like this, and that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.
It subdues all arrogance; for example, a king may be haughty and self-important, claiming there is no one equal to him.
Those who have attained liberation are not like this: they are free from all arrogance and devoid of the notions of "self" and "mine. These who have attained liberation are precisely the Tathāgata.

The eradication of ignorance is like the successive transformation of milk into curd and so forth until it reaches clarified butter (*sarpis*); this clarified butter is free from all dregs and impurities, its intrinsic nature being luminous and pure. Liberation is likewise; that which is liberation is the Tathāgata.

Detached from desire and dwelling in tranquility, peerless and without equal among the two classes of dharmas, he wanders alone like an elephant in the empty wilderness; liberation is thus, and that which is liberated is the Tathāgata.

Free from all deception, one enters the Tathāgatagarbha that is liberated from "mine-ness. The bodies of devas, humans, and asuras lack any solid core; they are like the *eranda*, reeds, and plantains, which have no solid core and are devoid of the Tathāgatagarbha.
