If the Tathāgata were eternally free from sorrow, he would not be called a Perfectly Awakened One. According to those sentient beings who are ready to be transformed, the Tathāgata, the Equally and Perfectly Awakened One, manifests before them. Therefore, one should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding, manifesting in various ways just like the birds known as geese, cranes, and śarabhas.
Chapter 16: The Parable of the Moon. In the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, Chapter Sixteen, "The Parable of the Moon," the Buddha again addressed Kāśyapa: "Good son!
Just as when the moon does not appear, people say it has set, and all the populace forms the thought that it has vanished."

When it appears in other directions, the people of those regions all say that the moon has risen; yet that moon neither sets nor rises, for its appearance and disappearance are manifested due to Mount Sumeru.

In this way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, within the great trichiliocosm or in Jambudvīpa, manifests birth as a son by depending upon parents; the people of Jambudvīpa all conceive the thought that he has been born.
Furthermore, when he manifests parinirvāṇa in Jambudvīpa, these sentient beings all conceive the thought that he has passed away; yet in reality, the Tathāgata is neither born nor does he perish.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as when the moon appears full in another region, the sentient beings of that region all perceive it as full;
yet while it appears newly risen here in Jambudvīpa, the people of this region perceive it as newly risen."

Gradually increasing until the month is full, people then form the perception that it is full; yet that moon neither increases nor decreases—it is only because of Mount Sumeru that its waxing and waning appear to exist.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise appears to enter *nirvāṇa* in Jambudvīpa, causing all sentient beings to perceive his extinction;
or he manifests birth in Jambudvīpa, appearing like the first day of the new moon.
The people of Jambudvīpa conceive the thought of being infants like the moon on its third day;
they manifest the practice of walking about like the moon on its fourth day;
they manifest the practice of learning to write like the moon on its eighth day.

Manifesting the act of renouncing the world until the completion of the full month, he displays great radiance that destroys immeasurable hosts of Māras; then, in the midst of darkness, he manifests *parinirvāṇa*.

Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his body is like the bright moon surrounded by the array of stars; yet when it sets and disappears, the people of Jambudvīpa may conceive the thought that it has been born or that it has perished. In reality, the Tathāgata neither increases nor decreases, remaining forever like the full moon. Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgata is eternally abiding.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like the bright moon, which is seen by all throughout cities, towns, villages, mountains, marshes, and forests; it appears reflected in all the waters according to the size of each vessel.
If a person travels for hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, the moon constantly follows them, and those people form this perception: [that the moon is following them]."
"Is this the same moon that followed me here, or is it another moon?

A fool sees the moon as being like the surface of a mirror; a person of middling capacity sees the moon as being like a chariot wheel; a superior person sees the moon as five yojanas in diameter; and other sentient beings see it according to their respective capacities.
The Tathāgata, like the bright moon, is likewise seen by all; yet each sentient being thinks to themselves, "The Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, is dwelling in my house."

It is likewise with those in the realm of animals; the deaf, the blind, the mute, and those who are crippled or deformed each consider the Tathāgata to be of their own kind. With their various languages, various scripts, and various bodies, they all think:
"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak only my language, write only my script, possess only my body, and eat only my food."

Furthermore, they may form various other conceptions: some may think of him as a śrāvaka, some as a pratyekabuddha, some as one who has left the household life in various heterodox paths, or some may think that a Tathāgata has appeared in the world for their sake. Yet, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is truly without change; for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests various forms through his body of skillful means, like a tree of medicinal herbs.

The Tathāgata is likewise: for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests hundreds of thousands of transformations in accordance with the world. Therefore, the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma.

"Furthermore, good son! When the asura Rāhu seizes the sun or the moon, sentient beings say that he is eclipsing the moon; when he releases the moon, they say he has disgorged it. When he obstructs the moonlight so that it does not appear in the world, people conceive the thought of an eclipse; when he releases the moon and it appears again in the world, they say he has disgorged it. Yet, whether the moon is hidden or revealed, in reality there is no increase or decrease."

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is also like this. Just as Devadatta injured and damaged the Buddha’s body and committed the ānantarya karmas, and even those who are icchantikas—all these acts are for the sake of future sentient beings. Thus, he manifests the injury of the Buddha’s body, the destruction of the Dharma, and the schism of the Saṅgha; yet the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is truly without injury or destruction. Even if there were hundreds of thousands of millions of celestial Māras, they could not sever the Dharma or destroy the Saṅgha. Therefore, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is truly without damage or ruin; he manifests the appearance of damage and ruin only in conformity with the world.

For example, when two people fight, the gravity of their offense is determined according to the extent of the injury inflicted; the Tathāgatas, Buddhas, act in the same way, manifesting the appearance of injury to represent the offenses of the Avīci hell, thereby establishing laws and regulations to admonish those who come after.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who well instructs his son to study medical arts and identify various medicinal herbs, causing him to fully understand their roots, stems, flowers, leaves, fragrance, taste, color, and appearance; after the physician’s death, the son continues the lineage and becomes proficient in the medical methods.

The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are also like this: they employ various transformations to heal sentient beings, manifesting even the five heinous crimes, slandering the sutras and the Dharma, and even appearing as those belonging to the icchantika class. This is for the sake of the future, so that after their parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣus may follow the sutras and the vinaya as the Tathāgata taught them, knowing the gravity of offenses and exercising self-restraint."
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as humans see the moon eat once every six months, the various devas above see the moon eat every day, or even see it eat in a mere instant."
Why is this so? Because the days and months of the heavens are long while those of the human realm are short.

It is the same with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas: some say their lifespan is as long as six months of eating, while others say it lasts but a brief moment before they enter parinirvāṇa. Yet they cannot be destroyed by the hundreds of thousands of millions of affliction-māras, aggregate-māras, death-māras, or the Māra of the Lord of Heaven; they manifest immeasurable births in accordance with the world. The lifespan of a Tathāgata is truly immeasurable; therefore, the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as all sentient beings love and delight in the bright moon, so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; those sentient beings who delight in the Dharma all love and delight in him."
"Furthermore, good son!

For example, when the sun rises, there are three seasonal transformations—spring, summer, and winter—which differ from one another. The winter days are short, the spring days are moderate, and the summer days are extremely long. The sun of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is also like this, manifesting three kinds of lifespans. For the sake of sentient beings, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, he manifests the appearance of a short lifespan.
When these see it, their hearts are filled with lamentation: 'How strange! How can the Tathāgata’s lifespan be so short?'"
“For the sake of the bodhisattvas, he manifests a lifespan therein, whether it be for one kalpa or exceeding one kalpa;
yet only when a Buddha contemplates a Buddha is that lifespan truly immeasurable.
Furthermore, son of good family!”

The subtle and secret teachings of the Vaipulya Mahāyāna spoken by the Tathāgata manifest the great rain of Dharma upon the world; those sentient beings who, in future ages, shall reveal this Mahāyāna chapter of the True Dharma to the world, you should know that these are true Bodhisattvas.
It is like summer rain and like winter days; when there is much cold affliction, it shortens one's lifespan.
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas hear the Buddha’s subtle and secret teaching on skillful means, he manifests for them the retribution of a short lifespan, which is like winter.
When the various Bodhisattvas have perfected subtle wisdom, he manifests for them the eternal dharma of the Tathāgata, which is like springtime.
In this way, the Tathāgata accords with the world by manifesting a lifespan across three periods of time.

Just as the various stars do not appear during the day but have not actually vanished, so too the Tathāgata appears together with the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the world and manifests nirvāṇa alongside them. It is not that only all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are subject to impermanence; one should know that he is likewise the eternally abiding Dharma, like the stars in the daytime.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

It is just as when the sky is overcast and the sun and moon do not appear; fools say that the sun and moon have set and perished. When the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is extinguished and the Three Jewels appear to vanish, it is likewise so: they are not eternally destroyed.
You should know that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma, neither subject to change nor to extinction, and cannot be defiled by those various faults."
"Furthermore, good son!

It is just as when the Dipper Star appears briefly with its light in the interval between darkness and dawn during the final watch of the night after the moon has waned; once people have seen it, it immediately vanishes again. People say it has perished, yet in reality it has not perished.
In this same way, good son!"

When the True Dharma of the Tathāgata has completely vanished, various Pratyekabuddhas will appear in the world to reveal and teach immeasurable sentient beings, establishing them in the True Dharma before they immediately enter parinirvāṇa; yet in reality, they abide forever and do not perish eternally, though sentient beings are unable to see them all.
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as when the sun rises, all darkness is completely dispelled; so it is!"
"Good son!
This Mahāyāna *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* has appeared in the world!
Any who hear it shall have all their accumulated, immeasurable karma of the immediate offenses completely extinguished."
Thus it is, son of good family!
This profound realm of the Mahāyāna Great Parinirvāṇa is inconceivable; it excellently expounds the subtle and wondrous nature of the Tathāgata.

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, that the True Dharma is inexhaustible, and that the Jewel of the Saṃgha is imperishable, they should diligently apply skillful means to study this sutra; I declare that such a person is near to the stage of Buddhahood.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Five;
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Volume Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Faxian of Pingyang during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Chapter Seventeen: Inquiry into Bodhisattvas The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What constitutes a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Those who have already resolved [to attain enlightenment] and those who have not yet resolved—all such as these are bodhisattvas. Good son!”

For example, just as ghee and oil congeal in winter and lack any luster or moisture, so it is with those who practice various other samādhis found in all the sūtras, generating the aspiration for results and seeking bodhi; such individuals are said to have not yet awakened the mind of the Way, and they cannot quickly accomplish the path of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because it lacks the application of effort, being like the winter sun.
Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as in the springtime the sun’s heat is fierce and intense, causing all ghee and oils to become liquid and moist, while everything else that was frozen melts away, and the waters of lakes and ponds likewise dry up;
even so, Kāśyapa!

If good sons or good daughters—whether followers of our own path or of external paths—listen to this *Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* with a sincere heart, even for the sake of fame or gain, and cause it to enter their ears and settle in their minds; whether they have already resolved upon Bodhi or have not yet resolved upon it, the bodies of all such persons will be moistened and nourished, serving as the cause for Bodhi. For this reason, I declare that these good sons and good daughters are all Bodhisattvas.
Thus, this *Vaipulya Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is an accumulation of merit with inexhaustible awakened wisdom; for this reason, I call it the "Spring Marsh. Why is that?
Because it develops the eternally abiding Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, good son!

Just as when the light of the sun and moon shines forth, all other lights no longer appear; so too, when the light of this *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* shines forth, the light of the merits of all other sūtras and samādhis no longer appears.
Therefore, good sons and good daughters!

Upon hearing this *Vaipulya Mahāparinirvāṇa*, even if they have not yet been able to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path, the sunlight of *nirvāṇa* has already entered within them as the cause for bodhi; for this reason, it is called the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If all sentient beings necessarily possess the causes and conditions for bodhi that enter into their bodies, for what reason does the World-Honored One say that those who commit the four *pārājika* offenses, those who commit the five *ānantarya* crimes, those who slander the sutras and the Dharma, and the *icchantikas* act as poisonous thorns within the True Dharma?”
"As the Buddha has said, if those who have not yet resolved their minds possess the cause for enlightenment, what distinction would there be?
Those four types of people should then be free from evil offenses.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Except for those of the icchantika nature, all other sentient beings who hear this Vaipulya Sūtra of the Mahāparinirvāṇa and take it as the cause for Bodhi—know that these individuals have already made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in the past; therefore, they have been able to hear this sūtra, and no other remaining sins can prevail against them."
"Why is this? Because this Mahāyāna possesses the power of great skillful means, which brings forth the nature of all Tathāgatas.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Those who have not yet resolved their minds for enlightenment have no inclination toward it; upon hearing of it, they turn away and abandon it.
By what means could such persons attain the cause of bodhi?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"As for those who have not yet resolved their minds [for enlightenment], even though they do not delight in it and turn away from it, they still remember this sutra and do not forget it in their hearts. When they lie down to sleep, they see great spirits and deities in their dreams manifesting terrifying forms, saying: 'Ho! Good son!'"
"You must contemplate Bodhi; if you do not take pleasure in turning toward it, I shall kill you.
He was immediately struck with terror and contemplated Bodhi, continuing to do so even after he had awakened.

Furthermore, after that person’s life has ended, they fall into the hells; they see their retribution for those sins and remember it. They likewise remember falling among the hungry ghosts and being born in the heavens. Therein, they are able to give rise to the mind of bodhi. Regarding this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the lack of joy [in the Lesser Vehicle] is forever extinguished from this point on. Such is the cause of bodhi; with such causes and such conditions, one establishes bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a great cloud rising in the void and raining upon the great earth; though the water does not remain upon withered trees, mountain rocks, or high ridges, it flows down to fill the low-lying fields, ponds, and reservoirs, which sentient beings then enjoy. This Mahāyāna rain of the Great Dharma falls equally upon icchantikas as it falls upon wood, stone, and high ridges, yet these do not receive the moisture of the conditions for Bodhi."
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a seed that has been parched until it is dry and scorched; even if there were timely rains for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, they could not cause it to sprout. The icchantikas are also like this: although they may hear this *Vaipulya Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they will ultimately be unable to produce the sprout of Bodhi."
Why is this? It is because their roots of goodness have been extinguished, like parched grain seeds.
Furthermore, son of good family!

For example, if a bright pearl is placed in turbid water, the water immediately becomes clear; yet if it is cast into the mud, it cannot make it clear. This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is also like this: even when placed within the turbid waters of the five sins of immediate retribution and the four offenses involving expulsion committed by sentient beings, it can still clarify them and cause them to resolve upon Bodhicitta; however, if it is cast into the mud of an icchantika, it cannot produce the cause for Bodhi even after hundreds of thousands of millions of years.
Why is this? Because they lack roots of goodness.
Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a medicinal tree called the "King of Medicine" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*), which can cure everything. Whether its roots, trunk, flowers, leaves, sap, or fragrance are consumed by someone, applied to the body, or even merely smelled, whether they find it pleasant or unpleasant, all their illnesses are eliminated—except for those that are inevitably fatal, which it cannot heal.
Thus it is, son of good family!

This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* can completely cure the heavy illnesses of the evil karma of all sentient beings. Even those who have committed the four defeats (*catur-āpatti*) or the crimes of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), as well as those among the various non-Buddhists who take no pleasure in Bodhi—if they hear even a single word of this Vaipulya sūtra, it shall become the cause for their Bodhi.
Why is this? Because this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* cures all evils, with the sole exception of the icchantikas.
Why is this? Because they lack the cause for awakening (*bodhi*).

It is like a human body: when there is a wound or a damaged area, medicinal ointment can be applied to eliminate various diseases; yet if there is no wound or damage, the ointment cannot take effect. The *icchantikas* are just like this: they cannot be wounded or damaged so as to receive the cause for awakening.
"Furthermore, good son!
For example, just as a diamond can destroy all manner of jewels, yet its power cannot break the horn of a white sheep;

so too this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* can destroy all evil dharmas that have been accomplished, establishing the causes for Bodhi, yet it alone cannot destroy the causes for Bodhi that arise from the evil of an icchantika."
"Furthermore, good son!

For example, when the branches and trunks of various trees are cut, they soon grow back as before. In the same way, if sentient beings who have committed various sinful deeds hear this *Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, the cause of Bodhi will arise within them. However, it is like the *tāla* tree, which does not grow back once its trunk is severed; the *icchantikas* are also like this, for they can never produce the branches and leaves of Bodhi."
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a great cloud and rain arising in the sky; yet those raindrops do not abide in the sky. Likewise, this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* universally rains down the rain of Dharma, but upon the rain of icchantikas, it does not abide."
"Not cultivating reality, one does not come; that ultimate state cannot be seen.
Those various evil and unwholesome karmas are what the world deems most base and contemptible."
"Those who cultivate it well are said to cultivate bodhi. As for 'not coming,' if one does not cultivate it oneself, one will ultimately not attain it oneself.
'Reality' refers to subtle and secret supreme karma; as for such supreme karma, toward whom would it not come?"
This refers to the icchantikas;
those who have forever abandoned the wholesome mind are called icchantikas.
What is the root of these various classes of icchantikas who are characterized by overweening pride?
The unwholesome karma of slandering the sutras and the Dharma takes this as its root; one should know that such slanderous, rebellious, violent, and harmful acts are what the wise fear.

For example, on a perilous road filled with many bandits, a violent, arrogant, and foolish person, unaware of the danger, proceeds recklessly and is harmed by the robbers; yet the Great Powerful Dharma King travels this same path without any fear.

Regarding "not seeing the ultimate limit": one never sees the ultimate limit of the evil karma of those icchantikas, nor does one see the ultimate limit of their immeasurable cycle of birth and death. I have briefly described this accumulation of evils; were one to hear it in full detail, it would be truly terrifying.

Even if all sentient beings were to simultaneously resolve their minds to attain the Unsurpassed Way, these Perfectly Enlightened Ones would still not see the ultimate end of the various evils of those icchantikas. At the time they attain perfect enlightenment, what further end would they not see? All sentient beings, having destroyed birth and death, shall all achieve the Buddha-way; yet they do not see the Buddhas entering *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

Impermanence and extinction are like the extinguishing of a lamp’s flame; those who commit various evil deeds and are greatly despicable in the world—such as the icchantikas who are forever severed from the causes, conditions, and merits of bodhi—are called the despicable of the world. Yet that they attain the name of "Buddha" through final awakening within this Mahāyāna is itself a form of despicableness.
Such is the nature of all Buddhas:
"One who has already committed evil deeds is like *sāja* milk curdling;
the fool is lightly burned, like fire covered by ashes."
"There are those who resemble Arhats yet act like icchantikas, and those who resemble icchantikas yet act with loving-kindness like Arhats.
Those who resemble Arhats yet are icchantikas are sentient beings who slander the Vaipulya sūtras.
Those who resemble icchantikas yet are Arhats disparage the Śrāvakas and extensively preach the Vaipulya, saying to sentient beings:"
"I and you all are equally Bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because everyone possesses the Tathāgata-nature."
"Yet those sentient beings who are called icchantikas shall say:
'The Tathāgata has bestowed upon us the prediction of our future enlightenment; you, too, are like this.

We and you shall all together cast off immeasurable afflictions, hordes of Māras, and evil karma, just as one breaks a water jar; we shall surely attain bodhi through this sūtra, so do not harbor further doubt.'"

"Just as a loyal warrior, commissioned by his king, enters a foreign land to extol the king's virtues, never wavering even at the cost of his own life, so too are we today. Since the Tathāgata has prophesied that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, we shall surely not spare our own lives to widely proclaim this sutra among the ignorant and foolish."
This is called a Mahāsattva who resembles an icchantika.

If there is one dwelling in the forest (āraṇyaka) who is foolish and lacks wisdom, appearing like an arhat yet slandering the Vaipulya sūtras, such a deluded ordinary person is taken by others to be a true arhat or a great being (mahāsattva). This evil bhikṣu manifests himself in a secluded forest hermitage and positions himself as if he were a true arhat; yet he never conforms to the practices of the forest, instead making heterodox claims based on four causes and conditions, saying that the Vaipulya sūtras are all the words of Māra, and declaring that the Mahāyāna is a spear and sword that pierces the true Dharma of the wise. He asserts that all Buddhas and World-Honored Ones are impermanent while preaching them to be eternally abiding. One should know that this is the mark of destroying the true Dharma and causing schism in the Saṅgha; one who makes such statements is called an icchantika.
Therefore it is said:
"One who has committed evil deeds is like *sajja* milk or curd;
the fool is lightly burned, like fire covered by ashes."
"In this way, son of good family!
You should know that the *Vaipulya Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is the definitive teaching of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
The Mahāyāna is the most unsurpassed, like a maṇi jewel—luminous, pure, and free from defilement."
Furthermore, good son!

Just as a lotus flower does not fail to bloom once it has been touched by the light of the sun, so it is with all sentient beings: upon hearing this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* even once, whether they have not yet resolved their minds or do not delight in bodhi, these individuals will certainly become causes for bodhi.

The reason that those icchantikas are eternally severed from the Tathāgata-nature is that they have committed great evil karma through slander; they are like silkworms who entangle themselves in their own cocoons, having no way out.
The icchantikas are likewise; they are unable to develop or give rise to the causes of bodhi regarding the tathāgata-nature, even until the very limit of all existence in saṃsāra.
"Furthermore, good son!

Just as the utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka grow from within the mud yet are not defiled by that mud, so too it is with sentient beings who cultivate the Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra; they likewise are not defiled by afflictions."
Why is this? Because the nature of the Tathāgata is not subject to defilement.
Furthermore, son of good family!
For example, when a cool breeze arises in a land, all sentient beings whose pores encounter this wind have their heat and afflictions entirely removed.
In the same way, son of good family!

This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, with its ambrosial flavor of the Dharma, moistens all sentient beings and causes them to give rise to the cause of Bodhi, with the sole exception of those who are icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a skilled physician who understands the eight branches of medical science and is able to cure all diseases, with the sole exception of the *asādhyā* (incurable) disease."
In this way, son of good family!

All sūtras and various samādhis can cure all the diseases of afflictions such as lust, anger, and ignorance, yet they cannot cure the transgression of the four grave prohibitions or the karma of the five immediate offenses.
"Good son!

Furthermore, there is a skilled physician who surpasses the eight branches of medicine; he is able to cure all the diseases of sentient beings as long as their life-force has not yet expired, but he cannot cause them to recover once their life-force has been exhausted."

This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is likewise: it can cure all the afflictions of sentient beings, even those who do not delight in bodhi and have not yet resolved to attain it, causing them all to give rise to the aspiration for bodhi—except for those who are icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!
It is like a blind person who cannot see the five colors; a skilled physician can treat them so that their eyes open and become clear, yet he alone cannot cure one who is born blind.

This *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is also like this: for all sentient beings, including śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who do not delight in bodhi and have not yet resolved to attain it, it treats them all so that they may open their eye of wisdom and resolve to attain bodhi, with the sole exception of those born blind—the icchantikas."
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who has mastered the eight branches of medicine; for all sentient beings who suffer from illness, he writes his incantations upon their bodies and is able to cause all diseases to be completely cured.

This *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is also like this: it can eliminate all the afflictions of sentient beings—those who do not delight in Bodhi and have not yet resolved their minds, as well as those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the karma of the five immediate offenses—and establish them securely in Bodhi."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Those who have committed the four grave offenses or the five crimes of immediate retribution are like a tāla tree that has been cut down; likewise, those who take no pleasure in bodhi and have not yet resolved to attain it—how can one cause them to give rise to the causes for bodhi?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If these sentient beings, whether in a dream or at the time of their death, fall into the hells and give rise to a mind of regret, thinking:
'Alas! We have violated the True Dharma and brought this sin upon ourselves.'"

Thus they give rise to a vow, thinking: "If I am to escape birth in other realms and be born here, I must, wherever I may be, resolve to practice the path of a Bodhisattva. By the majestic spiritual power of this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, these beings will surely give rise to the resolve for enlightenment when born among gods or humans; therefore, I say that even those who have committed the four grave offenses or the five acts of immediate retribution can all give rise to the resolve for enlightenment as the cause of Bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who compiles various medicines called *agada*. Wherever this excellent medicine is applied, all poisons are completely neutralized and eliminated, with the sole exception of one kind of supreme venomous snake, which it cannot subdue."

This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is likewise: all those with the four kinds of poisonous snakes of pride, those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the deeds of immediate retribution, and those who do not delight in bodhi nor have yet resolved their minds toward it—all are established upon the path to bodhi.
Why is this? Because this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is the most supreme and foremost of all excellent medicines; it is only those who are like the venomous snake—the icchantikas—who are excluded.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who mixes various medicines and applies them to a drum. If there are sentient beings wounded in battle, upon hearing the sound of that drum, all their wounds are healed, except for those whose life has ended and who must certainly die."

The sound of the Dharma drum of this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is likewise so: when all sentient beings hear its sound, the arrows of lust, anger, and delusion are removed; those who do not delight in Bodhi and have not yet resolved their minds, as well as those who have committed the four pārājika offenses and the ānantarya crimes, are all healed and restored—except for those of the icchantika class.
"Furthermore, good son!

For example, when it is dark at night, all household affairs of the people of Jambudvīpa are suspended; once the sun has risen, those people are able to attend to their domestic duties. In this way, for sentient beings, hearing various sūtras and samādhis is like the darkness of night. Hearing this subtle and secret teaching of the *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is like seeing the true Dharma when the sun rises, just as a farmer encounters the rains of summer."

In the Mahāyāna sūtras, immeasurable sentient beings all receive the prediction [of enlightenment] as they manifest their Tathāgata-nature; eight thousand śrāvakas likewise receive the prediction in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, with the sole exception of those icchantikas who are like ice in winter.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a person who is possessed by a non-human spirit or afflicted by a malignant poison, yet encounters a skilled physician who dispels the affliction through incantations or medicinal herbs. Thus, the ailment is immediately eliminated."
Thus it is, good son!

If this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*—whether by bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, or even non-Buddhists—is written as a scroll in various places and expounded for others, any sentient beings who read or hear it will all plant the causes for Bodhi. Even those who do not delight in Bodhi and have not yet resolved their minds on the Way, as well as those guilty of the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, shall have all their various evil poisons completely extinguished, with the sole exception of those belonging to the class of icchantikas.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

It is like a great king in whose body there are worms that secretly devour his flesh, yet the king does not perceive it. At that time, there is a skilled physician who, knowing the symptoms of the disease, says to the king:
'There is an ailment within your body; you should treat it with haste.'"

At that time, the king did not believe him and was unwilling to allow him to treat him; his teacher, out of fear, did not dare to give him medicine, but secretly employed incantations to cause the worms to fall off naturally. When the king saw that his illness had been cured, he finally believed the teacher’s words and treated him with great hospitality.

All sentient beings are likewise thus: upon hearing the *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, they may have no desire for Bodhi or have not yet resolved to attain it; yet the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ skillful means to preach for them. Although they do not accept it immediately, they will awaken to it and plant the causes for Bodhi either in their dreams or at the time of death—except for those who are icchantikas.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a skilled physician who well-instructs his son in the study of the eight branches of medicine, withholding the most essential and secret formulas until they are hidden from him; only after he knows that the son has mastered the eight branches and attained thorough proficiency does he then teach him all the most essential and secret formulas."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is likewise in this regard: he first instructs the sons of the Dharma—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—to train in the eradication of immeasurable afflictions, cultivating the perception of the body as lacking solidity, being an accumulation of manifold sufferings, impermanent, subject to decay, empty, and devoid of "mine-ness. Furthermore, he teaches them the ninefold scriptures so that they may master them thoroughly; only then does he teach them this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, enabling them to know that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata-nature, which is an eternally abiding dharma, thereby causing them all to give rise to the cause for unsurpassed bodhi, with the sole exception of those of icchantika nature.
Thus it is, son of good family!
This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* is immeasurable, incalculable, and inconceivable; you should know that this sutra is the unsurpassed art and the essential secret of the Great Physician.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a boatman who, having ferried people across by means of a boat, returns to ferry others once they have reached the other shore. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: they board the Mahāyāna boat of parinirvāṇa and deliver those sentient beings who are ready to be transformed; once they have entered parinirvāṇa, they again ferry sentient beings across in other places. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Great Boatman; for this reason, the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, yet he manifests appearing and disappearing for the sake of delivering sentient beings."
"Furthermore, good son! It is like a person who boards a ship wishing to cross the great ocean:

if they obtain a favorable wind, they will swiftly reach the other shore; if they do not obtain the wind, they may spend years or even drown. In the same way, if sentient beings obtain the wind of Mahāyāna parinirvāṇa, they will swiftly transcend birth and death to reach the shore of Bodhi; if they do not obtain it, they will forever drown in the bitter sea of saṃsāra."

"Furthermore, son of good family! It is like a person who enters the sea and encounters turbulent waves; seeing no way to escape, he sits upright and awaits death. Suddenly, he is encountered by a wind-king who blows him to a certain land, arriving there without even realizing it was dark. He rejoices immeasurably and conceives a sense of wonder. In this same way, this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* acts as a great wind-king. Sentient beings do not know of it and take no pleasure in turning toward it to resolve upon bodhicitta; yet, the wind of parinirvāṇa blows secretly until they reach the realm of bodhi, whereupon they finally realize the truth and conceive a sense of wonder."
"Furthermore, good son!
Just as a snake sheds its skin and moves elsewhere yet does not actually die;
so it is, good son!"

The Tathāgata, having entered parinirvāṇa, has cast off that former body as one discards a sloughed-off skin; for this reason, the Tathāgata is called the Sugata. Having abandoned the provisional body that was like a poisonous tree, he may again manifest transformations through skillful means in other Jambudvīpas.
Therefore, O son of good family!
"You should know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma.

Furthermore, son of good family, it is like a goldsmith who, having obtained fine, genuine gold, can fashion various ornaments, vessels, and garments according to his will; so too it is with the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas. Following those to be transformed within the twenty-five states of existence, they are able to manifest their bodies to deliver and liberate them. For this reason, the Tathāgata is called the 'immeasurable body' and is also called 'eternally abiding.'"
"Furthermore, son of good family!

Just as the *āmra* tree and the *jambu* tree undergo transformations through three seasons—sometimes having lush foliage, sometimes flowers and fruit, and sometimes withering and falling away—it is not that those trees die and are born anew;
in the same way, son of good family!"

The body of skillful means of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, also manifests at the three times for the sake of teaching and transforming others; it displays birth, the attainment of Buddhahood, and the manifestation of parinirvāṇa, yet in reality it is eternally present and never extinguished.
"Good son!
Such is the secret body of the Tathāgata; likewise, the secret speech of the Tathāgata and the esoteric teachings of his skillful means are also difficult to know.
As for these esoteric teachings of skillful means, good son!"

For example, when a great king issues commands to his ministers, there are likewise such secret instructions; as when he might say, "Bring the *saindhava*," and yet the single term *saindhava* has four actual referents: first, salt;
second, a washbasin; third, a horse; [and fourth, a person from the Sindhu region].
Fourth is the sword.
These four items are all called *saindhava*.
If, when the king is about to eat, he commands his attendants to bring *saindhava*, the ministers should know that the king must be seeking salt.
If, after the king has finished his meal, he asks for *sindhuva*, the ministers should know that he must be asking for a washing basin;
if he wishes to go to the park and asks for *sindhuva*, the ministers should know that the king must be asking for a horse;
when on the verge of battle, if he asks for *sindhuva*, the ministers should know that he must be asking for a sharp sword.
When a king has such concealed speech, his ministers should likewise understand its underlying intent.
In this same way, son of good family,
this hidden teaching of the Mahāyāna also possesses four kinds of impermanence as described.

Those good sons should know that when the Tathāgata is born in Jambudvīpa and manifests *nirvāṇa*, this is the Mahāyāna practice of the perception of impermanence. If the Tathāgata speaks of the extinction of the True Dharma, his disciples should understand it thus: when the Tathāgata speaks of suffering, this is the Mahāyāna cultivation of the perception of suffering. When the Tathāgata says that the body is a vessel of manifold afflictions, and further says that even the Sangha Jewel shall eventually pass into extinction, his disciples should understand it thus.

The Buddha taught that there is no self; this Mahāyāna cultivates the perception of non-self. If it speaks of non-perception, emptiness, nothingness, and liberation, his disciples should understand this: this Mahāyāna teaches that one attains liberation from the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).

Therefore, emptiness is taught so that all sufferings may be extinguished; it is taught as non-existence, as ultimate bliss, and as signless—a state that cannot be destroyed by impermanence or change. For this reason, it is called the eternally abiding dharma, the unchanging dharma.

You should know that liberation is itself the Tathāgata, and that which is the Tathāgata is the Tathāgata-nature (tathāgatagarbha), which exists within the bodies of all sentient beings. One who knows this is my disciple and is well-versed in the subtle and esoteric teachings of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, good son!

It is like a drought, when medicinal herbs, fragrant flowers, sweet fruits, and trees all wither and fail to produce fruit; all other water and land plants and trees likewise become parched and lose their luster, and it will be difficult for them to grow again the following year."
Thus it is, son of good family!

After my parinirvāṇa, these disciples of the *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* will be like flowers and fruits in a drought that cannot bear fruit; they will be like those in a city plundered by bandits who have lost their true treasures and guard only heaps of chaff and husks. Once these wicked bhikṣus have lost the treasure, they will abridge and compile [the teachings] without properly understanding the meaning, becoming lax, arrogant, and indolent. Alas, what a great peril! The future age shall be most terrifying.

How great is this benefit! Sentient beings of the future who hear this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* with their ears, and who, according to what they have heard, uphold, recite, and explain its meaning and purport extensively for others, shall thereby attain true bodhi.
"Furthermore, good son!

Suppose there is a country, city, or village where there are those who sell milk; some mix water with it to deceive others in order to obtain wealth. The sellers of milk act in the same way, mixing water and selling it, deceiving one another in succession, so that when people buy and consume it, it has no flavor of milk."

Thus it is, good son! After my parinirvāṇa, during the eighty-odd years before the True Dharma has perished, this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* shall circulate in the world in Jambudvīpa. At that time, wicked bhikṣus will be lax and indolent; they will associate with the factions of Māras to subvert and disrupt the True Dharma. They will compose their own sūtras, treatises, verses, and hymns of praise, taking what is not right to be right and what is right to be wrong. They will abridge, expand, add to, or subtract from the text for the sake of gain and profit, desiring to amass many unrighteous goods.

They will corrupt the true flavor of the Dharma, making it thin and tasteless. Furthermore, they will employ heterodox teachings and incorrect terminology to mislead those who receive them; they will neither respect nor honor [the Dharma], harboring internal deceit and hypocrisy while putting on the appearance of delighting in the Dharma for the sake of gain and profit.
"At that time, this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* shall be subjected to slander and humiliation by such people as these.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa!"
For this reason, sons and daughters of good family should diligently apply skillful means and establish the resolve of a true man regarding the *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

Why is this so? Because the nature of a Tathāgata is the dharma of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*), whereas the disposition of women gives rise to much defiled attachment toward all dharmas; their power is insufficient to give rise to the wondrous flavor of the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.

Good son! It is like the moisture exuded from the body of a mosquito, which cannot moisten this great earth. The nature of women is like this great earth, abounding in many cravings and attachments. Just as all the rains of heaven and the myriad currents of the hundred rivers flow into the great ocean, yet that great ocean is never satisfied, so too is the nature of women: they greedily receive the five desires without ever reaching satiety.
Therefore, Kāśyapa,
if a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to skillfully distance themselves from the dharma of women, they should diligently practice this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Why is this? Because this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* explains the nature of the Tathāgata as the dharma of the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
If there are sentient beings who do not know that they themselves possess the nature of the Tathāgata, although the world calls them men, I say that such people are women.
If there are women who are able to know that they possess the Tathāgata-nature, although the world may call them by the name "women," I declare that such individuals are men.
Thus it is, son of good family!

This *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is an accumulation of immeasurable and boundless merit; it extensively explains that all sentient beings possess the Tathāgata-nature. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to swiftly realize this Tathāgata-nature, they should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate this sūtra.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
Having now practiced the *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*, I have for the first time realized that my own body possesses the Tathāgata-nature; only now am I definitively a man.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Good son!
You should diligently apply skillful means to study this profound Dharma, extracting the deep flavor of the Dharma just as a bee gathers nectar from flowers.
For example, Kāśyapa!"
The moisture from mosquitoes and gnats cannot saturate this great earth.

In the same way, son of good family, in future ages, the wicked bhikṣus who corrupt and disrupt the sūtras and the Dharma are as numerous and immeasurable as a high, parched land; they cannot be moistened by this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Why is this? You should know that it is because the signs of the extinction and decline of the True Dharma have appeared.
"Furthermore, son of good family!
For example, at the end of summer and the beginning of winter, after the continuous downpours of autumn rain, the warm moisture remains latent.

In the same way, son of good family, after my parinirvāṇa, when the True Dharma has declined and perished, this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* shall circulate in the south. At that time, it will be submerged by the clouds of rain of various heterodox and false teachings that are not the Dharma. Then, those Bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma in the south shall take this sūtra and all other Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras and come to Kaśmīra, where they shall remain latent within the earth.

Alas! At this time, the signs of the total extinction of the Dharma appear; clouds of non-Dharma rain down, filling the world. Those who cultivate the Dharma-rain of the Tathāgata’s grace—the Dharma-protecting Bodhisattvas, the heroes among men—all remain hidden.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The natures of all Buddhas, Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are without distinction; we only pray that you will explain this extensively so that all sentient beings may attain understanding."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"Suppose there is a person who raises many milch cows, keeping those that are blue, yellow, red, and white in separate herds. When he wishes to perform a sacrifice to the heavens, he gathers all the cows together and milks them all into a single vessel, so that they become one uniform color like that of a conch shell."
In this way, good son!
The Buddhas, Tathāgatas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas are pure in nature and are all of one color. Why is this so?
Because their outflows are likewise exhausted.
It is like a goldsmith who takes various colored gold ores and, by smelting and refining them, produces pure gold of a single color. Why is this so?

Because immeasurable and innumerable coarse and mineral-like afflictions are all extinguished, one should therefore believe this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*: all sentient beings possess the true nature of the Tathāgata, and they are all of one and the same color.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature without distinction.’”
Since this point is not yet understood, let us for now set aside the matter of sentient beings.
As the World-Honored One has said:
"Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas do not attain the Great Parinirvāṇa; only the Tathāgata attains this Great Parinirvāṇa."
"Therefore, you should know that the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas are not the same as the Tathāgata.
If there were no distinction, why would the World-Honored One alone have practiced skillful means and accumulated merit for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"What I previously spoke was the Tathāgata’s skillful and esoteric teaching, stating that the śrāvakas do not attain nirvāṇa."

Therefore, one should know that all [beings] attain parinirvāṇa by means of this *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*; yet parinirvāṇa is exclusively the domain of the Buddha. For this reason, this sutra is named the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

This is indeed a distinction. As the Buddha has taught, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas shall all return to the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, just as the hundred rivers flow into the great ocean, which is the eternally abiding Dharma.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I am the most constant.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
“How is it, World-Honored One, is the nature of the Tathāgata not different from difference?
The Buddha said,
“There is difference.”
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha,
"In what way are they different?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Just as with cow’s milk, so too is the Tathāgata-nature of all śrāvakas;
just as when it has become curdled milk, so too is the Tathāgata-nature of all pratyekabuddhas;
just as when it has become clarified butter (sarpis), so too is the Tathāgata-nature of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.”
Just as it is with clarified butter, so too is the nature of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
In this way, son of good family,
there are four kinds of distinctions in this Mahāyāna *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is the nature of all sentient beings?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
“Just as when milk has not yet formed, it is mixed with water and blood, so too are the Tathāgata’s true nature covered by immeasurable afflictions.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“As the World-Honored One has said:
‘In the city of Kauśāmbī there is a candāla named Nanda who shall attain the Buddha-way.
Among the number of the thousand Buddhas of this world-system, the World-Honored One has prophesied that he will attain the Buddha-way in the mere duration of a single thought-moment.”
"For what reason did the World-Honored One not prophesy that the Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others would swiftly attain the Buddha-way?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"There are some śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who do not make a vow for swiftness in order to protect and uphold the True Dharma; yet there are those who do make such a vow for swiftness. Because these vows differ in their degree of intensity, the World-Honored One, by the power of their bodhi, has prophesied that they will swiftly attain the Buddha-way."
Furthermore, good son!
It is like a merchant carrying a maṇi jewel who, traveling along a road through a village of wild folk, shouts for sale of his precious treasure.
When the wild folk hear the sound and come to look, they see the jewel but do not recognize it; they immediately laugh loudly, calling it a mere brick or stone.
In this way, good son!
The Tathāgata bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas that they shall attain the Buddha-way and reach the most supreme state.

In a future age, there will be bhikṣus who are lax and indolent, who do not recognize true jewels and are like common folk; they have left the household life out of illness, hardship, or poverty, their faith is shallow, and they subsist by wrong livelihood through flattery and crookedness. If they hear the Tathāgata grant a prediction to a śrāvaka, they will laugh aloud. You should know that such people are merely the semblance of śramaṇas, not true śramaṇas.

Therefore, noble son, there are those who make a vow to swiftly uphold the True Dharma, and others who do not make such a vow for swift upholding; for this reason, the Tathāgata bestows predictions upon them according to their respective pace, whether slow or fast.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how should a bodhisattva-mahāsattva obtain an indestructible retinue?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Diligently practicing skillful means to protect and uphold the True Dharma—this constitutes the indestructible retinue of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the hero among men."
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What kind of sentient beings do not know the six flavors?”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Those who do not know that the Three Jewels endure forever from beginning to end are sentient beings who do not know the six flavors.

Just as a person with a disordered sense of taste cannot distinguish between the six flavors—sweet, bitter, pungent, sour, salty, and bland—all sentient beings are likewise; being ignorant and lacking wisdom, they do not know that the Three Jewels are eternal dharmas. For this reason, they are called those who do not know the flavor."
"Furthermore, good son!

Those sentient beings who do not know that the Tathāgata is an eternally abiding dharma—I call them those born blind. Those sentient beings with physical eyes who know that the nature of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding—I call them those with the divine eye."
If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the Mahāyāna, are able to believe and rejoice in it, I say that these individuals are also called those with the "divine eye.
Even if sentient beings possess the divine eye, if they do not know that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, I say that such individuals are called those with the "fleshly eye."
Why is this? Because the nature of the Tathāgata is eternally abiding and truly real, yet they are unable to diligently cultivate it.
"Furthermore, good son!
You should know that the Tathāgata acts as a father and mother to all sentient beings. Why is this?

He is able to manifest in all the various forms and types of sentient beings, entering their respective realms to preach the Dharma for them; with a single voice he preaches the Dharma, yet each different species understands it according to its own kind, exclaiming:
“Excellent! The Tathāgata expounds the Dharma through my voice.
“Furthermore, good son!”

It is like a person who has given birth to a child; when the child is sixteen months old and its speech is not yet correct, the parents, wishing to teach it to speak, first mimic its sounds and gradually instruct it. One should know that it is not the parents who are truly incorrect.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are also like this: for the sake of teaching and transforming others, they assume the same physical forms, voices, and languages as those beings; yet these Tathāgatas do not truly become identical to them, but rather manifest through skillful means in accordance with the world.

Chapter 18: Rejoicing The Great Parinirvāṇa Sūtra, Chapter Eighteen: Rejoicing At that time, the World-Honored One emitted various colored rays of light from his face, which illuminated the fourfold assembly. Once the radiance had shone forth, the elder Cunda promptly presented the final offering to the Tathāgata and the great assembly.
At that time, Cunda and his retinue were filled with great joy and raised their voices in praise, saying:
"How tragic and rare! To make offerings to the Tathāgata is a feat difficult to encounter again."
He then took various bowls made of many kinds of jewels, filled them with food of the finest flavor, and brought them toward the Buddha.
At that moment, a deity of great majesty and supernatural power appeared before him and addressed Cunda, saying:
"Do not yet present these offerings; I pray that you allow us to behold the Tathāgata for even a brief moment longer."
At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted a radiance that illuminated that devaputra; the deity, receiving the Buddha’s sacred intent, permitted Cunda to approach.

Then, the devas and all the various classes of sentient beings, each with their own distinct voices, harbored feelings of sorrow within and their mournful cries shook the earth; together with Cunda, they made offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, presenting the final *dānapāramitā*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to let the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and the entire assembly know that the time had arrived, again emitted a radiance that illuminated the entire gathering.
Then the bhikṣus, knowing that the time had come, each adjusted their dignified deportment and took up their alms bowls according to the ritual for receiving offerings.
The elder Cunda prepared various seats made of many jewels for the Buddha and the Sangha, hanging silk banners, canopies, incense, flowers, and necklaces of pearls.
At that time, the adornments of the trichiliocosm were so exquisite and wonderful that it was like the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The elder Cunda stood before the Buddha and, filled with grief and sorrowful despondency, addressed the Buddha once more:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will still take pity on us and remain for a kalpa, or even longer than a kalpa."
The Buddha told Cunda:
"If you wish for me to remain long in the world, you should know that the time has come; you ought to quickly provide the final *dānapāramitā*."
Cunda replied to the Buddha,
"So be it, World-Honored One!
At that time, all sentient beings of various kinds— devas, humans, and bodhisattvas— cried out in unison:
"How marvelous, Cunda!
This is your final offering;
how marvelous, Cunda!"
"This would have been a most magnificent offering; yet now, these provisions we have prepared shall become useless here.
Thus they each lamented, grieving, sorrowing, and suffering in distress.

At that time, from every single pore of the World-Honored One’s own body, there emerged immeasurable transformation Buddhas, each accompanied by a retinue of bhikṣus; they caused all those beings to receive offerings, and at that moment, all sentient beings were filled with great joy.
At that time, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the offerings provided by Cunda sufficed for the entire great assembly that had gathered.
Cunda was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"Today, the Tathāgata and the entire great assembly have all accepted my final offering; thereafter, the Tathāgata shall enter parinirvāṇa."
The other sentient beings also thought to themselves:
"Today the Tathāgata, together with the great assembly, accepts my final offering of food; thereafter he will enter nirvāṇa and accept no further invitations."

At that time, the ground beside the Sāla Grove was narrow; yet, by the Buddha’s supernatural power, even in spaces as small as the point of a needle, there were immeasurable Buddhas with their retinues sitting and eating therein.
At that time, the assembly of devas, humans, and asuras all sighed with great compassion and spoke these words:
"Today the Tathāgata accepts our final offering of food before he enters parinirvāṇa."
"What further service shall we perform?
Alas! We are orphaned and without protection.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for all of them:
"Do not lament, for such is the nature of all Buddhas;
though it is called nirvāṇa, it is not yet ultimate extinction.
The Tathāgata abides eternally in the Dharma, forever dwelling in the most profound peace."
All you who have doubts, listen attentively as I now speak.
Having already abandoned the perception of food, my body is free from the affliction of hunger and thirst;
I shall now, for your sake, explain the Dharma of sympathetic joy.
May all sentient beings attain peace and happiness.
The nature of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is the true, eternally abiding Dharma;
now that you have heard this, you should diligently cultivate it through skillful means.
Just as the crow and the owl, whose natures are utterly opposed,
can be made to travel in a single flock and dwell together in mutual enjoyment;
so does the Tathāgata regard all beings, just as he regards Rāhula.
One should abandon compassion and enter forever into Nirvana;
one can cause the fierce venomous snake and the hare to share the same burrow.
When the Tathāgata abandons compassion, he enters forever into Nirvana.
He can cause the eranda tree to possess the fragrance of the hundred-petaled flower;
yet if the Tathāgata were to abandon his compassion, he would enter parinirvāṇa forever.
He can cause the kārūṣaka fruit to have a flavor equal to that of the tāmalī.
If the Tathāgata were to abandon his compassion and enter nirvāṇa forever,
he could not cause even the icchantikas to attain equal enlightenment;
yet if the Tathāgata were to abandon his compassion and enter nirvāṇa forever, [he would fail in this].
If all sentient beings were to attain the Buddha-way at once,
the Tathāgata would abandon his compassion and enter parinirvāṇa forever.
Even if the water of mosquitoes and gnats were to submerge and destroy this great earth;
The hundred rivers all overflow, and the great ocean is completely filled;
yet the Tathāgata has relinquished his compassion and entered forever into nirvāṇa.
Because you, all sentient beings, deeply delight in the True Dharma;
It is said that the Tathāgata has forever extinguished sorrow, lamentation, and grief;
from this day forth, do not harbor thoughts of impermanence regarding the Tathāgata.
You should know that the nature of the Tathāgata is eternally present and unchanging.
The Dharma and the Saṅgha are likewise; they are all not subject to destruction.

"In this way, son of good family, these three dharmas are the words of the eternal, unchanging True Dharma (satya). When all sentient beings encounter various terrors, this teaching of the True Dharma can bring them peace and security."
To cross over all perilous wildernesses, this declaration of the Truth can cause one to attain deliverance;
this declaration of the Truth can cause even withered trees to sprout flowers and leaves once more.

If these four assemblies hear that these three dharmas are eternally abiding and speak with sympathetic joy, even if they have not yet resolved their minds or take pleasure in turning toward it, all such persons shall become causes for bodhi.
The three dharmas are eternally abiding; this is the Tathāgata’s most wondrous, sympathetic rejoicing, and his truthful teaching.

If bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs can explain the eternal abiding of these three dharmas for the sake of all sentient beings, it should be known that such individuals are worthy of receiving the offerings of all arhats;
if they differ from this, they are not so worthy.
"Even all those such as the *caṇḍālas* who take pleasure in hearing the Tathāgata’s words of rejoicing shall likewise be freed from all sorrow, fear, and terror.

At that time, the devas, humans, *asuras*, and others, hearing it said that the Tathāgata is the eternally abiding Dharma, felt joy in their hearts, their hearts became supple, their hearts attained truth, their hearts were freed from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), and their hearts became pure. Their countenances were serene and joyful like blooming lotuses; they scattered celestial flowers, burned various famous incenses, and played heavenly music as offerings to the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"Good son! What rare and extraordinary thing have you seen?"
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Indeed, World-Honored One!

I have witnessed a marvelous and unprecedented event: I saw all the devas, humans, asuras, and others who had prepared offerings, each receiving the Tathāgata and the great assembly partaking of their food and drink.”

Furthermore, they saw that within this space, though the ground was narrow, it accommodated the seats for the great assembly of Tathāgatas; even at the point of a single needle’s tip, there were immeasurable retinues of Buddhas receiving offerings and reciting verses of sympathetic joy.

Those sentient beings did not know one another, each thinking, "The Tathāgata alone has accepted my invitation. Yet now, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for Cunda, accepts his final *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving). By the Buddha's supernatural power, he causes this entire great assembly to be fully satisfied, yet the World-Honored One does not actually consume any food.

Only the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—such as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the prince of the Dharma, and other lions among men—can understand the Tathāgata’s skillful means in manifesting these transformations. This is a marvelous and unprecedented event, which Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are unable to know.
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
This is the eternal dharma of the Tathāgatas, infinite and immeasurable.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Cunda, saying:
“Have you seen anything extraordinary or unprecedented?
Cunda replied to the Buddha, “Indeed, I have seen it.
Just now I saw the Tathāgata’s body adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.”

In this way, the Tathāgatas are immeasurable and innumerable, surrounded by their retinues of bodhisattvas; now we behold the true body of the World-Honored One, dwelling alone amidst the great assembly like a medicinal tree, with the bodhisattvas surrounding him before and behind.
The Buddha told Cunda:

"The Buddhas mentioned earlier were all manifested transformations. Out of compassion and for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, they manifested these transformations so that their merits could not be exhausted; yet, all sentient beings were unable to know them."
Only those bodhisattvas who have accomplished immeasurable bodhisattva merits, the heroes among men, are able to know the Tathāgata’s skillful means of manifesting transformations.
You now, Cunda, likewise have accomplished the bodhisattva merits and the practices of the ten stages.
Cunda addressed the Buddha:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
We shall all practice the bodhisattva’s universal sympathetic joy.”
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Do not follow after the fruit of greed as you do in other sūtras.
Cunda addressed the Buddha:
"Are all other sūtras, then, not sūtras?
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Those [sūtras] speak of what remains."
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What is the meaning of this?
The Buddha told Cunda:
"As I have said: 'All praise giving; there is no one who censures giving.
Giving to those who violate the precepts brings little merit, while giving to those who uphold the precepts increases merit.'"

"I have taught this sutra; although it praises all forms of giving, there are distinctions among them. Giving to one who violates the precepts yields not even a hair’s breadth of merit, whereas giving to one who upholds the precepts brings about great fruits, though these do not necessarily all result in the same way."
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One, why have you spoken this verse praising the merit of all forms of giving?
The Buddha told Cunda:
"Except for one kind of person, I praise all forms of giving.
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Except for what kind of person do you praise all forms of giving?"
The Buddha told Cunda:
"With the exception of those who are icchantikas, who break the precepts, and who slander the Dharma, I praise all forms of giving.
Cunda addressed the Buddha:
“What is meant by ‘icchantika’?
The Buddha told Cunda:

“If bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās slander the sūtras and the Dharma, uttering evil words from their mouths without ever repenting or reforming, and have no heart of refuge in the sūtras and the Dharma—such persons as these are headed toward the path of the icchantika.”

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five crimes of immediate retribution, yet do not reform or repent, lacking a sense of shame; who never cherish or protect the True Dharma; who do not regard those who protect the Dharma as their spiritual friends; and who have never praised any virtuous deeds.
"If there are those with false views who deny the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, I say that such people are headed for the path of the icchantika.
Setting aside such types, I praise all forms of giving.
Cunda addressed the Buddha:
“What is meant by ‘violating the precepts’?
The Buddha told Cunda:
“Violating the four grave prohibitions, committing the five deeds of immediate retribution, and slandering the true Dharma.”
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Are there degrees of mitigation for such grave offenses?
The Buddha said:
"There is a distinction [in their status]: although they have violated the precepts, they still wear the Dharma robes and feel shame and remorse, thinking:
'Alas! I have now committed this grave offense; how strange it is that I have created such great suffering!'"
"Yet, harboring fear, they give rise to a mind that protects the Dharma.

I shall praise those who protect all dharmas and shall further subdue those who act contrary to the Dharma. They diligently cultivate the skillful means of the various meditative concentrations and samādhis within the Vaipulya sūtras; if they act in this manner, I declare that such persons have not violated the precepts."

Why is this so? Just as when the sunlight emerges, even the most subtle particles and obscurations no longer appear, so too, when one cultivates the sunlight of this Mahāyāna sūtra, the accumulated masses of countless and immeasurable sins are all utterly extinguished. For this reason, this sūtra states that those who protect the Dharma obtain great rewards.
If it were otherwise, this would be called the greatest violation of the precepts; to give to such as these brings not even a hair’s breadth of merit.
Furthermore, good son!

If those who have committed the four grave prohibitions can know the true nature of the Tathāgata and give rise to the mind that protects the Dharma, why is it that by bestowing [gifts] upon such as these, one obtains a great karmic fruit?

It is like a woman whose country was in turmoil who, taking an infant, wished to go to another land. On the way, she encountered a great flood with surging, overflowing waters. Carrying her child, she attempted to cross; as the current rushed swiftly, she did not let go of her child, and both mother and son were drowned.
Yet, because that woman had committed great evils in the past, through the merit of protecting her child, she was reborn in heaven at the end of her life.
Thus it is, son of good family!

Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five deeds of immediate retribution, if they deeply repent and reproach themselves, giving rise to a mind that protects the Dharma, then for the sake of having protected the Dharma, the unwholesome karma they originally committed and the evil results thereof will be transformed; they shall become a field of merit capable of receiving faithful offerings, and the merit of protecting the Dharma shall likewise yield a great fruit.
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If an icchantika should again give rise to faith and repent before the Triple Gem, would one who makes an offering to such a person obtain a great fruit?”
The Buddha told Cunda:

"Do not speak such words. It is like a person who eats an amra fruit and, having taken its seed, crushes it while eating; if one were to take that empty husk and plant it in the ground, even though one were to irrigate it, it would ultimately never sprout."
The icchantika is also like this: it is impossible for one who has destroyed the seeds of goodness to be made to repent and give rise to a wholesome mind; therefore, they are called icchantikas.
Regarding those who obtain great fruits through giving and observing the precepts, these fruits are likewise not the same. Why is this?
The retributive fruits obtained from giving to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all possess distinctions; only by giving to the Tathāgata does one obtain the supreme fruit.
Therefore it is said: "Not all giving yields a great fruit.
Cunda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"For what reason, World-Honored One, did you speak this verse?"
The Buddha told Cunda:
"There was a cause and there was a condition.

At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a faithless upāsaka who served the Nirgranthas; he came to ask me about the meaning of giving, and because I wished to guide him, I spoke these verses."
One should know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means and secret teachings are intended for bodhisattvas; they are not something that everyone is able to fully comprehend.

Therefore, bodhisattvas—heroes among men—should discern the meaning within the Tathāgata’s intentional (sāvaśeṣa) teachings, thereby subduing all those who violate the precepts, just as one removes tares and weeds that harm the good grain.
Furthermore, good son!
As I have said in verse:
"All rivers must be winding; All thickets must consist of trees."
"All women are necessarily deceitful; all who possess great power are necessarily at peace.
At that time, Mañjuśrī rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, paid homage to the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
"Not all rivers are necessarily winding; not all forests are necessarily filled with trees."
"It is not that the minds of all women are deceitful, nor is it that those with great power are entirely at peace.
Thus, World-Honored One, this brief teaching of the Dharma-gate is not a definitive statement."

Why is this so? Within this trichiliocosm, outside of Jambudvīpa, there are other Jambudvīpas where there is a straight river as straight as a cord, extending from the western ocean directly to the eastern ocean, as described in the Vaipulya and Āgama sūtras; this, however, is a statement made by the Tathāgata with intentional ambiguity.
Regarding the statement that "all groves must consist of trees," there is also another explanation. Why is this?
Because there are two kinds of groves.
There are also groves of trees made of gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.
As for the statement that all women are necessarily deceitful and hypocritical, there is another explanation: there are women who maintain pure precepts and whose minds are upright and sincere.

Regarding the statement that "all who possess great power will surely find peace and happiness," there is also another explanation: the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, possesses the supreme great power and is called "peaceful and happy. Although the Wheel-Turning Kings and various celestial deities are also said to possess great power, they do not possess peace and happiness. Therefore, one should know that not all who possess great power are peaceful and happy; only the great power of Nirvāṇa—which is eternally abiding, unchanging, and characterized by the dharma—is truly secure, blissful, and joyful.
For example, it is like a skilled physician who gives clarified butter (sarpis) to a patient to consume; then that patient requests of the physician, saying:
"Please give me another medicine, for I am able to eat it."
The skilled physician replied, "Eat only this much;
once it has been digested, you may eat more. If you were to eat all at once, it might not be digested and could even kill you.
At that time, the skilled physician truly felt compassion for the patient, fearing he would die.
Thus, out of compassion and pity, and wishing to extinguish the arrogance of the queen of King Prasenajit’s minister, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"All rivers must wind and turn; All thickets must have trees;
All women must be deceitful; All who possess great power must find peace."
"You should know that the World-Honored One’s words are free from error; even if this great earth were to be overturned, the Tathāgata’s words would never be in error.
Therefore, whether with remainder or without remainder, all [teachings] are for the sake of the Tathāgata’s gathering in of sentient beings."
The Buddha said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
“Mañjuśrī! Out of compassion for all sentient beings, you have extensively explained the Tathāgata’s having remainder and being without remainder.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again spoke in verse before the Buddha:
“Conform well to others, without observing what they do or do not do;
but observe your own conduct alone, clearly discerning what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
“It is so, Blessed One!”
