The teaching of this True Dharma is likewise not the ultimate teaching. Why is this?
All heterodox outsiders head toward hell (*niraya*), whereas the World-Honored Buddha teaches his disciples to all head toward *nirvāṇa*.
If one is born in the heavens, this is called the discourse of praise and blame; such various [discourses] are not in accordance with the truth.
Why, then, does the World-Honored One say in his verses:
"How does one accord well with others?"
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī:
"There is a cause and there is a condition for why I have spoken of 'skillful compliance.
At that time, after King Ajātaśatru had killed his father, the king, he came to where I was and asked me: "
"How is it, World-Honored One? Are you omniscient or not omniscient?
If you are omniscient, Devadatta harbored malicious intent toward the Tathāgata throughout a hundred thousand lifetimes; why did you permit him to go forth as a monk?"
I then spoke this verse for his sake, in order to accord with him well.

King Ajātaśatru had committed the crime of patricide yet remained unaware of it; the Tathāgata wished to lead him to reflect upon his own transgressions so that his offense might be lightened. Therefore, he said:
"But observe your own conduct; examine closely what is wholesome and what is unwholesome."
"How is it that you now see this as being discordant?

If one maintains the precepts and practices a mind of loving-kindness yet observes the faults of others, this is the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, intended to bring peace and happiness to oneself and all sentient beings. Therefore, one should observe whether others act or do not act, and likewise for oneself; one who constantly practices such observation is my disciple."
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"As I have said in verse:
'All fear death; none do not dread the pain of the staff.'"
"Use yourself as a metaphor: do not kill, and do not inflict punishment.
At that time, Mañjuśrī again spoke a verse before the Buddha:
"It is not that all fear death; it is that all dread the pain of the rod."
Nor do they fully compare themselves with others, yet they exercise forbearance toward those sentient beings.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
This brief teaching of the Dharma-gate is likewise not ultimate."

Why is this so? It is because, just as it is impossible for any gods, humans, or other sentient beings to inflict harm upon an Arhat or the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning Sage King—namely, the queen, the elephant, the horse, and the minister—so too do the brave warrior, the virtuous woman, the wild horse, the king of beasts, and the precept-keeping bhikṣu remain unafraid even when confronted by adversaries. While all fear death and none fail to dread the pain of a staff, this is merely a statement made with remainder.
Furthermore, one should not use oneself as an analogy for others. Why is this?

If an Arhat uses himself as an analogy for others, it constitutes the notion of a life-principle (*jīva-saṃjñā*). One who possesses the notion of a life-principle is not a superior person (*uttama-puruṣa*); to conceive of a life-principle is the false view of a fool that leads toward the gates of the evil destinies.
Furthermore, O Arhat, since both the self and sentient beings are empty and non-existent, who could die and who could kill? For one to give rise to a harmful intention is impossible.
As for that analogy you have cited, does it refer to an existing self as an analogy?
Is it an analogy for non-self?
If it were an analogy for self, it would be inferior; if it were an analogy for non-self, it would mean that the Arhat has no analogy at all.
Yet the Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not teach the Dharma falsely or without cause.

In Rājagṛha, there was a great master hunter who, having slaughtered living beings for an offering, invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, saying, "I pray that you will compassionately accept [this meal].
However, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has never eaten meat; he regards all beings equally, as he does Rāhula.
He immediately became a hunter and spoke this verse:
"One should observe those who live long lives: it is because they do not harm living beings.
All fear death; there is none who does not dread the pain of the staff."
"Use yourself as a metaphor: do not kill, and do not inflict punishment.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
Excellent, Mañjuśrī! You,
a seer among men, comfort all sentient beings and skillfully expound the Tathāgata’s esoteric teachings on expedient means.
At that time, Mañjuśrī spoke again in verse:
"Revering one's parents and increasing their offerings—
Because of such filial conduct, Upon death, one falls into the Avīci Hell."
“World-Honored One!

This verse states that ignorance and craving serve as one’s parents; sentient beings follow along with them, causing them to increase and create various evil karmas, so that upon death they shall fall into the Avīci Hell.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Mañjuśrī:
“As I have stated in verse:
‘All suffering arises from the power of others; all bliss arises from mastery over one’s own power.’”
"All arrogance is violent and harmful; all that is virtuous and good is loved by others.
Mañjuśrī spoke again in verse:
"Not all suffering arises from the power of another, nor is all happiness attained through one's own independent power."
"Not all forms of pride are violent and harmful; not all [who possess pride] are beloved by the wise.
This is the World-Honored One’s brief manifestation of the Dharma-gate, not a definitive teaching."

Why is this so? It is like the child of a commoner who follows a teacher to study; every movement—whether looking up, looking down, advancing, or retreating—is entirely dependent upon the teacher. Once his Way and arts are perfected, he will forever attain peace and happiness.
Just as the son of a king possesses sovereign power through his own strength and does not follow the instructions of others, whereas those who are ignorant and dark remain in constant suffering;
for this reason, the Tathāgata spoke this verse. Those sentient beings who are possessed by Māra and lack such sovereignty—it was for them that the Tathāgata spoke this verse.
Therefore, one should know that suffering does not arise solely from the power of others, nor does happiness arise solely from one's own power.

As for the statement that "all those with the force of pride are violent and harmful," this is also a partial teaching; it is not the case that all pride is entirely violent and harmful. For example, there may be someone who is proud and arrogant toward worldly people, yet has left the household life to study the Path, or who calculates their own merit, maintaining pure precepts. One should know that although such persons possess pride, they do not act with violence or harm.

Regarding those who are loved by all virtuous and good people, there is also another teaching: for instance, within the internal Dharma, if one commits the four grave offenses (*caturmahāpatti*), even if one can exert self-discipline to maintain dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) and cultivate noble conduct, because one has destroyed right action (*samyakkarmānta*), such a person is not loved by others.
"For what reason, World-Honored One, did you speak this verse?
At that time, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī:
"The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, do not falsely preach the Dharma without cause."
At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, there was a maiden named Subhadrā, daughter of Kauṇḍinya. Loathing the mundane world, she came to where the Buddha was with the desire to seek ordination.
According to the nature of women, one cannot attain independence; such matters are governed by men. She thus took refuge in the Triple Gem.
The Buddha, knowing his intention and that this was the opportune time, spoke these verses: "All suffering arises from the power of others.
Excellent! Excellent!"
“Mañjuśrī, the sage among men, is able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the esoteric teachings on skillful means.
Mañjuśrī then spoke in verse:
“All classes of sentient beings Exist in dependence upon food and drink;”
All infants are entirely free from the mind of stinginess.
In all worlds, the consumption of solid food increases one's ailments;
yet those who practice the Dharma dwell together in peace and happiness.
“Is it not the case, World-Honored One, that by now accepting Cunda’s offering of food, you will suffer an increase in affliction?
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke in verse to Mañjuśrī:
“It is not the case that all sentient beings Exist solely by depending on food and drink.”
Not all infants are entirely free from a heart of stinginess;
not all in the world find that physical food increases their illness;
and not all who practice the Dharma attain peace and happiness while dwelling together.
“Mañjuśrī! If you fall ill, I shall also fall ill; for all Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas do not consume solid food—this is the fixed law of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.”
If one were to say that Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas have ever partaken of solid food, it would contradict the meaning of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

Yet, they accept hundreds of thousands of offerings from sentient beings and praise all the merit of giving; desiring to rescue sentient beings and ferry them across the boundless ocean of suffering of the three evil realms, they constantly extol generosity even though they do not partake of solid food.

Desiring to cause sentient beings to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*, he sat upright beneath the tree for six years of ascetic practice; how could it be said that his body became emaciated from not eating?

Do not say that the Tathāgata is of the same category as ordinary beings; the Tathāgata has already crossed over the floods of craving and desire, and his sphere and range of activity do not coincide with those of worldly people. The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable, and it is the same for his śrāvaka disciples.
To speak of "edible food" is a statement made with intentional reservation;
to say that all infants are free from stinginess and attachment is also a statement made with intentional reservation;

furthermore, there are immeasurable beings who have forever abandoned the mind of stinginess and dwell in unshakable bliss, and the claim that all edible food increases one's afflictions is likewise a statement made with intentional reservation.

The external diseases, such as sword wounds, sores, and warts, are immeasurable in number; that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-dharma) abide together in peace and happiness is likewise a statement made by the Tathāgata with intentional meaning (saṃdhāya-vacana).

The methods therein are manifold; there are those who cultivate mundane wholesome dharmas, various purifying practices of body, speech, and mind, and various forms of faith, yet they dwell together without being in accord with one another.

Therefore, you should know that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not speak in contradiction to the truth without cause or condition; rather, for the sake of transformation, they teach the Dharma through skillful means.

At that time, there was a half-headed brahmin who, together with his fellow residents, was practicing the ritual of fasting for the heavenly deities. He came to where the Buddha was, and in order to subdue him and cause him to abandon his heterodox views, [the Buddha] spoke this verse.
At that time, Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it, World-Honored One, that all other sūtras are merely the Tathāgata’s teachings of incomplete meaning?"
The Buddha said:
"No, son of good family!"

If there are sentient beings who have accomplished merit and are well-versed in the profound Dharma, the Tathāgata preaches for them the Dharma of eternal abiding, peace, and bliss without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
For other sentient beings who delight in hearing the Dharma, the Tathāgata preaches for them either with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) or without remainder.
Bodhisattva Kāśyapa was immediately filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How marvelous!
World-Honored One!"
“Regard all sentient beings as equal, just like an only son.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
“Excellent!”
“Good son! You should thus correctly understand this profound Dharma.
Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We only pray that the Tathāgata will explain the merit obtained from this *Vaipulya Parinirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Regarding this *Mahāyāna-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the merit obtained by those who hear its name cannot be fully described even by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
"The merit produced by this *Mahāyāna Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* is inconceivable; it is the domain of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas alone.
At that time, the devas, humans, and asuras, before the Buddha, with single-mindedness and in unison, spoke in verse:
"The Tathāgata, God among Gods, Is profoundly deep and inconceivable."
The Vaipulya Nirvāṇa Sūtra spoken by the Tathāgata,
which gives birth to all merits, is likewise inconceivable.
The True Dharma is difficult to conceive, and the Jewel of the Saṅgha is likewise so.
I only pray that the God among Gods, out of compassion, will remain for a short while.
The Venerable Elder Kāśyapa and his retinue are approaching;
so too is the Venerable Ānanda, the great sage of vast learning.
As well as the King of Magadha, King Ajātaśatru—
these are the most intimate disciples of the Tathāgata.
Those noble beings will surely harbor thoughts of doubt.
The Tathāgata will enter nirvāṇa, or shall he remain forever in the world?
Such doubts have arisen in our minds; where can we find certainty?
We pray that out of compassion you will stay for a moment, so that we may wait until our doubts are resolved.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the great assembly:
“O you who harbor doubts and suspicions, do not be anxious or worried.
The eldest son born from my Dharma is the Elder Mahākāśyapa.”
Ānanda, the man of great learning—such as these will arrive in an instant;
I must first let them see me before I enter parinirvāṇa.
Such a man of wisdom as this beholds the Tathāgata’s two feet.
"He himself knows that my body is truly both eternal and impermanent.

At that time, the entire assembly of followers made offerings to the Tathāgata with celestial silk canopies and flowers, burning various famous incenses and performing celestial music, in numbers so immeasurable they could not be compared.

Having made offerings to the Buddha, beings as numerous as the sands of ten thousand Ganges Rivers resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and dwelt in the first stage of the bodhisattva path.
The elder Cunda was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, as the nectar of Bodhi was poured upon his crown.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Kāśyapa, and the Bodhisattva Cunda:
"O sons of good family!..."
Cultivate your own mind and be careful not to be negligent. I now suffer from back pain and my entire body aches; I wish to lie down in rest. You, Mañjuśrī!

You should preach the Dharma for the sake of the fourfold assembly. I now entrust the True Dharma of the Tathāgata to you; until the arrival of the Elder Mahākāśyapa and Ānanda, you should expound it extensively.
Thereupon, for the sake of transforming sentient beings, the World-Honored One manifested that he was ill; he lay on his right side upon the ground, fixing his mindfulness on the perception of light.
*The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, Fascicle Six.
